pages.description: Status: implemented in the relay Worker (2026-07). Desktop/host wiring for release + merge announcements is a follow-up (the relay endpoint is live).
pages.markdown:
# ActivityPub federation (fediverse interop)

Status: implemented in the relay Worker (2026-07). Desktop/host wiring for
release + merge announcements is a follow-up (the relay endpoint is live).

## What federates

ForkMesh joins the ActivityPub network (Mastodon-compatible) with two kinds of
followable actors on the relay's domain:

| Actor | Handle | Actor URL | Type |
|---|---|---|---|
| User profile | `@alice@forkmesh.com` | `/ap/users/alice` | `Person` |
| Repository | `@owner.repo@forkmesh.com` | `/ap/repos/owner/repo` | `Group` |
| Service actor | `@forkmesh.com@forkmesh.com` | `/ap/actor` | `Application` |

User names can never contain a dot, so `owner.repo` splits unambiguously on
the first dot (repo names may themselves contain dots). Handles and actor ids
are lowercase-normalized. Only active, public user accounts and published,
non-private repos federate; the visibility checks mirror the public-profile
and catalog rules.

Outbound: verified signed-inbox submissions federate as `Create(Note)` —
issue opens/comments, PR opens/comments/reviews, discussion opens/comments.
The repo actor posts to its followers; when the event's
author maps to a local account, the user actor posts to theirs as well.
Releases and merges never pass through the relay inboxes (they are canonical
on the owner's node), so the owner-signed `POST
/api/repo/{owner}/{repo}/ap-publish` endpoint lets the desktop push those
announcements; until the desktop adopts it they simply don't federate.

Images attached to an issue/comment travel as inline `![name](data:...)`
markdown in the body (there is no separate upload channel). Since remote
servers can't fetch a `data:` URL, `ap.extract_body_images` pulls up to 4 of
them out of the body before it becomes note text, and each is re-served at
`/ap/o/{uuid}/media/{n}` (from the same encrypted `ap_objects` row) so it can
be listed as a proper `Image` `attachment` on the Note.

Inbound: `Follow` (auto-accepted), `Undo(Follow)`, `Create(Note)` replies to
our objects, `Create(Note)` posts that Mention a repo actor, `Delete`. Remote
replies become **federated comments** — stored in `ap_comments`, surfaced via
`GET /api/repo/{owner}/{repo}/fedi-comments?kind=issue&number=N`, and shown
as clearly-marked fediverse comments. They are deliberately kept OUTSIDE the
Ed25519-signed event log: a remote reply can never carry a forkmesh author
signature, so it must never enter the signed spine that nodes replicate.

**Repo mentions → manual issue review.** A post whose Mention tag points at a
repo actor ("@owner.repo@forkmesh.com the save button crashes") never creates
an issue automatically. After ActivityPub HTTP-signature verification and the
public-repository/federation gates, the Create or embedded Note must explicitly
address the ActivityStreams Public collection before a sanitized projection
enters the World's verified-public-feedback feed. A valid signature alone
does not publish a direct/private Note. Remote content, repository routing,
consent, and failure detail remain in an encrypted review record; its
blind-indexed remote-note id deduplicates redelivery.

An authenticated repository owner can open a preview, edit the proposed title
and body, and explicitly authorize a pending issue-inbox submission. Follow-up
consent is a separate, default-off checkbox. The feed says `pending` while the
encrypted inbox row waits for the owner node. The Qt node reports the real
issue number in its signed acknowledgement only after `IssueStore` has
materialized and committed the open event; only then does the feed say
`created`. If separately authorized, the repo actor queues one deduplicated
public reply with the confirmed issue backlink. Failures keep a generalized
retry/delayed status and never turn a proposal or proposed number into a
creation claim.

Legacy `ap_mentions` rows are still honored as dedupe tombstones, so a note
auto-processed by an older deployment cannot reappear as a new review item.
New notes use `world_fediverse_mentions`; no AI classification or attachment
fetch occurs during inbox handling.

## Wire protocol

Follows Mastodon/Wildebeest practice:

* RSA-2048 keypair per actor, public key published as `publicKeyPem`
  (`<actor>#main-key`), private key stored AES-GCM-encrypted under `DATA_KEY`
  (the standard `encrypt_row` pattern) in `ap_actors`.
* draft-cavage HTTP signatures. Outbound signs
  `(request-target) host date digest content-type` (GETs:
  `(request-target) host date accept`), `algorithm="rsa-sha256"`. Inbound
  verifies whatever header list the peer signed but REQUIRES
  `(request-target)` and `digest`, checks `Digest: SHA-256=<b64>`
  byte-for-byte, enforces a ±12 h date window, and requires the `keyId` host
  to match the activity actor's host. Key fetches are signed with the
  service actor (secure-mode servers answer) and cached in
  `ap_remote_actors` for 24 h with one forced refresh on verify failure
  (key rotation).
* Discovery: `/.well-known/webfinger`, `/.well-known/nodeinfo` →
  `/nodeinfo/2.1`, and content negotiation on `/@name` (users) and
  `/@owner.repo` (repos): an ActivityPub `Accept` header gets the actor
  document, a browser gets the HTML profile page.

The pure protocol spine (documents, signing strings, digest, sanitization)
lives in `app/src/activitypub.py` — stdlib-only, imported
directly by `tests/test_activitypub.py`. WebCrypto RSA glue, D1 state and
handlers live in `entry.py` (section "ActivityPub federation").

## Delivery without Queues (free plan)

There is no Cloudflare Queues binding. A publish writes one `ap_outbox` row
per unique destination inbox (sharedInbox preferred), best-effort drains 5
inline, and the per-minute cron's `minute % 5 == 0` slot drains 20 more with
exponential backoff (5 m → 24 h cap, 8 attempts, 404/410 drop immediately).
Cost while unused is near zero: actor rows are minted lazily on the first
WebFinger lookup, so an unfollowed repo's publish path is two indexed
SELECT misses.

## Branding

Every actor ships an avatar (`icon`) and profile header (`image`):

* Defaults: the brand images at `/assets/fediverse-avatar.png` (400×400) and
  `/assets/fediverse-banner.png` (1500×500 — Mastodon's exact header size).
  These are the **instance's own** identity, so only the instance actor and
  user actors fall back to them. A repo actor never does: a ForkMesh-branded
  header on somebody else's project reads as the project being ours.
* Per-repo overrides: the repo owner uploads `logoPng` / `bannerPng` (base64
  PNG, ≤256 KB / ≤1 MB) through the existing About endpoint
  (`POST /api/repo/{o}/{r}/about`, session-auth, `""` clears). They are stored
  encrypted in `repo_media` (one row per image so a banner never nears D1's
  2 MB value cap) and served at `/api/repo/{o}/{r}/media/{logo|banner}.png`
  with a `?v=<updated_at>` cache-buster in the actor document. The About
  `description` doubles as the repo actor's fediverse bio, and a user actor's
  bio comes from their profile `profile_bio`.
* Committed repo artwork (`_committed_repository_banner_url`): with no
  uploaded banner, a repo actor's `image` is the project's own
  **`.forkmesh/banner.png`**, served immutably as
  `/api/repo/{o}/{r}/raw?path=.forkmesh%2Fbanner.png&ref=<commit>` — the
  pinned commit is the cache-buster, so pushing new artwork refreshes it.
  Catalog metadata only lists top-level names, so the URL is a *candidate*:
  it is skipped outright when the repo has no `.forkmesh` directory, and a
  404 from the mirror means "no banner" (the actor then ships no `image` at
  all, and the About card / fediverse profile page drop the header strip
  rather than substitute brand artwork). The avatar keeps its own
  precedence — uploaded, then committed root `logo.png`, then approved
  artwork, then the brand default.
* Profile metadata (verified links): every actor ships `attachment`
  PropertyValue rows — the canonical page (`Repository` for repo actors,
  `Profile` for users) and the `Relay` it lives on (origin-derived, so
  self-hosted relays advertise their own domain). The row is
  Mastodon-verifiable: the served page carries a reciprocal `<link rel="me">`
  pointing back at the actor's `url` (injected per-page at serve time by
  `_serve_repo_page` / `_serve_repo_profile_page`, and baked into
  `_public_profile_html`), which is what turns the row green.
* Actor `url` (click-through target): Mastodon sends anyone who clicks a
  handle — a mention in a post, or the profile's external-link — to the
  actor's `url`. For **users** that is the `/@name` profile page. For **repos**
  it is the `/@owner.repo` **fediverse profile page** (`_serve_repo_profile_page`:
  banner, avatar, bio, follower/post counts and a feed of the repo's federated
  posts), *not* the raw git page — landing a social-timeline visitor on a code
  forge was jarring (adhoc #50). The git page stays the verified `Repository`
  row and is linked prominently on the profile; because the `Repository` row
  now differs from `url`, the git page's `rel="me"` points at `/@owner.repo`.
* Change propagation: saving the repo About (or a user profile) broadcasts an
  `Update(actor)` activity to all existing followers, so remote servers
  refetch the avatar/header/bio immediately instead of waiting out their
  actor-cache TTL.
* Web surface: `GET /api/repo/{o}/{r}/about` (public) returns the description,
  logo/banner URLs and `{handle, followers}` for the repo actor. The dashboard
  repo page uses it for the social badge header above About and the Watch
  button, whose count IS the fediverse follower count (the button opens a
  follow-from-Mastodon card with the copyable handle). The gear editor
  uploads/removes the logo and banner and edits the description; the page's
  displayed About text prefers the repo's committed `.forkmesh/info.json`
  (about + website), matching the desktop app. `bannerUrl` may be empty and
  has no default, so the card probes the image and drops the header strip
  (releasing the logo's overlap offset) when the repo has no banner of its
  own — it never substitutes brand artwork. The About rail also carries an
  owner-only **Fediverse posts** dropdown (issue #426): `POST /api/repo/{o}/{r}
  /ap-posts` (session/owner-key authed, `action: list|delete`) lists the repo
  actor's federated posts and deletes one. A delete drops the local `ap_objects`
  row (the `/ap/o/{uuid}` Note starts 404ing and it leaves the profile feed) and
  queues a `Delete(Tombstone)` to every follower inbox through `ap_outbox`, so
  the post disappears from Mastodon timelines too. The `actor_bi` filter keeps
  one owner's token from reaching another actor's objects.

## Configuration

Operator config is admin-managed (signed admin API, same gate as the relay
allowlist — the caller signs with their node key and must carry `is_admin`):

* `GET /api/accounts/admin-ap?node=&ts=&sig=` — signature over
  `forkmesh-admin-ap-v1\n<node>\n<ts>`. Returns `{enabled, blockedDomains,
  stats}` (actors, followers, remote actors, objects, comments, queued
  deliveries).
* `POST /api/accounts/admin-ap-update` — body `{node, ts, sig, action,
  domain?}`, signature over
  `forkmesh-admin-ap-update-v1\n<node>\n<action>\n<domain>\n<ts>`. Actions:
  `enable` / `disable` (global switch — while disabled every AP endpoint 404s,
  publish hooks no-op and the cron drain pauses) and `block` / `unblock`
  (defederation — blocking a domain rejects its inbound activities, refuses
  actor fetches, and purges its followers, cached actors and queued
  deliveries, subdomains included).

Settings live in `ap_settings` / `ap_blocked_domains` with a 60 s per-isolate
cache. Deployment-level config stays in wrangler vars: `PUBLIC_BASE_URL`
(actor-id origin for self-hosted relays; defaults to the request host).

The Solana payout relay mesh is a separate system; its canonical routes moved
to `/api/relay-mesh/*` with `/api/federation/*` kept as a served legacy alias
(federated relays also retry the legacy path against older main relays), so
the two federations no longer share a name.

## Known limitations / follow-ups

* Desktop node should call `ap-publish` on release publish + PR merge, and
  render federated comments in issue/PR/discussion views (API is live).
* Local users cannot yet follow remote fediverse accounts (no outbound
  Follow); Like/Announce/Update inbound are acknowledged and dropped.
* Followers collections expose `totalItems` only (no paging) — Mastodon is
  fine with this.
* Object content is public by design (public repos only), stored encrypted
  at rest like everything else.

pages.title: Conflict-safe signed collaboration objects
pages.description: Status: normative protocol version 1, part of the ForkMesh protocol suite. Suite version: 1.0.0-rc.1. The machine-readable envelope schema is collaboration-event-v1.schema.json.…
pages.markdown:
# Conflict-safe signed collaboration objects

Status: normative protocol version 1, part of the
[ForkMesh protocol suite](../protocol/README.md). Suite version: `1.0.0-rc.1`. The machine-readable envelope schema is
[`collaboration-event-v1.schema.json`](../../public/docs/protocol/collaboration-event-v1.schema.json).
The dependency-free reference fold is `app/src/collaboration.py`; the independent
WebCrypto fold is `app/public/collaboration.js`.

## Invariants

ForkMesh collaboration state is a deterministic projection of an immutable set
of signed events. A relay, mirror, or database may transport and index those
events, but is never authoritative for their meaning. Given the same policy and
event set, implementations MUST produce the same state when events are
permuted, duplicated, delayed, or replayed.

Implementations MUST retain each canonical raw envelope. Materialized fields,
search indexes, counts, and notification views are disposable caches. Invalid
input is retained only in a bounded quarantine/audit channel and MUST NOT enter
the state fold.

## Repository, object, and event identity

A repository identity is:

```text
urn:forkmesh:repository:sha256:<sha256(
  "forkmesh-repository-identity-v1\n" || verified repository root
)>
```

The verified root is deployment-specific (for example a signed repository
manifest), but aliases and mutable URLs are not identities.

Every object's first event carries a random 16-byte `objectKey`, base64url
without padding. The object ID is:

```text
urn:forkmesh:collaboration:<family>:sha256:<sha256(
  "forkmesh-collaboration-object-v1\n" || canonical-json({
    repository, family, creator, objectKey, references
  })
)>
```

This binds the repository, family, creator, and immutable references before an
event is signed. For reactions, clients SHOULD derive `objectKey` from subject,
author, and normalized emoji to make one logical reaction idempotent. For
notifications, clients SHOULD derive it from recipient and causing event.

The event ID binds both the signed meaning and its deterministic Ed25519
signature:

```text
signingBytes = utf8("forkmesh-collaboration-event-v1\n") ||
               canonical-json(unsigned envelope)
eventId = "sha256:" || hex(sha256(signingBytes || 0x00 || rawSignature))
```

Ed25519 public keys are raw 32-byte keys and signatures are raw 64-byte values,
both base64url without padding. Schema/domain prefixes are frozen; changed
meaning requires a new version.

## Canonical encoding

The wire envelope is canonical JSON encoded as UTF-8 with no BOM or trailing
newline. Object keys are ASCII, sorted lexicographically; there is no
insignificant whitespace. Strings are NFC-normalized and lone surrogates are
forbidden. Values are objects, arrays, strings, booleans, null, or integers whose
magnitude is at most 2^53-1 (envelope counters are additionally
non-negative); floating point and duplicate object keys are forbidden. Arrays
whose semantics are sets (`parents`, `references`, observed IDs, and set
values) are sorted and duplicate-free. An envelope is at most 1 MiB and JSON
nesting is at most 32 levels, so malformed input cannot force unbounded parser
or canonicalizer work.

A receiver MUST parse with duplicate-key detection, reproduce the exact
canonical bytes, recompute `eventId`, and verify Ed25519 before considering
causality or authorization. Noncanonical encodings fail closed even if they
would parse to the same JSON value.

## Causality and replay defense

`parents` names the events observed when an author made an event. The Lamport
`clock` is zero without parents and otherwise exactly one plus the greatest
parent clock. `issuedAt` is display/audit time only and never decides a winner.

Each signing key allocates a repository-wide monotonically increasing
`sequence`. Gaps and concurrent slots from different keys are valid. Two
different events signed by one key in the same sequence slot are equivocation:
both are excluded and surfaced in audit telemetry. A sequence lower than or
equal to a same-author ancestor is a rollback and is rejected.

Missing-parent events remain pending, with their raw bytes retained. A child of
a rejected event is rejected; it cannot bypass validation by arriving first.
Duplicate event IDs are one logical event and only increment the replay metric.
Repository, object, policy, and schema binding prevents a valid signature from
being replayed into another context.

## References and policy

References are sorted `{relation, family, object}` triples. A comment has one
issue/PR/comment subject; a reaction has one issue/PR/comment/review subject; a
review has one PR subject; a moderation object has one non-notification,
non-moderation subject. References on every event for one object must exactly
match its first event, preventing later retargeting.

Every event binds the SHA-256 ID of a canonical repository policy document:

```json
{
  "schema": "forkmesh-collaboration-policy-v1",
  "repository": "urn:forkmesh:repository:sha256:…",
  "maintainers": ["<Ed25519 key>"],
  "moderators": ["<Ed25519 key>"],
  "notifiers": ["<Ed25519 key>"]
}
```

The repository trust root pins this document. Version 1 deliberately treats a
policy change as a new collaboration epoch; clients must retain the old epoch
and policy to verify history rather than re-authorizing old events under a new
role list.

| Family | Create | Later mutation / tombstone |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Issue, pull request | Any signed identity | Creator or maintainer |
| Comment, reaction | Any signed identity | Creator; moderation is a separate decision |
| Review | Any signed identity | Creator; maintainer may dismiss via tombstone |
| Label, milestone, board | Maintainer | Maintainer |
| Notification | Recipient or policy notifier | Recipient |
| Moderation decision/resolution | Moderator | Moderator; subject creator may appeal |

Unauthorized events remain auditable but never influence state. Renderers MUST
NOT infer moderator power from an author name, server origin, arrival channel,
or possession of a database row.

Authority comes only from the policy document's keys. Implementations MUST NOT
infer any role from asset ownership or transaction history, and MUST NOT
require a wallet, token, blockchain account, payment, reward, tip, or bounty to
create, fold, authorize, moderate, or govern a collaboration object. Incentive
adapters may read folded state, but folded state never reads them; see
[incentive independence](../incentive-independence.md). Changing this rule is a
breaking protocol change.

## Fold and conflict rules

All families use the same primitives, with family-specific fields and role
rules:

| Family | Scalar registers | Observed-remove sets | Required reference |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Issue | title, body, status, priority, dueAt | labels, assignees | — |
| Pull request | title, body, status, base, head, mergeCommit | labels, reviewers | — |
| Comment | body | — | subject |
| Label | name, color, description | subjects | — |
| Reaction | emoji (immutable) | — | subject |
| Review | state, body, revision (immutable) | — | pull request |
| Milestone | title, description, status, dueAt | subjects | — |
| Board | name, description, status | items | — |
| Notification | kind/recipient (immutable), status, message | — | optional subject |
| Moderation | decision, reasonCode, note | — | subject |

For a scalar field, discard a candidate only when another write causally
descends it. One remaining value is current. Concurrent candidates with equal
values coalesce; concurrent differing values produce an explicit `conflicts`
entry and no current value. A resolving event names every conflicting head as a
parent and therefore causally dominates them. Timestamp, lexical author order,
or arrival order never silently resolves ambiguity.

`add` gives each set value an `(eventId, value)` tag. `remove` names the exact
ancestor add events it observed. A concurrent add survives. Tombstones use the
same rule: `restore` removes only the ancestor tombstone IDs it names, so an
unobserved concurrent tombstone continues to hide the object. History is never
erased.

## Moderation lineage

The first `decide` event is moderator-signed and binds its subject. An `appeal`
must be signed by the subject creator, name an ancestor `decide`/`resolve` as
`predecessor`, and descend from it. A moderator `resolve` names both that
predecessor and appeal as ancestors. Skipped, cross-object, or forged lineage is
rejected.

Concurrent differing active decisions never pick a quiet winner: the subject
is visibly `quarantined` with `moderationConflict`. Equal decisions coalesce.
Resolved `hide`, `quarantine`, and `allow` project to hidden, quarantined, and
visible respectively; the signed decision and appeal history remains readable
to authorized audit tools.

## Storage, migration, and recovery

The portable log format is one canonical envelope per NDJSON line with LF
record separators. Export sorts unique raw records by their raw SHA-256 digest.
Import verifies every line and recomputes state; it does not trust an exported
snapshot or silently normalize CRLF records.

Legacy `forkmesh-issue-v1`, `forkmesh-pull-v1`, comment, label, reaction,
review, milestone, project/board, notification, and moderation records migrate
through an importer-signed `create`/`decide` event. That event binds the exact
legacy record digest and records `valid`, `invalid`, or `unavailable` legacy
signature status. It never claims the legacy author made a new signature. The
original bytes stay beside the new log until retention policy permits archival.

Roll back readers before writers: stop emitting v1, keep accepting and
preserving raw envelopes, and project the prior snapshot format read-only. Do
not down-convert or delete v1 events because that loses causality. Recovery is
to restore policy plus NDJSON, run the independent verifier, and compare the
state digest. Corrupt lines remain quarantined while valid independent objects
continue folding.

Use the verifier locally:

```bash
python3 tools/verify_collaboration.py \
  --policy repository-collaboration-policy.json \
  --require-complete collaboration.ndjson
```

`tools/export_collaboration_log.py export --repository IDENTITY --signing-key
SEED` performs this import for a checkout's `forkmesh-issue-v1` records. It
writes `.forkmesh/collaboration/policy.json` and `issues.ndjson`, which can be
committed so a visitor verifies them from a plain clone. The digest binds the
exact record file bytes, and each record's legacy status is `valid` only when
every legacy event signature in it verifies.

The exporter carries its own copy of `issue_event_content` from
`app/src/events.py`, because that module needs the Worker's js bridge and a
stdlib tool cannot import it; `app/tests/test_export_collaboration_log.py` pins
the two byte-for-byte. A legacy `open` event is signed before the issue has a
number, so its signature may bind either 0 or the assigned number; every other
event binds the number. Signing uses `cryptography` when installed and falls
back to pure-Python RFC 8032. A record that v1 cannot represent, such as a
title over the 512-byte limit, is skipped and named in the export summary
rather than truncated, so the log never misstates an issue.

## Threat, abuse, privacy, and telemetry

The main threats are forged authorship, replay across repositories, malicious
clock/timestamp choice, key equivocation, reference retargeting, unauthorized
moderation, deletion races, and a relay omitting events. Signatures and domain
binding address forgery/replay; DAG validation and explicit conflicts address
ordering; role policy and lineage address moderation; observed tombstones
address deletion races. Omission requires peer exchange/availability receipts
and cannot be solved by a fold over an incomplete set.

Raw events can contain private issue text, notification recipients, moderation
notes, and relationship metadata. Private logs stay inside the repository's
authorization/encryption boundary. Telemetry exports counts only:
`received`, `uniqueRaw`, `signatureValid`, `accepted`, `pending`, `rejected`,
`duplicateDeliveries`, `equivocations`, `conflicts`, rejection reason, and
accepted family. It MUST NOT export bodies, object IDs, public keys, refs, or
raw signatures.

## Automated evidence and supported runtimes

`app/tests/test_collaboration_protocol.py` supplies the signed convergence
corpus, randomized permutations/replays, byte mutation fuzzing, adversarial
authorization/signature/sequence cases, all-family legacy migration,
rollback/recovery, telemetry, and Python↔WebCrypto parity. The dedicated
`collaboration-conformance.yml` workflow runs it with Python 3.12 and Node 24 on
Linux, macOS, and Windows and retains JUnit evidence. The same focused suite is
part of the core quality gate.

No network service, wall clock, or database is required. This is intentional:
an implementation passes only by deriving state from retained signed bytes.

pages.description: Status: shipped (desktop, web, mobile signing, Worker, SSH gateway, Go mirror) · Issue: #483 (closure gate "review conversations remain attached to the right lines or expose an…
pages.markdown:
# Pull request review threads across patchsets

Status: shipped (desktop, web, mobile signing, Worker, SSH gateway, Go mirror)
· Issue: #483 (closure gate "review conversations remain attached to the right
lines or expose an explicit outdated state across patchsets")

## Problem

A review thread is pinned to `path`, `side` (`old`/`new`) and a line range of
the diff the reviewer was looking at. When the author pushes again, the diff
is re-cut: lines shift, the commented code may move or disappear. Before this
change a thread was either painted on whatever line now had its number, or
dropped from the diff view entirely when that number no longer existed. The
conversation itself survived in the ledger, but the reviewer's claim ("this
code, at this revision") was neither recorded nor verifiable.

## The anchor

Every line-anchored review event (`line-comment`, `thread-comment`) may carry
two more fields:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `patchset` | The head commit the reviewer's diff was cut against. The desktop uses the head it derived the patch from (falling back to the pull's signed `creationHeadOid`); the web uses `creationHeadOid`, because it renders the signed creation diff. Empty when no client can name one (a portable patch-backed pull). |
| `anchorLines` | The exact text of the commented lines on that side, diff prefix stripped, newline-joined, capped at 12 lines. Empty when the range is not in the diff. |

Both are **signed**. When either is present, the event's signed content
appends `NUL patchset NUL anchorLines` to the existing per-type content
(`forkmesh-pull-comment-v1` is unchanged as the canonical label). An event
without an anchor signs exactly the bytes it signed before, so every existing
signature stays valid and every pre-anchor verifier keeps accepting
pre-anchor events. Verifiers that predate this change reject *anchored*
events with `bad_signature`; the relay, the SSH gateway, the Go mirror
intake, the desktop and the mobile client all carry the rule.

On disk (`.forkmesh/pulls/<n>/NNNN-<type>.md`) the fields are front-matter
keys `patchset: <oid>` and `anchorLinesB64: <base64url>`, the latter using
the same blob encoding as `suggestionPatchB64`. The Go mirror's intake and
the desktop's inbox drain both write them.

Cross-language vectors for the anchored content live in
`desktop/tests/test_crypto.cpp` and `app/tests/test_crypto.py` (same hashes
in both).

## Placement

When a client shows a pull's diff it places every thread against that diff.
The rule is the same on the desktop (`PullReviewModel.cpp`) and the web
(`06-repo-content.js`):

1. **Own patchset.** `patchset` equals the patchset on screen: the thread is
   *current* at the lines it names. No text search is needed.
2. **Text search.** Otherwise, if `anchorLines` is present, look for that
   exact run of consecutive lines on the thread's side of the file, nearest
   to the original line. Found at the same line: *current*. Found elsewhere:
   *moved* to the new line range. Not found: *outdated*.
3. **Patchset only.** A different patchset with no anchored text is
   *outdated*: nothing proves the line still holds the same code. If the diff
   on screen has no named patchset at all (an immutable patch-backed pull) and
   the line exists, the thread is *current*.
4. **Legacy.** A thread with no anchor is painted where it says while that
   line exists and is *outdated* once it does not.

What each state looks like:

- **Current** — the thread sits on its line, as before.
- **Moved** — the thread sits on the line its text now occupies, with a
  `Moved` badge and "Written on new lines 10–12 of revision `abc1234…`; the
  same code now sits here."
- **Outdated** — the thread is never painted on a line. On the desktop it is
  shown at the top of its file's diff table (it cannot fold away, since there
  is no gutter marker to reopen it from); on the web it appears in an
  "outdated review threads" block at the top of the file. Both carry an
  `Outdated` badge and say which revision and lines it was written on. The
  conversation timeline marks the opening event "(outdated)" or "(moved from
  line N)". Per-file counts in the desktop file list include outdated
  threads.

Applying a suggested change uses the thread's *current* line, and refuses
when the thread is outdated ("the lines it changes are no longer in the
diff").

## Branch review threads (desktop and phones)

A branch with no pull request can be reviewed the same way. In the desktop's
branch compare view, click a line number to comment on that line, or press
on one and drag down the gutter or the code to select a range. The inline
composer opens under the selection. The file header's comment pill starts
a thread about the whole file. Replies, Resolve and Reopen work the same as
on a pull request. Without this, the only way to leave feedback on an agent's
branch was to open a pull request first.

Branch threads use the same event shapes as pull threads (`thread-comment`,
`thread-reply`, `thread-state`, with the same anchor fields). They are stored
in the `forkmesh/pulls` ledger branch at
`.forkmesh/branch-reviews/<first 24 hex of sha256(branch)>/`, next to a
`branch.md` that names the branch. That ledger is pushed with every other
head, so anyone viewing the branch from a mirror sees the threads. Keeping
them out of `.forkmesh/pulls/` means pull loaders, catalog counts and the
strict mirror reader (which rejects any non-numeric directory there) never
treat them as pull requests.

Signatures use the `branch-comment` prefix, with the branch name in place of
the pull number:
`forkmesh-branch-comment-v2\n<owner/name>\n<type>\n<branch>\n<author>\n<ts>\n<sha256 hex of contentForSigning>`.
Rendering a branch diff only reads these threads from a ledger checkout that
already exists. It never creates the `forkmesh/pulls` branch or its
checkout: that is a write, and it ran git (which pumps the event loop) in
the middle of a render. Only posting a comment creates the ledger. Because
every plain branch diff now carries the per-line comment links that PR
diffs already had, a small diff's HTML is larger and can stream in over
more than one page.

Placement uses the anchor text only (the current patchset is left empty),
because a branch view can include uncommitted work-tree changes that no
commit names.

File-level threads (line 0), on a branch or on a pull request, are shown at
the top of their file in the diff, in the same place as outdated threads.

### From a phone or any node that cannot write the ledger

The iOS and Android apps offer the same thing in their branch diff screen:
tap a line to select it, tap a second line on the same side to extend the
range, then comment. They read threads with the ordinary repository reads
(`tree` and `blob` on `ref=forkmesh/pulls`, path
`.forkmesh/branch-reviews/<key>`), the same way they read pull threads.

A phone cannot write git, so it sends the signed event through the pull
inbox:
`POST /api/repo/<owner>/<name>/pulls` with `{"branch": "<name>", "event": {...}}`
and no `number`. The app server checks the branch name and verifies the
`branch-comment` signature against this repository. Only the v2 form is
accepted, because the kind is new and has no legacy signatures. The server
then queues the event in `pull_inbox` with `number: 0` and the branch, and
rings the host and mirror doorbells. Whichever node drains the inbox stores
it in `.forkmesh/branch-reviews/<key>/`, creating `branch.md` the first
time. That is either the owner's desktop (`PullStore::applyRemoteBranchEvent`)
or a Go mirror (`writeBranchReviewItem` in `server/intake.go`). Both skip an
event id that is already stored, so a replayed inbox row is harmless. Until
it lands, the phone shows its own comment as pending, the same as a pull
comment.

Shared test vectors (the event `thread-comment-ios-1` on `src/app.txt`,
lines 3–5, branch `feature/review`, repository `alice/demo`) are pinned in
`app/tests/test_branch_review_intake.py`, `server/intake_test.go`, the iOS
`BranchReviewTests` and the Android `ReviewToolsTest`.

## What is not covered

- The web compare page does not show or take branch review threads yet.

- Threads on the web are placed against the signed creation diff. A pull
  updated on the desktop (re-push, apply-fix, agent edit) therefore shows its
  desktop-written threads as *moved* or *outdated* on the web until the web
  renders the current head; the anchor makes that explicit rather than wrong.
- Whitespace-only or renamed-file changes are treated like any other edit to
  the anchored text: the thread becomes outdated rather than following a
  fuzzy match. Exact matching is deliberate; a thread should never be shown
  on code it did not talk about.
- Comparing two patchsets side by side is a separate epic item (#483, "compare
  between patchsets") and is not part of this change.

## Verification

- Desktop: `forkmesh-tests` — anchored canonical vectors, front-matter
  round-trip of a multi-line anchor, and placement across a re-cut diff
  (current / moved / outdated / legacy, block moves, per-file counts,
  same-patchset shortcut, patchset-only rules).
- Worker: `app/tests/test_crypto.py` (vectors), `test_pull_review_frontend.py`
  (web placement and authoring contract), `test_ssh_independent_writes.py`,
  `test_pull_submission_inbox.py`, `test_org_pull_inbox_auth.py`.
- Mirror: `server/intake_test.go` — anchored keys persist, unanchored files
  are byte-identical to before.

pages.title: Release binary publishing
pages.description: Issue #304. Release binaries are never committed to git. A release is two things kept apart on purpose
pages.markdown:
# Release binary publishing

Issue #304. Release binaries are never committed to git. A release is two
things kept apart on purpose:

- **Metadata**: small, signed text committed to the repository and synced
  across the mesh like issues and pull requests.
- **Payloads**: the binary bytes, kept in a content-addressed store (CAS) on
  the node that serves the repository, and fetched by their SHA-256.

A mirror can carry the bytes, but it cannot change them without breaking the
signed hash, and git history never grows by the size of a build.

## Two kinds of release

**Repository releases.** Any repository can publish releases from the web or
the desktop. The manifest's canonical body is built by
`release_manifest_content` in `app/src/releases.py`: repository, tag, the
commit the tag pointed to (`tag_commit`), the commit embedded in the artifact
(`build_commit`, when present), and one line per asset (name, blob SHA-256,
size, content type, OS, architecture, label), sorted. The creator signs
`release_signing_message`:

```text
forkmesh-release-v1\n<repo>\n<tag>\n<author>\n<ts>\n<sha256 of the content>
```

with their Ed25519 identity; `verify_release_manifest` in `app/src/events.py`
checks it. Release name, notes and the prerelease flag are not signed, so they
can be edited without invalidating the release. Download counts are not
signed either.

**ForkMesh's own desktop releases.** Channels under
`.forkmesh/releases/<channel>/` (`latest`, `candidate-<version>`) hold
`SHASUMS256.txt`, `release.json` and `release.json.sig`: a raw 64-byte Ed25519
signature over the exact `release.json` bytes, made with the release publisher
key (not a user identity). `tools/forkmesh-release-publish.sh` writes them;
`www/public/install.sh` and the desktop updater verify them. Operating
instructions are in
[`.forkmesh/releases/README.md`](../../../.forkmesh/releases/README.md) and the
developer overview in [`docs/release/README.md`](../../../docs/release/README.md).

## The content-addressed store

Blob path, relative to the store root (`cas_blob_relpath` in
`app/src/releases.py`):

```text
sha256/<first two hex digits>/<full sha256>/data
```

The served store is `<bare repository>/forkmesh-releases/` on each mirror
(`server/bootstrap.go`, `server/gateway.go`). A local publish without
`--cas-dir` writes to `.forkmesh/release-blobs/`, which `.gitignore` excludes.

## Download

```text
GET /api/repo/<owner>/<repo>/releases/blob/sha256/<sha256>?filename=<asset name>
```

The route is matched in `app/src/urls.py`. The response is immutable and can
be cached forever at the edge; the App forwards it to a node holding the blob.
`filename` only sets the download name and never changes which bytes are
returned. Installers ask the repository recorded in the manifest (`repo`),
because only that node is guaranteed to hold the blob.

## Verification order

1. Authenticate the metadata: the release signature against a trust anchor
   (the publisher key built into `install.sh`, a local PEM, or a digest from
   an authenticated controller).
2. Check that the manifest binds `SHASUMS256.txt` (`checksums_sha256`).
3. Download the blob by hash and check its SHA-256 before installing or
   running it.

Nothing downloaded is executed to decide whether it is trustworthy.

## Related

- `app/src/releases.py`: tag and asset-name validation, CAS layout, canonical
  manifest, `SHASUMS256.txt` generation, semver ordering for `latest`, and the
  re-upload decision for an asset name.
- `app/tests/test_releases.py`

pages.markdown:
# Scoped community trust lists

Status: protocol version 1, candidate. The dependency-free reference resolver
is `app/src/trust_lists.py`. The vectors in
`conformance/trust-lists/v1/vectors.json` bind four independent resolvers to
it byte for byte: the web client (`app/public/trust-lists.js`), the iOS client
(`native/ios/ForkMeshCore/Sources/FMAccount/TrustLists.swift`, tested by
`native/ios/ForkMeshCore/Tests/FMAccountTests/ConformanceTests.swift`), the
Android client
(`native/android/core/src/main/kotlin/com/forkmesh/nativeapp/security/TrustLists.kt`,
tested by
`native/android/core/src/test/kotlin/com/forkmesh/nativeapp/security/TrustListsCryptoTest.kt`),
and the desktop client (`desktop/src/TrustLists.cpp`). The user guide is
[Trust lists](../trust-lists.md).

## Goals and non-goals

A trust list is a signed statement that says, for example, "in the `forkmesh`
organization, these keys are security researchers whose advisories I stand
behind". People follow the lists they find useful. ForkMesh does not run a
global list, and no list is followed by default.

- **Reputation is scoped.** Every entry names one role and one repository,
  organization, or community. There is no wildcard or global scope. A follow,
  an include, or a delegation can only narrow scope, never widen it.
- **Nothing essential depends on a list.** Cloning, reading, identity,
  sign-in, pushing, and opening issues or pull requests never consult trust
  lists. A client with no follows behaves exactly as it does today. Lists
  inform ranking, review routing, badges, and moderation queues.
- **Disagreement stays visible.** When followed lists disagree, the result is
  `conflict`. Only the user's local override picks a side.
- **Compromise is recoverable locally.** Equivocation, a forked history, or
  a revocation cuts a list back to its last good version. The client shows
  the list as `recovered` instead of silently following the newest document.

## Documents

Documents are canonical JSON. Every string is printable ASCII other than `"`
and `\`. Object keys are sorted by code point, there is no whitespace, and
integers are at most 2^53−1 in magnitude, with no fractions, exponents, or
`-0`. A receiver accepts a document only when re-encoding its parse
reproduces the received bytes exactly. The restricted alphabet lets every
language write this encoding with a plain sorted-key writer. A raw document
is at most 262,144 UTF-8 bytes.

A document's identifier is `sha256:<hex SHA-256 of the raw bytes>`. Because
the raw bytes include the signature, two documents with the same meaning but
different signatures have different identifiers.

The signed message is the document's `schema` value, a newline, and the
canonical JSON of the document without its `signature` key. Signatures are
Ed25519 over those bytes. The rules of FM-SIG-001 in the
[protocol suite](../protocol/signatures-and-authentication.md#ed25519) apply.
Every resolver also rejects a scalar `S ≥ L` explicitly before calling a
platform verifier. It also rejects non-canonical key encodings (including
x = 0 with the sign bit set), the identity, and small-order and mixed-order
keys. Platform verifiers such as WebCrypto and OpenSSL do not, so the iOS and
Android resolvers use their own strict verifier (`Ed25519.verifyStrict`).
The `forged-weak-keys` vector carries signatures that pass lax verification
for each of those keys. Keys are 43-character and signatures 86-character
unpadded base64url, and both must round-trip.

A list is identified by issuer key and name, not by any single version:

```text
listId = "urn:forkmesh:trust-list:sha256:" ||
         hex(sha256("forkmesh-trust-list-id-v1\n" || issuer || "\n" || name))
```

### List version (`forkmesh-trust-list-v1`)

| Field | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `issuer` | Signing key of the list owner |
| `name` | Slug `[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{0,63}` |
| `version` | Integer ≥ 1 |
| `previous` | `null` for version 1; otherwise the document identifier of version − 1 |
| `issuedAt`, `expiresAt` | Milliseconds; `expiresAt > issuedAt`; lifetime at most 400 days |
| `roles` | Sorted, non-empty set of `maintainer`, `moderator`, `mirror-operator`, `organization`, `reviewer`, `security-researcher` |
| `communities` | Sorted, non-empty set of at most 64 scopes, none covered by another |
| `revocationKeys` | Sorted set of at most 4 keys, not including `issuer`, that may revoke later versions |
| `entries` | At most 2,000 `{subject, role, scope, stance, note}` entries, strictly sorted by subject, role, scope |
| `edges` | At most 16 `{kind, issuer, name, roles, communities, expiresAt}` edges, strictly sorted by issuer, name |
| `signature` | By `issuer` |

An entry's `stance` is `trust` or `distrust`. Its `note` is at most 280
characters. Its subject is never the issuer. An entry's role must be one of
the list's roles, and its scope must be covered by the list's communities.

An edge whose `kind` is `include` composes another list and has
`expiresAt: null`. An edge whose `kind` is `delegate` grants another key
authority to publish entries for this list and carries an integer
`expiresAt`. Either way, the edge's roles must be a subset of the list's
roles, its communities must be covered by the list's communities, and it
cannot name its own list.

### Scopes

| Scope | Covers |
| --- | --- |
| `repo:<owner>/<repository>` | That repository |
| `org:<owner>` | Itself and every `repo:<owner>/…` |
| `community:<slug>` | Itself |

Owners match `[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{0,38}`. Repositories match
`[A-Za-z0-9._-]{1,100}` other than `.` and `..`. The intersection of two
scope sets keeps each member of one set that the other set covers. It then
removes duplicates and any member covered by another member.

### Revocation (`forkmesh-trust-list-revocation-v1`)

`{list, issuer, name, fromVersion, revokedBy, revokedAt, reason, successor}`,
signed by `revokedBy`. `list` must equal the listId of `issuer` and `name`.
`reason` is `compromised`, `malicious`, `retired`, or `superseded`.
`successor` is `null` or `{issuer, name}` of a different list.

A revocation is authorized when `revokedBy` is the issuer, or when a verified
version of the list with `version < fromVersion` names `revokedBy` in
`revocationKeys`. A recovery key committed before a compromise can therefore
revoke everything the attacker publishes. An attacker who adds keys in a
malicious version cannot use them to revoke the versions before it.
Revocations have no expiry. Revocation is monotonic, so no document can undo
one.

### Appeal (`forkmesh-trust-list-appeal-v1`)

`{subject, list, version, role, scope, statement, issuedAt}`, signed by the
`subject` it concerns, with a statement of 1–1,000 characters. Nobody can
appeal on someone else's behalf.

## Verification order

A resolver rejects a document at the first failing step and records
`{documentId, code}`:

1. `too_large`; bracket nesting deeper than 8 outside strings, found by a
   scan before any parser runs, or unparseable JSON: `invalid_json`;
   `noncanonical`; a top level that is not an object, or a `schema` that is
   not a known string: `unsupported_schema`; wrong key set: `invalid_keys`.
2. List version: `invalid_issuer`, `invalid_name`, `invalid_version`,
   `invalid_previous`, `invalid_time`, `invalid_scope` (roles, then
   communities), `invalid_revocation_keys`. Then, entry by entry,
   `invalid_entry`, `entry_outside_scope`, `unsorted_entries`. Then, edge by
   edge, `invalid_edge`, `edge_outside_scope`, `unsorted_edges`. Last,
   `invalid_signature_encoding` and `invalid_signature`.
3. Revocation: `invalid_issuer`, `invalid_name`, `list_mismatch`,
   `invalid_version`, `invalid_revoker`, `invalid_time`, `invalid_reason`,
   `invalid_successor`, then the signature.
4. Appeal: `invalid_subject`, `invalid_list`, `invalid_version`,
   `invalid_scope`, `invalid_statement`, `invalid_time`, then the signature.
5. In context: a list version or appeal whose `issuedAt` is more than
   300,000 ms after the resolver's clock is rejected as `issued_in_future`,
   and an unauthorized revocation as `unauthorized_revoker`.

Duplicate raw documents are counted once.

## Version history

For each list, a resolver considers every verified version it holds:

- two different documents with the same `version` are an **equivocation** at
  that version;
- a document whose `previous` does not equal the identifier of the single
  held document for `version − 1` is a **history fork** at that version;
- an authorized revocation cuts at its `fromVersion`.

The cutoff is the lowest of these versions. The head is the highest held
version below the cutoff that has exactly one document. The list state is:

| State | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `active` | A head exists, it has not expired, and nothing was cut |
| `recovered` | A head exists below a cutoff; `cutoffReasons` says why |
| `expired` | The head's `expiresAt` has passed; older versions are never revived |
| `revoked` | An authorized revocation left no usable version |
| `conflicted` | Equivocation or a fork left no usable version |
| `missing` | The list is followed or referenced, but no verified version is held |

Only `active` and `recovered` lists contribute entries and edges. A
revocation's `successor` is shown to the user and never followed
automatically. A compromised issuer key might have been used to revoke too,
so the user decides.

## Composition and merge

Local inputs are **follows**, `{issuer, name, roles, communities}` where a
`null` narrowing means the list's own scope, and **overrides**,
`{subject, role, scope, stance}` where the stance is `trust`, `distrust`, or
`ignore`. Neither is published or signed. They stay on the device. The client
that stores them validates them before resolving: keys and names use the
document field rules, and each override tuple appears at most once.
Resolvers do not re-validate local input.

1. Each follow starts a walk at its list, scoped to the intersection of the
   list's roles and communities with the follow's narrowing.
2. A walk admits each head entry whose role is in the walk's roles and whose
   scope is covered by the walk's communities.
3. A walk follows each edge. An expired delegation is skipped and counted.
   An edge back to a list already on the path is skipped as a cycle. An edge
   from a path that already holds 4 lists is skipped as depth-limited.
   Otherwise the child walk's scope is the intersection of the current scope,
   the edge's scope, and the child's own scope. The walk stops if that scope
   is empty.
4. Each `(subject, role, scope)` tuple collects at most one source per list,
   the one reached by the shortest path, with ties broken by the
   newline-joined path. Its `stance` is the shared stance of its sources,
   `conflict` when they differ, or `none` when only an override names it.
   `effective` is the override when present, otherwise the stance.
5. A verified appeal attaches to the tuple's assertion when one of that
   assertion's sources is the appealed list. The appeal is `resolved` when the
   list's head is newer than the appealed version and no longer distrusts the
   tuple, and `open` otherwise. Appeals that match no assertion are counted as
   unattached.

The resolution is canonical JSON with `lists` sorted by `listId`,
`assertions` by subject, role, and scope, `sources` by `listId`, `appeals` by
identifier, `rejected` by identifier and code, and `conflicts` by their
canonical JSON. `conflicts` holds `stance` conflicts, noting whether an
override resolved them, plus `equivocation` and `history_fork` records. The
result does not depend on the order of documents, follows, or overrides.

## Telemetry

`telemetry` contains only counts, never keys, list names, or follows:
documents, duplicates, rejections by code, revocations, lists by state,
followed and reachable lists, assertions, stance conflicts, overrides, appeals
by status, expired delegations, and cycle and depth-limited edges. These are
the issue's primary measures (active lists, cross-client verification,
overrides, appeals). A client that reports them upstream reports this object
unchanged, or a subset of it.

## Privacy

Follows and overrides never leave the device and never appear in telemetry.
Fetching lists one at a time by `listId` from a relay tells that relay which
lists interest you. Clients SHOULD fetch the whole public bundle, or fetch
through a mirror they operate. Entries name keys, not account names, so a list
cannot change its meaning when an account is renamed.

## Threats

| Threat | Mitigation |
| --- | --- |
| Stolen issuer key publishes a malicious version | Recovery key revokes `fromVersion`; followers fall back to the last good version as `recovered` |
| Issuer shows different versions to different followers | Equivocation cuts below the disputed version once both copies meet |
| Rewritten history | `previous` digest chain; a fork cuts the list |
| A list claims global authority | No global scope; entries and edges must stay inside the list's own scope |
| Delegate or included list overreaches | Scope intersection at every hop; delegations expire |
| Attacker revokes with a key added in a malicious version | Only keys named in a version *before* `fromVersion` may revoke |
| Stolen issuer key revokes the whole list | Accepted as a denial of service; the owner publishes a successor under a new key and followers choose to follow it |
| Signature malleability and canonicalization tricks | Byte-exact canonical re-encoding, strict base64url, and explicit `S < L` |
| Resource exhaustion | Size, entry, edge, community, and path-depth limits |
| Silent winner between lists | `conflict` until the user overrides |
| Forged appeals | Appeals must be signed by their subject |

## Rollout and rollback

Version 1 is additive: no existing route, table, or authorization decision
reads it. Rolling back means removing the resolvers. No stored state migrates,
because follows and overrides are local and documents are immutable. Any
change to meaning requires a new schema string. Changing the vectors requires
regenerating them with `generate_vectors.py` and passing all four resolvers.

Not yet implemented: publishing and fetching lists over relays and mirrors,
authoring and signing UI in the clients, follow and override settings UI,
and upstream reporting of telemetry.

pages.markdown:
# Daily interface validation

The daily interface has one shared contract for the responsive web surface and
the web content embedded by desktop and mobile shells. Numeric limits live in
[`daily-interface-budgets.json`](daily-interface-budgets.json); changes that
make a limit weaker use the same expiring waiver process as other quality
budgets.

## Automated evidence

`npm run test:daily-interface` exercises the checked-in production dashboard in
Chromium at desktop and mobile viewports. It blocks CI when startup, repository
browse, in-memory search, diff construction, navigation handoff, or perceived
feedback exceed their limits. The journey also verifies:

- keyboard entry through Control/Command+K, roving command selection, Escape,
  focus restoration, repository-card activation, and skip navigation;
- semantic dialog, combobox, listbox, status, main, and navigation landmarks;
- visible focus, light/dark contrast, 200% zoom reflow, 44 CSS-pixel coarse
  pointer targets, and global reduced-motion behavior;
- readable unified diffs with non-color line signs, labelled line-comment
  controls, virtualized large-file layout, and announced copy feedback;
- empty, API-error, offline/retry, and recovery paths without losing the page;
- page-local performance events that carry only operation, duration, budget,
  source class (`local` or `remote`), and pass/fail. They contain no account,
  repository, route, search query, or content and are not persisted.

Run it locally after installing the pinned browser dependencies:

```bash
cd app/browser_tests
npm ci
npx playwright install --with-deps --only-shell chromium
npm run test:daily-interface
```

CI retains the Playwright report for 30 days even on failure. The static
`app/tests/test_daily_interface_contract.py` suite keeps the runtime constants,
workflow, documentation, and central quality-gate registry in sync.

## Representative-user release gate

Automation is necessary but does not substitute for representative users. Each
public-alpha candidate must link a dated, consented study report covering at
least two keyboard-only participants, two screen-reader participants, two
touch/mobile participants, and two pointer users. A participant may belong to
more than one cohort, but results stay disaggregated by access need.

Use a fresh supported build and a seeded repository. Do not collect repository
contents, assistive-technology speech logs, IP addresses, or participant
identity in telemetry. Record only consented aggregate duration, completion,
error count, and a 1–5 satisfaction score.

| Task | Target time | Maximum user errors | Required completion |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Browse to and open a file | 45 seconds | 1 | 90% |
| Copy a clone command | 45 seconds | 1 | 90% |
| Find and open an issue | 60 seconds | 1 | 90% |
| Review a diff and submit feedback | 120 seconds | 2 | 85% |
| Inspect mirrors and recover from offline | 90 seconds | 2 | 85% |

A release owner links the test run, cohort summary, supported platform matrix,
rollback/recovery drill, current user documentation, and privacy-reviewed
telemetry snapshot from the release checklist. Missing or placeholder evidence
means the adoption gate remains open.

## Rollback and recovery

The command palette and local measurement trail are additive and keep no server
state. Rollback is the previous static dashboard asset set. If catalog loading
fails, the page remains operable, exposes a semantic status, and offers an
explicit retry that bypasses cached data. Copy failures preserve selectable
commands and announce the manual fallback. Theme selection and cached catalog
data remain local and can be cleared by the existing sign-out/browser-state
cleanup path.

pages.markdown:
# ForkMesh feature definition of done

A feature is complete only when its implementation and the evidence below are
reviewable together. This applies to application code, infrastructure, protocol
changes, and visible World behavior.

## Required evidence

1. **Threat review.** Identify trust boundaries, sensitive inputs, authority
   changes, failure behavior, and likely attacker goals. State why the feature
   fails closed where authorization, identity, custody, or repository privacy is
   uncertain.
2. **Abuse and privacy review.** Record the data collected, its visibility,
   retention and deletion behavior, consent controls, moderation/appeal path,
   and abuse cases. Raw IP addresses, wallet secrets, private repository
   existence, and private agent data must not become public observability data.
3. **Benchmark and budget evidence.** Run the applicable performance budget or
   provide a reproducible measurement. A feature with no relevant hot path may
   say so, but must explain why.
4. **Regression-test evidence.** Add tests for the success path, denied path,
   malformed input, and material privacy or authorization boundary. Record the
   exact commands and results.
5. **Operational evidence.** Document deployment, configuration, rollback,
   monitoring, recovery, and any external operation that was intentionally not
   performed.

The pull-request template exposes these five sections. CI rejects a pull request
when a section is missing or contains only the template placeholder.

## Running the gates

From the repository root:

```bash
python3 tools/quality_gate.py validate
python3 tools/quality_gate.py run --profile core
python3 tools/quality_gate.py run --profile release
```

The `core` profile is the fast local and CI gate. The `release` profile also
runs the real-browser World suite and therefore requires its pinned Playwright
dependencies and Chromium installation. Native Qt, iOS and Android suites remain
required when their toolchains are available; the completion report must name
any unavailable toolchain rather than silently treating it as passed.

For a desktop change, also build the `forkmesh` app target
(`./desktop/run.sh` or `cmake --build desktop/build --target forkmesh`). The
desktop workflow (`.forkmesh/desktop-ci.yml`) builds only the critical test
targets; `forkmesh-window-tests` among them compiles the `MainWindow*.cpp`
units, but no CI job compiles `desktop/src/main.cpp` or links the app. See [docs/desktop/build-and-test.md](../../../docs/desktop/build-and-test.md).

CI runs the core profile on pushes, pull requests, a weekly schedule, and manual
dispatch. The separate World browser workflow runs the browser portion on every
push and pull request, including the blocking responsive daily-interface timing
and accessibility journey documented in
[`daily-interface-validation.md`](daily-interface-validation.md).

## Changing a budget

Improving a maximum needs no exception. Removing a budget or raising a maximum
is a weakening and must be explicit:

1. Add a JSON record under `www/docs/engineering/quality-gate-waivers/` using the
   budget ID as the file name.
2. Include every field listed in `quality-gates.json`, a concrete risk review,
   a UTC expiry date, and the approving reviewer identity.
3. Pass the base commit to
   `python3 tools/quality_gate.py compare --base-ref <sha>`.
4. Replace the waiver with a restored or tighter budget before it expires.

The comparison command rejects silent removals or increases. Waivers are an
auditable temporary exception, not a way to make a failing test green.

pages.markdown:
# Network-log badge audit — which categories still earn their slot

> Snapshot of 2026-08-06. File references below are to the code as it was
> then and some have moved since (`RepoHost.cpp` no longer exists; helper
> bodies left `MainWindowInternal.h` for `MainWindowInternal1-4.cpp`). Today the
> classifier is `kNetworkLogRules` / `networkLogStyleFor()` in
> `desktop/src/MainWindowSettings.cpp`, the single sink is
> `MainWindow::logSystem()` in the same file, and the live log is
> `~/projects/forkmesh/data/network_log.txt` in the default layout. See
> [docs/desktop/diagnostics.md](../../../docs/desktop/diagnostics.md).

Audit of the 30 log categories in the desktop client's Log view: the coloured
badge on every entry, the quick-filter chip row, and the icon legend in the
footer/header strip. The question asked was "which of these do we no longer
use?"

Three lists have to agree for a category to work, and they do — no category is
missing from one of them:

| List | Where |
| --- | --- |
| classification rules (substring → badge) | `desktop/src/MainWindowSettings.cpp` (`kNetworkLogRules`) |
| quick-filter chip order | `desktop/src/MainWindowSettings.cpp` (`order[]` at the time of the audit; no longer present under that name) |
| legend icons + accents | `desktop/src/MainWindowInternal.h` (`categories()`) |

Every log line reaches the classifier through one sink, `MainWindow::logSystem()`
(`MainWindowSettings.cpp`), so "is this category still produced?" is
answerable by looking at what feeds that function.

## Method

Two independent passes, because either one alone is misleading:

1. **Static** — extract the message text of all 690 distinct string-literal log
   messages passed to `logSystem()` / `flashMessage()` across `desktop/src`,
   and run each through a faithful re-implementation of `networkLogStyleFor()`
   (stall check → error precedence → `[body: …]` stripping → first-matching
   rule). This answers "could this badge ever be produced?"
2. **Empirical** — classify every line of a real retained log,
   `~/.local/share/ForkMesh/ForkMesh/network_log.txt`: 27,165 entries spanning
   2026-08-05 22:52 → 2026-08-06 12:45 on the deploy box. This answers "does
   this badge actually appear?"

The empirical window is only ~14 hours of one mostly-headless machine, so a zero
there is weak evidence on its own. The static pass is what settles whether code
still emits a category at all.

## Verdict

### 1. `HOST` is dead — no producer anywhere in the tree

The rule is `{"host: ", "#76e3ea", "HOST"}`. It was added in `1f0a992a3` to
catch `RepoHost`'s own log lines, which at that commit were:

```
RepoHost.cpp:547   emit log("Host: connection to relay went stale for …")
RepoHost.cpp:700   emit log("Host: serving " + m_owner + "/" + m_name + " live to the web.")
RepoHost.cpp:972   QStringLiteral("Host: served %1 for %2/%3.")
```

`RepoHost` and its desktop server/publisher pipeline have since been deleted.
The managed Go service owns serving, catalog publication, and native
collaboration intake. No string reaching `logSystem()` in the entire
codebase contains `"host: "`, and the badge scored 0 across 27,165 real
entries.

`HOST` now costs a permanently-dark legend cell and a chip that can never
appear. It is also the 30th category, which is exactly what fills the legend's
`10 × 3` compact grid (`kCompactColumns`/`kCompactRows`,
`MainWindowInternal.h:7698`) — dropping it leaves a hole to lay out, so removal
should adjust that grid rather than just delete the row.

Note that "hosting" *events* are not gone, only this badge: host-online /
host-offline lines exist, they just don't use a `Host: ` prefix, so they land in
other categories.

### 2. Two `BOUNTY` rules are redundant — they can never change a badge

| Rule | Status |
| --- | --- |
| `{"escrow", …, "BOUNTY"}` (index 11) | never wins |
| `{"funded", …, "BOUNTY"}` (index 13) | never wins |

Every message containing `escrow` or `funded` also contains an earlier needle:

- `"Bounty escrow for issue #%1 ready to fund …"` → `bounty` (index 10) wins
- `"Bounty for %1 funded and split to the author + treasury …"` → `bounty` wins
- `"Reward escrow for pull #%1 ready to fund …"` → `pull #` (index 8) wins → `PULL`
- `"Pull #%1 merged, but no inbuilt bounty wallet is funded yet …"` → `pull #` wins → `PULL`

Both scored 0 hits statically and 0 hits over the real log. They are harmless,
but they are dead weight in a list whose ordering is already load-bearing.

### 3. `FORK` is 31% of the log and almost none of it means "a fork happened"

This is the biggest problem the audit turned up, and it is a *misclassification*
problem, not a dead-category one.

- `FORK` badged 8,424 of 27,165 entries (31.0%).
- In **8,422 of those 8,424**, the substring `fork` appears *only* inside the
  word `forkmesh` — a URL host, an account name, or the `forkmesh/forkmesh`
  repo name. Two entries were about an actual fork.

Because `{"fork", …, "FORK"}` sits at index 26, it pre-empts all eleven rules
below it — `PROMPT`, `ISSUE`, `ADMIN`, `IDENTITY`, `CRYPTO`, `PEER`, `NETWORK`,
`STATUS`, `NODE`, `CLIP`, `SAVE` — for any message that so much as mentions
ForkMesh. The rule already carries a comment acknowledging it is a catch-all
that other rules must be hoisted above; in practice nearly every line qualifies.

The measurable damage:

- **`NODE` is effectively unreachable.** Its needles `connected` and `peer`
  scored **0** wins in 27,165 entries; `node` won 9 times, and the samples are
  incidental build-output text (`sh-control-tests.dir/src/ControlNode.cpp.o`),
  not node events. 7,288 entries did contain `connected` / `peer` / `node` —
  5,644 went to `FORK`, the rest to `ERROR`/`STATUS`/`ACCOUNT`/`NETWORK`/`MIRROR`.
- **`ISSUE` never won.** 70 entries contained `issue`; all 70 went elsewhere
  (`BGTASK` 45, `ERROR` 17, `FORK` 4, `GIT` 3, `MERGE` 1).

A narrower needle (`fork` as a whole word, or `forked`/`forking`/`fork location`)
would let the eleven shadowed rules fire and would stop a third of the log
reading as a fork.

### 4. `ADMIN` never wins in practice, for a different reason

177 entries contained `admin`; **155** were `GET …/api/accounts/admin-pending`
polls that match `account` (index 16) first, and 20 more were errors. `ADMIN`
has four live producers (`MainWindowSetup.cpp:2088`, `:2352`,
`MainWindowChat.cpp:15148`, `MainWindowMessages.cpp:601`) — the badge works, it
is just drowned by an endpoint name.

### 5. Live but simply not exercised in this window

Every one of these has a confirmed producer feeding `logSystem()`; each scored 0
in the 14-hour deploy-box log only because that box did no such work. **Not**
candidates for removal:

| Badge | Producer |
| --- | --- |
| `PEER` | `MainWindowMessages.cpp:841` — `"Node connected: %1 is online"` |
| `FORKED` | `MainWindowRepoDetail.cpp:1205` — `"Forked into %1/%2."` |
| `PULL` | 33 producers, e.g. `MainWindowBranches.cpp:5266` `"Opened pull #%1 …"` |
| `BOUNTY` | `MainWindowPulls.cpp:7242`, `:7457`, `:7461` |
| `WALLET` | `MainWindowChat.cpp:22341`, `MainWindowSettings.cpp:3332`, + validation paths |
| `CLIP` | 10 producers, e.g. `MainWindowActions.cpp:4762` `"Copied %1 to clipboard."` |
| `ISSUE` | 13 producers (see §3 for why it still loses) |

The log contains no `Issue #`, `Copied`, `Forked into` or `Node connected` line
at all, which is consistent: this machine self-merges agent branches rather than
opening pull requests, and has no interactive clipboard use.

## Observed distribution (27,165 entries)

| Badge | Count | Share |
| --- | --- | --- |
| BGTASK | 9,285 | 34.2% |
| FORK | 8,424 | 31.0% |
| ACCOUNT | 3,161 | 11.6% |
| ERROR | 2,039 | 7.5% |
| INFO | 1,033 | 3.8% |
| PUBLISH | 739 | 2.7% |
| MIRROR | 716 | 2.6% |
| STATUS | 624 | 2.3% |
| GIT | 540 | 2.0% |
| ACTIONS | 309 | 1.1% |
| SYNC | 83 | 0.3% |
| STALL | 52 | 0.2% |
| PIN | 46 | 0.2% |
| NETWORK | 38 | 0.1% |
| SAVE | 24 | 0.1% |
| MERGE | 15 | 0.1% |
| SESSION | 11 | <0.1% |
| PROMPT | 11 | <0.1% |
| NODE | 9 | <0.1% |
| CRYPTO | 3 | <0.1% |
| IDENTITY | 3 | <0.1% |
| PEER, FORKED, HOST, PULL, ISSUE, BOUNTY, WALLET, ADMIN, CLIP | 0 | — |

Two-thirds of the log is `BGTASK` + `FORK`, and `FORK` is noise. `ACCOUNT`'s
11.6% is likewise almost entirely `/api/accounts/*` polling.

## Recommended follow-ups

Nothing here is applied — this is the audit only.

1. Remove the `HOST` rule, its `order[]` entry and its legend row, and re-lay
   the legend's compact grid for 29 categories.
2. Delete the redundant `escrow` and `funded` rules.
3. Narrow the `fork` needle so it stops matching `forkmesh`. This is the change
   that recovers `NODE`, `ISSUE` and nine other categories.
4. Consider whether `ADMIN` should be checked above `account`, so
   admin-ownership lines aren't lost to the polling endpoint's name.

## Note for a future audit: the stored line gained a tail

Since adhoc #1587 every entry ends with the file and line that logged it —
`2026-08-06 12:45:01  Mirror sync finished  [desktop/src/MainWindowRepos.cpp:812]`
— in `network_log.txt` as well as on screen. Anything re-implementing
`networkLogStyleFor()` over a captured log must strip that tail first
(`forkmesh::logMessageBody()`, `desktop/src/LogSource.h`): the path is not
part of what the caller wrote, and a line logged from `MainWindowIssues.cpp`
would otherwise badge as `ISSUE`. The app itself strips it in
`MainWindow::logBadgeFor()` / `logAccentFor()` and never appends it to the text
handed to the classifier.

# Quality-gate waivers

This directory contains temporary, reviewed exceptions for a removed or
weakened performance budget. A waiver file is named `<budget-id>.json`; it must
contain every field required by `../quality-gates.json`, use an ISO-8601 UTC
expiry time, and explain the measured risk.

Do not add a waiver for a tighter budget.

pages.description: ForkMesh chat always has an outer AES-256-GCM room cipher. Its passphrase is normally derived from the controller deployment's DATA_KEY, so it protects the wire and retained…
pages.markdown:
# Chat encryption and public integrations

ForkMesh chat always has an outer AES-256-GCM room cipher. Its passphrase is
normally derived from the controller deployment's `DATA_KEY`, so it protects
the wire and retained storage from third parties but not from the controller
operator.

The application layer applies one of two explicit policies:

| Conversation | Content policy | Controller integrations |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Public `#` channel | Controller-readable room encryption | ForkBot and public-channel webhooks; MCP for `mainnode/forkmesh #general` |
| Private channel or direct message | Automatic device-to-device encryption inside the room cipher | Unavailable |

Browser channels use their stored `visibility` field. Public World `#general`
is public by definition. Desktop and mobile `#` channels are public unless the
desktop channel is marked private; direct messages are protected. Authenticated
dashboard spaces are protected.

Changing a channel to Public is an intentional disclosure decision for new
messages. It does not decrypt already retained private history. Changing it to
Private rotates the room key and revokes its incoming webhooks.

## Why public channels are controller-readable

ForkBot, MCP, and incoming webhooks run on or through the controller. They
cannot read or create a recipient-sealed message without a participant device's
private key. Public channels therefore stop at the authenticated room cipher so
those integrations can read and post there.

This is not end-to-end encryption from the controller operator. The UI labels
these conversations **Public** and explains that they are controller-readable.
MCP is deliberately narrower than the general channel system: its chat tools
accept only public `mainnode/forkmesh #general`.

During migration, a public channel can contain older recipient-sealed frames
and newer controller-readable frames. Participant clients try to open both;
MCP skips old sealed frames and returns the public history it can read.

## Protected conversation device identities

There is no phrase or setup step. On first use, each installation creates an
X25519 private key:

- the browser keeps it in same-origin local storage;
- desktop keeps it in local application settings; and
- mobile keeps it in the platform secure store.

The private key never appears in a request or frame. Clients exchange this
public announcement through the ordinary room cipher:

```json
{ "type": "e2ee-key", "v": 2, "kid": "…", "pub": "…" }
```

`pub` is the raw 32-byte X25519 public key in unpadded base64url. `kid` is the
first 16 characters of `base64url(SHA-256(pub))`. Clients retain at most one
announcement per room per day so an offline device can be discovered. Live
announcements are sent on connection and answered when a new device is learned.
Learned keys are scoped locally to both controller and room.

The controller can read these public announcements. They are not content keys
and do not enable passive decryption.

## Protected message envelope

For every protected application frame, the sender:

1. generates a fresh random 32-byte content key;
2. encrypts the complete JSON frame with AES-256-GCM;
3. derives an X25519 shared secret with each known room device;
4. runs that secret through HKDF-SHA256 to obtain a pairwise wrapping key; and
5. wraps the content key for every recipient, including the sender's device.

The inner frame is:

```json
{
  "type": "sealed",
  "v": 2,
  "kid": "sender key id",
  "pub": "sender X25519 public key",
  "nonce": "…",
  "tag": "…",
  "body": "…",
  "keys": [
    { "kid": "recipient key id", "nonce": "…", "tag": "…", "key": "…" }
  ]
}
```

That frame is then encrypted by the room cipher. The durable flag stays on the
outer envelope, so retention and replay work without exposing the protected
message's type, sender, or content.

### Exact derivation

For sender key id `S`, recipient key id `R`, room `ROOM`, and content nonce
`N`:

| Value | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Shared secret | `X25519(senderPrivate, recipientPublic)` |
| HKDF salt | `SHA-256("ForkMesh chat e2ee salt:" + ROOM)` |
| HKDF info | `"forkmesh-chat-e2ee-kek-v2\n" + ROOM + "\n" + S + "\n" + R` |
| Wrapping key | HKDF-SHA256, 32 bytes |
| Content AAD | `"forkmesh-chat-e2ee-content-v2\n" + ROOM + "\n" + S` |
| Wrap AAD | `"forkmesh-chat-e2ee-wrap-v2\n" + ROOM + "\n" + S + "\n" + R + "\n" + base64url(N)` |

The AAD prevents a controller from moving a frame to another room, relabelling
its sender or recipient, or moving a wrapped key to another message without
failing authentication. A protected conversation refuses an application frame
that is not a valid v2 recipient envelope. Recipient lists are capped at 64
device keys, favoring the most recently announcing devices.

## User-visible behavior

The web and desktop access badges are informational:

- **Public** means the controller can read and author messages for integrations.
- **End-to-end** means device-to-device encryption is automatic and the
  controller's room key cannot read or inject the protected content.

A new installation can open protected messages sent after other participants
learn its public key. It cannot retroactively decrypt retained messages whose
content keys were never wrapped for it. Clients report that condition instead
of silently presenting an empty conversation.

## Security boundary and limits

For private channels and DMs, the protocol removes the controller's `DATA_KEY`
as a passive message-decryption key. An operator inspecting the relay database,
WebSocket traffic, or retained envelopes sees only recipient ciphertext.

Automatic public-key discovery is not authenticated membership. A controller
that actively injects a new public key can make future senders treat that key
as another device. Preventing that requires an independently authenticated
participant directory or human verification, neither of which exists uniformly
across browser, desktop, and mobile. An operator serving modified JavaScript can
also read a browser client's local data and plaintext.

Other limits:

- public channels are intentionally readable and writable by the controller;
- timing, sizes, connection metadata, public device keys, and durable flags
  remain visible even for protected conversations;
- this is not a double ratchet and provides no post-compromise security;
- compromise of one device exposes content keys wrapped for that device;
- losing a device private key loses history addressed only to it; and
- the controller can drop, delay, replay, or withhold frames and key
  announcements, causing denial of service.

## Implementations and contracts

| Piece | File |
| --- | --- |
| Browser primitives and identity store | `app/public/chat-seal.js` |
| Browser policy, send, receive, and discovery | `app/public/chat-room-transport.js` |
| Web surfaces | `app/public/chat.js`, `app/public/dashboard-chat.js` |
| Desktop primitives and transport | `desktop/src/RoomSeal.{h,cpp}`, `ServerNode.cpp` |
| iOS primitives and transport | `native/ios/ForkMeshCore/Sources/FMCrypto/RoomSeal.swift`, `native/ios/ForkMeshCore/Sources/FMChat/Relay/RelayService.swift` |
| Android primitives and transport | `native/android/core/src/main/kotlin/com/forkmesh/nativeapp/crypto/RoomSeal.kt`, `native/android/core/src/main/kotlin/com/forkmesh/nativeapp/chat/RelayRoom.kt` |
| MCP public-channel bridge | `tools/forkmesh_mcp_server.py` |
| Cross-client contracts | `app/tests/test_chat_room_seal_frontend.py`, `desktop/tests/test_crypto.cpp`, `desktop/tests/test_chat_transport.cpp`, `native/ios/ForkMeshCore/Tests/FMCryptoTests/RoomSealTests.swift`, `native/android/core/src/test/kotlin/com/forkmesh/nativeapp/crypto/RoomSealCryptoTest.kt` |

Browser, desktop, iOS, and Android pin the same v2 recipient-envelope fixture. A
change to X25519/HKDF derivation, AAD, base64 encoding, or the wire shape fails
the interoperability tests before protected conversations on different client
releases silently stop understanding one another.
