pages.markdown:
# Dependency security audit

Every third-party component the ForkMesh repository resolves, across all
ecosystems, with who publishes it, how it has been maintained, and a security
score. The full, filterable report is a styled page:

**[Open the dependency audit report](/docs/dependency-audit/)** (all 128 Dart
packages, 12 npm packages, the CI Python pin, Android and iOS build plugins,
vendored browser libraries, desktop system libraries and toolchains).

Data was pulled live on 13 September 2026 from pub.dev, registry.npmjs.org,
PyPI, go.dev, the Google and Maven Central plugin indexes and the OSV
vulnerability database. The method, rubric and raw tables are also kept in the
repository at `docs/dependency-security-audit-2026-09-13.md`.

## What the audit found

| Finding | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Open advisories on pinned versions | None, in any ecosystem. OSV was queried per package and exact version. |
| Advisories in package histories | Four (archive ×2, http, shared_preferences_android), all fixed years before the versions in use. |
| The one real exposure | The mirror node is built with go1.24.4, which carries 47 open Go standard-library advisories (net/http, crypto/tls, net/url, os). go1.27.1 carries none. |
| Staleness | 52 Dart packages have newer releases; nothing in use has gone more than 20 months without an upstream release. |
| Publisher concentration | 106 of 128 Dart packages come from Google-run publishers; the community publishers are verified and active. |

## Top publishers

| Publisher | Packages | Tier |
| --- | --- | --- |
| tools.dart.dev | 36 | core (Dart team) |
| flutter.dev | 34 | core (Flutter team) |
| dart.dev | 29 | core (Dart SDK team) |
| steenbakker.dev | 6 | community: the flutter_secure_storage family, which holds the app's keys |
| google.dev | 5 | core |

## Scoring rubric

Each package starts at 100 and loses points for measurable risk signals.
Grades: A ≥ 90, B 80–89, C 70–79, D 60–69, F below 60.

| Signal | Deduction |
| --- | --- |
| Open advisory matching the pinned version | −40 |
| Advisory in the package's history, pinned version not affected | −5 |
| Discontinued or deprecated | −30 |
| No verified publisher | −15 |
| Verified community publisher (not Google-run) | −5 |
| No release in more than 24 / 12 months | −20 / −10 |
| Pinned version over 18 months old and a major version behind | −5 |
| pub.dev points below 100 / below 140 of 160, or analysis pending | −10 / −5 |
| Ships native code (Flutter plugin or FFI) | −5 |
| npm: fewer than two maintainers | −10 |

## Recommended actions, in order

1. Rebuild `forkmesh-mirror-node` with go1.27.1 and roll the mirror fleet.
2. Upgrade `flutter_secure_storage` to 11.x, `file_picker` to 12.x,
   `device_info_plus` to 13.x and `archive` to 4.3.0; run the mobile suite and
   refresh the iOS pod.
3. Bump Flutter to 3.47.4, Kotlin to 2.4.20 and the Android Gradle Plugin to
   9.4.0.
4. `npm update` in both browser-test projects and the VS Code extension,
   checking the extension's `engines.vscode` floor.
5. Narrow the Worker CSP `script-src` if the jsdelivr allowance is unused.

## Not covered by this audit

The audit is a snapshot of 13 September 2026. Dependencies added since then
have not been scored:

- the native iOS app's Swift packages, pinned in
  `native/ios/ForkMesh.xcodeproj/project.xcworkspace/xcshareddata/swiftpm/Package.resolved`
  (13 pins, including `mlx-swift`, `mlx-swift-lm`, `swift-transformers` and
  `swift-crypto` for on-device Gemma 4 and cryptography);
- the native Android app's Gradle dependencies in
  `native/android/app/build.gradle.kts` and `native/android/core/build.gradle.kts`
  (AndroidX Compose BOM, kotlinx coroutines).

`server/go.mod` still declares `go 1.24`; the Go standard-library exposure
above depends on the toolchain a release is built with, so check the Go
version of the release host before relying on the finding being fixed.

pages.markdown:
# Organization roles and the authorization matrix

Every organization request in the Worker is decided by one deny-by-default
table, `app/src/organization_rbac.py`. A role holds a capability only when
the matrix names it; an unknown role, an empty role, or a capability the
matrix does not list is refused for everyone, owners included. This page is
generated from that module and checked against it by
`app/tests/test_organization_rbac.py`, so the table below is the policy the
deployed Worker enforces.

## Roles

Strongest first.

| Role | Purpose | Repository permission on linked repositories |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `owner` | Runs the organization. The only role that can dissolve it or grant and revoke `owner`/`admin`. | `admin` |
| `admin` | Administers members, teams, linked repositories, integrations and bot tokens. Cannot promote anyone to `owner`/`admin` or demote them. | `admin` |
| `maintainer` | Ships code: may queue agents and manage bots it links, administers nothing. | `maintain`, a team grant can raise it to `admin` |
| `member` | Collaborates. | `read`, a team grant can raise it to `admin` |
| `auditor` | Read-only observer: sees the roster, agent work and internal surfaces, never writes, pushes or votes. | `read`, a team grant cannot raise it |
| `guest` | Outside collaborator: sees the public profile and only the repositories a team grants, read-only. Not an insider for world floors, office chat channels, task boards or succession votes. | none, a team grant raises it to `read` at most |

## Capabilities

`read` capabilities never change organization state; `write` capabilities
do, and no `write` row lists `auditor` or `guest`. The Engineering-floor team
check still applies on top of the agent rows, exactly as before.

| Capability | Kind | owner | admin | maintainer | member | auditor | guest |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `organization.agents.queue` | write | yes | yes | yes | yes | no | no |
| `organization.agents.read` | read | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes | no |
| `organization.bots.link` | write | yes | yes | yes | yes | no | no |
| `organization.bots.manage` | write | yes | yes | no | no | no | no |
| `organization.chat.channels` | write | yes | yes | yes | yes | no | no |
| `organization.dissolve` | write | yes | no | no | no | no | no |
| `organization.fediverse.manage` | write | yes | yes | no | no | no | no |
| `organization.issues.manage` | write | yes | yes | no | no | no | no |
| `organization.members.manage` | write | yes | yes | no | no | no | no |
| `organization.pull_rules.manage` | write | yes | yes | no | no | no | no |
| `organization.read` | read | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| `organization.repositories.import` | write | yes | yes | no | no | no | no |
| `organization.repositories.link` | write | yes | yes | no | no | no | no |
| `organization.roles.administer` | write | yes | no | no | no | no | no |
| `organization.roster.read` | read | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes | no |
| `organization.settings.write` | write | yes | yes | no | no | no | no |
| `organization.succession.approve` | write | yes | yes | yes | yes | no | no |
| `organization.tasks.administer` | write | yes | yes | no | no | no | no |
| `organization.teams.manage` | write | yes | yes | no | no | no | no |
| `organization.world.private` | read | yes | yes | no | no | no | no |
| `organization.world.restricted` | read | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes | no |

## Role administration

`organization.members.manage` says who may add, re-role or remove members;
`organization.roles.administer` restricts the administrative roles:

- an `owner` may assign or remove any role;
- an `admin` may add, re-role and remove `maintainer`, `member`, `auditor`
  and `guest` accounts, but can neither hand out `owner`/`admin` nor touch an
  account that currently holds one;
- every other role may assign nothing;
- the last `owner` can never be removed or demoted.

Every denied write is recorded in the sensitive-action audit log with the
reason (`insufficient_role`, `owner_role_required`, `last_owner`).

## Where the matrix is enforced

- `/api/orgs/<org>` settings, `/members`, `/teams`, `/teams/<team>/members`,
  `/repos`, the fediverse toggle, bot tokens, and repository imports into an
  organization.
- `_org_permission`, which the git push gate and every repository-permission
  check use: the role's baseline, raised by team grants up to the role's
  ceiling.
- World building access (`restricted` admits insiders, `private` admits
  administrators), office chat channel creation, task boards and the
  Engineering floor roster, which enumerate the insider roles in SQL.
- Succession votes: the D1 triggers enumerate the
  `organization.succession.approve` roles (migration
  `0183_organization_rbac_roles.sql`).

## Rollback

The role vocabulary is plain text in `org_members.role`, so a rollback
needs no data migration: a Worker build that predates a role treats it as no
membership, which is the deny-by-default behaviour. The down migration
restores the previous succession triggers.

pages.title: Private repository confidentiality boundary
pages.description: This document is the normative leakage and recovery contract for private ForkMesh repositories. A commercial-GA claim requires a keyless inspection report for the deployed…
pages.markdown:
# Private repository confidentiality boundary

This document is the normative leakage and recovery contract for private
ForkMesh repositories. A commercial-GA claim requires a keyless inspection
report for the deployed database backup and replica fleet, successful
revocation/recovery drills, and an independent cryptographic and tenant
isolation review. Passing repository tests alone is not that external review.

## Protected data

The protected set includes repository objects and refs, artifact bytes and
names, repository and organization names, source-device labels, discussions,
issues, pull requests, review bodies and decisions, agent prompts and
transcripts, notification text, security findings, media, and search terms or
indexes derived from any of them.

ForkMesh uses two different confidentiality boundaries:

- Private repository objects are sealed on an authorized device as
  `forkmesh.private-replica` ciphertext. A storage or replication operator has
  no recipient key and can copy, hash, retain, and restore the bytes without
  learning the repository identity or contents.
- Relay collaboration rows are AES-256-GCM encrypted under the instance
  `DATA_KEY`; equality lookups use a separately derived HMAC blind-index key.
  Owner-agent payloads and private/direct room frames add recipient encryption
  before reaching that layer. An instance operator controlling the live Worker
  and `DATA_KEY` is inside the relay-row trust boundary, but a database,
  snapshot, log, or backup operator without that secret is not.

There is no plaintext fallback when a required owner or room recipient key is
missing. Legacy agent rows are held for an explicit owner-device migration and
are not decrypted by a policy that requires end-to-end encryption.

## Declared metadata envelope

At-rest inspection may reveal only:

- random row, request, scan, queue, and opaque replica identifiers;
- keyed 256-bit blind indexes used for exact equality and tenant joins;
- bounded row counts, ciphertext sizes, coarse status enums, and timestamps;
- read/lease state, retry counts, and non-content feature flags;
- ciphertext and exact-file SHA-256 digests, key epochs, algorithms, and public
  recipient key identifiers; and
- whether a catalog row is private, needed to reject it before decryption on
  anonymous paths.

These fields leak existence, approximate activity time and volume, recipient
set cardinality, and equality within one instance-key lifetime. They must not
contain names, paths, device labels, message snippets, Git refs, object IDs, or
hashes derived from private Git refs. A `DATA_KEY` rotation changes blind
indexes and therefore breaks equality across independently exported epochs.

Private source authority is stored in encrypted `data`; its legacy `node_id`
and `machine_name` columns are blank. Private secondary-device lookup uses a
blind index. `repo_state_history` is public-mirror machinery and must have no
row for a private repository. Private integrity instead binds an opaque route
to the owner-signed encrypted-manifest hash and monotonically increasing key
epoch.

Authorized runtime plaintext can still reach memory, an explicitly exported
working copy, an unlocked device's swap/crash dump, or an old copy retained by
a former collaborator. Application encryption cannot retract data a recipient
already copied. Use device disk encryption and operating-system crash-dump
controls in addition to ForkMesh keys.

## Key lifecycle

The first recipient bundle is the owner authority. It contains public X25519
and ML-KEM-768 material; private halves stay in the local encrypted identity
vault. Every repository update and recipient rotation creates a fresh random
AES-256-GCM content key and advances `keyEpoch` atomically.

For device revocation or collaborator removal:

1. Revoke the recipient key or remove the share while an owner device remains
   available.
2. Fetch the fresh, owner-signed recipient set and reseal to exactly that set.
3. Publish the new encrypted manifest and opaque route at the new epoch.
4. Verify the removed key cannot open the new bytes and that every retained
   recipient can.
5. Import the new ciphertext into a second replica and verify an older epoch
   cannot overwrite it.

Revocation denies future epochs and downloads. It cannot erase an older
ciphertext or materialized checkout already held by the removed recipient.
Audit history is retained as signed, content-free key/share events rather than
by retaining removed recipient access.

Organization-managed deployments should escrow an organization recipient
private key in their approved HSM/KMS and enroll only its public bundle. The
KMS wrapping, quorum, export, and deletion policy remain organization-owned;
ForkMesh never accepts the private key through its relay APIs. Keep at least
two current owner recipients before rotation so one failed device does not
make the ciphertext unavailable.

## Backup and recovery

Back up exact `.fm-private` files, the encrypted D1 export, configuration, and
the separately protected identity recovery kit. Never place a plaintext Git
materialization or raw `DATA_KEY` in the ciphertext backup. Protect the
`DATA_KEY` recovery copy with a different administrative control and verify its
mode/ownership using the bootstrap runbook.

A quarterly recovery drill restores the D1 export and opaque replicas into an
isolated environment, runs the keyless audit, restores one authorized identity,
opens the newest epoch, and checks Git refs and collaboration event signatures.
It then attempts the same open with a revoked identity and attempts an older
epoch import. Record durations and only content-free outcomes; do not attach
repository names, object IDs, paths, ciphertext, keys, or decrypted output.

## Keyless inspection

Restore the D1 SQL export to a SQLite file, mount replica directories read-only,
and run:

```bash
python tools/audit_private_surfaces.py backup.sqlite3 \
  --replica-root /read-only/private-replicas \
  --output artifacts/private-surface-audit.json
```

The command takes no key. It validates every declared table column, blind-index
shape, encrypted payload framing, absence of private refs indexes and authority
labels, replica hybrid-envelope framing and digest, and monotonic duplicate
epochs. Reports contain only counts, row ordinals, and stable finding codes.
Exit `0` means complete inspection passed; `1` means a confidentiality finding;
`2` means input or inspection failure. `coverage_incomplete`, a missing table,
or an undeclared new column fails closed.

Run the audit on the primary export, each backup class, and a sample from every
replica operator. A rollback restores ciphertext and schema together; never
roll back only the database after a recipient rotation because epoch rollback
protection will correctly reject the older row.

## GA evidence

Before commercial GA, link all of the following to the release candidate:

- Linux, macOS, and Windows private-surface CI artifacts;
- production-like primary, backup, index, log, and replica inspection reports;
- add/remove/revoke/rotate drills with rotation time and denial outcomes;
- encrypted backup restore and owner-loss recovery duration and success;
- rollback, corrupt ciphertext, wrong key, missing key, stale epoch, and partial
  outage failure-path runs;
- current user and operator documentation;
- content-free telemetry for coverage percentage, rotation duration, recovery
  success, plaintext finding count, and unresolved security findings; and
- an independent review report covering the algorithms, implementation,
  recipient authentication, nonce/key generation, key erasure limits, tenant
  authorization, blind-index leakage, caches/logging, and operator threat model.

Any unresolved critical/high finding, plaintext finding, incomplete supported
platform, missing recovery run, or absent independent review blocks GA. Review
artifacts may be access-controlled, but their reviewer, scope, candidate commit,
date, disposition, and report digest must be recorded publicly.

pages.title: Secret scanning before replication
pages.description: A ForkMesh node copies every object it receives to the mirrors, forks, clones, and backups that replicate the repository. Nobody can recall a pushed object. Quarantine and…
pages.markdown:
# Secret scanning before replication

A ForkMesh node copies every object it receives to the mirrors, forks,
clones, and backups that replicate the repository. **Nobody can recall a
pushed object.** Quarantine and history rewrites stop future serving on nodes
you control. They cannot erase copies that already exist elsewhere. So the
only reliable remediation for a leaked credential is to rotate it, and the
only reliable prevention is to stop it before the first remote receives it.

Every boundary below prints the same permanence warning whenever it reports
a finding.

## One scanner contract

`tools/secret_gate.py` is the contract (`forkmesh-secret-scan-v1`). It uses
only the standard library, so it runs as `python3 -I` beside the gateway
tools. `python3 tools/secret_gate.py contract` prints it. It defines:

- **Rules.** 19 patterns: GitHub classic and fine-grained tokens, AWS access
  and temporary keys, Slack, OpenAI, Anthropic, Stripe secret and restricted
  keys, Google API keys, OAuth tokens and client secrets, SendGrid, Twilio,
  npm, HashiCorp Vault, Cloudflare API tokens, PEM private keys, and a
  generic password/token assignment. Every rule also carries rotation
  guidance for its issuer.
- **Placeholder filter.** The generic assignment rule skips values that
  advertise themselves as placeholders ("example", "changeme", `${VAR}`,
  `{{ }}`, `$VAR`, and similar). Provider-prefixed rules have no filter.
- **Inline ignore marker.** A `forkmesh-secret-scan:ignore-line` comment on
  a line skips matches on it. The marker covers a whole logical line, so a
  marker at the end of a backslash-continued command applies to every
  physical line in it. An organization can refuse markers.
- **Value-free findings.** A finding names the rule, path, line, Git blob id,
  and a fingerprint. The fingerprint is derived from the rule, path, and blob
  id, never from the matched value, so no report, audit record, or evidence
  file holds the value or a digest of it.

The desktop scanner (`RepoSecurity::secretPatterns()`) carries the same
patterns and placeholder markers. `app/tests/test_secret_gate.py` fails if
they drift apart.

## Where it runs

| Boundary | What happens | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Local commit | Blocks or warns on added lines before the commit exists | `secret_gate.py install-hooks` (pre-commit) |
| Local push | Blocks or warns on every object the push would send, before the remote receives any of them. This catches commits made with `--no-verify`. | `secret_gate.py install-hooks` (pre-push) |
| Desktop push | Blocks with a review dialog | `RepoSecurity::findSecretsInPush` |
| Review diff | Grades the added lines of a patch. The desktop's branch review, Source Control and agent Code diffs show a red banner above the diff listing each match, with a button that appends the ignore marker to that line | desktop `findSecretsInDiff`, `SecretDiffBanner`, `secret_gate.py scan-diff` |
| Node receipt (HTTPS and SSH gateways) | Refuses the push before the node stores anything; Git discards its receive quarantine | `secrets` in the [node operator policy](../operations/node-operator-policy.md) |
| Sync and mirror intake | Detection is **after replication**. `enforce` reports the repository, quarantines it under `block`, and returns the response plan below. | `node_operator_policy.py enforce` |
| Public security report | Reports findings without values | `tools/security_scan.py` |

The desktop's diff banner writes the marker with `RepoSecurity::markFindingSafe`,
the same call as the push dialog's "Mark safe & commit". It edits the
checkout the diff was read from (the branch's worktree, the working tree, or
the agent's worktree) and leaves the change uncommitted. It refuses a line
that no longer holds a match and a file type with no comment syntax. A
branch with no checkout on this machine shows the banner with the buttons
disabled.

Install the client hooks once per checkout:

```sh
python3 tools/secret_gate.py install-hooks --repo . \
  --repository alice/app --org-policy ~/.config/forkmesh/secret-policy.json
```

The installer never overwrites a hook it did not write. It lists preserved
hooks in `preservedForeignHooks`.

## Organization and repository policy

The organization policy is a file the operator or organization owns. With no
policy, every rule blocks.

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "mode": "block",
  "rules": {"generic-secret-assignment": "warn"},
  "customRules": [
    {"id": "custom-acme-key", "title": "Acme deploy key",
     "pattern": "acme_live_[A-Za-z0-9]{32}", "severity": "critical",
     "action": "block", "rotation": "Revoke it in the Acme console."}
  ],
  "allowlist": [
    {"paths": ["tests/fixtures/fake/*"], "rules": ["*"],
     "reason": "synthetic credentials for parser tests"}
  ],
  "honorIgnoreMarkers": true,
  "allowRepositoryAllowlist": false,
  "allowRepositoryCustomRules": false,
  "overrides": {
    "allowedSignersPath": "/etc/forkmesh/secret-override-signers",
    "maxLifetimeDays": 90
  }
}
```

- `mode` and `rules` take `off`, `warn`, or `block`. A rule without an entry
  uses `mode`.
- A repository may commit `.forkmesh/secret-scan.json` with `mode`, `rules`,
  `customRules`, and `allowlist`. It can only **tighten** a rule, from off to
  warn or from warn to block. Whoever pushes controls that file, so its
  allowlist and custom patterns count only when the organization sets
  `allowRepositoryAllowlist` or `allowRepositoryCustomRules`. The scanner
  merges the repository policy from the pushed commits and from the stored
  default branch. Deleting the file in a push does not loosen anything.
- Allowlist entries need a reason and cannot cover every path. Allowlisted
  findings are still counted.
- Invalid regular expressions, patterns that match empty text, unknown rule
  ids, and unknown fields are refused.

## Signed overrides

A block can be lifted only by an override that an allowed signer signed with
an SSH key. The override names the exact finding fingerprints. A warning
needs no override.

```sh
python3 tools/secret_gate.py sign-override --key ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 \
  --signer alice@example.com --repository alice/app --days 30 \
  --reason "synthetic token for the webhook parser test" \
  --fingerprint <fingerprint from the blocked output> \
  > .forkmesh/secret-overrides/webhook-parser.json
```

The allowed signers file uses the OpenSSH format, restricted to the override
namespace:

```text
alice@example.com namespaces="forkmesh-secret-override" ssh-ed25519 AAAA...
```

Commit the override next to the fixture. It travels with the repository, so
every node that shares the organization's signers accepts the same push.

An override is **ignored**, and the reason is printed, if any of these hold:

- the signature does not verify for the named signer
- it names another repository
- it has expired, or its lifetime is longer than `maxLifetimeDays`
- the policy has no `allowedSignersPath`

Accepted overrides are written to the node audit log (`admit-push-secrets`)
with the signer, reason, expiry, and fingerprints.

## Measured accuracy

`conformance/secrets/v1/corpus.json` is the maintained corpus. It is
generated from the readable `build_corpus.py`, and every credential in it is
synthetic. `python3 tools/secret_gate.py corpus` runs the corpus through the
publication, review-diff, pre-commit, and git-objects boundaries.
Git-objects is the boundary that pre-push, node receipt, and stored-data
enforcement share.

| Boundary | Malicious | Benign | False negatives | False positives |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| publication | 28 | 19 | 3 (10.7%) | 1 (5.3%) |
| review-diff | 28 | 19 | 3 (10.7%) | 1 (5.3%) |
| pre-commit | 28 | 19 | 3 (10.7%) | 1 (5.3%) |
| git-objects | 28 | 19 | 3 (10.7%) | 1 (5.3%) |

The bounds are at most 15% false negatives and 10% false positives. Every
misclassified case is a documented known limitation:

- A JSON object key (`"api_key": "..."`). The closing quote between the name
  and the colon defeats the assignment pattern.
- A token split by string concatenation.
- A key wrapped in base64.
- AWS's published documentation key id, which provider rules flag because
  they have no placeholder filter.

The test suite fails if any other case is misclassified, if a rule has no
malicious case, or if a scanner change fixes a known limitation without the
corpus saying so. To change the corpus, edit `build_corpus.py`, run it, and
commit both files.

## When a secret is found after replication

`enforce` output (and `python3 tools/secret_gate.py respond --report
<scan.json>`) returns this plan with per-rule rotation steps:

1. **Containment.** Quarantine the repository on every node you operate so
   it stops being served there. Remove the value from the default branch in a
   new commit. Pause automation that could reuse the credential.
2. **Rotation.** Revoke or roll the credential at its issuer first, deploy
   the replacement from a secret store, and review the issuer's audit log
   since first publication.
3. **Notification.** Tell the repository owner and security contact. Share
   the evidence record (rule, path, blob id, fingerprint), never the value.
   Follow third-party disclosure and breach-notification duties, and record
   the notice in the node case log.
4. **Residual risk.** Clones, forks, mirrors, backups, and caches that
   already received the objects keep them. Treat the secret as compromised
   until it is rotated.

## Telemetry

Everything is counted without values:

- **Scan reports.** Hooks and CLI commands carry per-boundary `counts`
  (`block`, `warn`, `overridden`, `allowlisted`), `invalidOverrides`, and
  skipped-file counts.
- **Node counters.** `node_operator_policy.py status` reports `secrets`:
  - `blockedPushes`, `warnedPushes`, and `warnings`
  - `overriddenFindings` and `allowlistedFindings`
  - `invalidOverrides`
  - `storedDetections`, which counts detections after replication
- **Audit log.** The hash-chained node audit log records `reject-push`
  (rule `secret`), `admit-push-secrets`, and `secret-detected-stored`.

## Not covered yet

- **Worker surfaces.** Browser uploads, provider imports, and other
  Worker-hosted writes do not run the contract yet. Content from those paths
  is scanned only when it reaches a node's `enforce`, which is after
  replication.
- **Desktop.** The desktop push dialog's "Push anyway" is an unsigned local
  bypass. The desktop does not read organization policy or signed overrides.
- **Upstream fetches.** The Go daemon's fetches are not scanned before they
  land. Run `enforce` after sync.
- **Scan limits.** Blobs larger than 1 MiB and binary blobs are skipped and
  counted, not scanned. Encoded or split secrets are missed (see Measured
  accuracy).
- **Owner notification.** It is a documented step, not an automatic message.

pages.title: World-to-desktop speech bridge
pages.description: ForkMesh World can use the Qt client’s locally installed Whisper or Parakeet engine without sending microphone audio to the Worker, a relay, another mirror, or the browser. The…
pages.markdown:
# World-to-desktop speech bridge

ForkMesh World can use the Qt client’s locally installed Whisper or Parakeet
engine without sending microphone audio to the Worker, a relay, another mirror,
or the browser. The browser is a controller and transcript recipient only. Audio
capture and speech-to-text remain inside the desktop client.

## Pairing

1. The user opens the World from the Qt client and explicitly enables voice
   control for that exact World origin.
2. Qt binds an ephemeral port on `127.0.0.1` and displays a short-lived pairing
   capability. Qt stores only its SHA-256 digest.
3. The user pastes the capability into the World voice panel. The World sends it
   once in an `Authorization: Bearer …` header to `POST /v1/pair`.
4. The one-use pairing capability is consumed before Qt returns an
   origin-bound, ten-minute browser-session capability in the JSON response.

Neither capability is placed in a URL, query string, fragment, referrer, cookie,
Worker request, analytics event, or browser storage that survives the tab.
Closing the panel or choosing **Revoke** invalidates the browser session. Closing
Qt stops the loopback listener and removes all capabilities.

## Capture protocol

The World asks the user to choose `chat`, `issue`, or `note` before enabling the
microphone control. Each start, stop, cancel, or revoke request carries a unique
`X-ForkMesh-Request-Id`; replayed mutation IDs are rejected. The Qt client:

- starts its normal local recorder only after `POST /v1/transcription/start`;
- changes the state to `transcribing` after an explicit stop;
- cancels and deletes the temporary recording after an explicit cancel;
- exposes status and transcript text through authenticated
  `GET /v1/transcription`; and
- inserts text into the chosen World composer only after the browser receives a
  completed transcript and the user confirms that destination.

The protocol intentionally has no audio upload or download endpoint and reports
`audioRelayed: false`. Request bodies are limited to 8 KiB, transfer encoding
and query strings are rejected, mutation IDs are single use, responses are
`no-store`, and transcript/error text is bounded and stripped of control
characters.

## Origin and browser boundary

Qt records the exact `http` or `https` origin at pairing time. It does not use
suffix, wildcard, substring, or `null` origin matching. CORS responses echo only
that known exact origin and never enable credential cookies. Chromium private
network preflights are accepted only for a still-active exact origin. The TCP
listener and every accepted peer are independently required to be loopback.

The Worker must never proxy this API. Deployments may change their public World
origin, but the desktop user must issue a new capability for that exact origin.

## Operational evidence

The bridge emits generalized audit events (issued, paired, started, stopped,
cancelled, completed, failed, revoked) without capability values, transcript
contents, audio, microphone names, or browsing history. Tests cover loopback
binding, exact-origin enforcement, one-use pairing and mutation capabilities,
expiry/revocation, cancellation, absence of audio transport, and transcript
status delivery.

## Completion-gate evidence

- **Threat review:** the protected assets are microphone control and transcript
  text. The reviewed threats are non-loopback access, DNS-rebinding/origin
  confusion, capability disclosure, replay, request smuggling, unbounded input,
  concurrent capture, capture surviving expiry, and a late process result
  crossing sessions. The controls are independent loopback listener/peer
  checks, exact canonical origins, digest-only capability retention, one-use
  pairing and mutation IDs, bounded single-request HTTP parsing, one active
  desktop capture, a monotonic periodic expiry sweep, and capture-ID binding.
- **Abuse/privacy review:** no IP-derived identity, browsing detail, audio,
  microphone label, transcript, or capability enters audit events. The bridge
  cannot submit a draft. Pairing, recording, stopping, cancellation,
  destination choice, copying, and revocation are explicit user actions.
- **Benchmark/budget evidence:** the protocol allows at most 16 KiB of headers
  and 8 KiB of body, retains at most 512 nonces during a ten-minute session,
  permits one local capture, polls status no faster than 450 ms, and adds no
  socket, audio upload, model execution, or Worker work. These are hard bounds,
  not advisory targets.
- **Current product state:** the World does not load a speech bridge script,
  stylesheet, launcher, pairing panel, or microphone control. The Qt bridge is
  retained as dormant local infrastructure for a possible future interface.
- **Regression evidence:** `forkmesh-world-speech-tests` drives the real Qt
  loopback server, while `test_world_speech_bridge_frontend.py` enforces that
  ForkMesh World exposes no browser speech entry point.

pages.title: Breakout authorization replica
pages.description: ForkMesh mirrors use Git and signed repository ledgers as the replicated data plane. Repository management during a controller outage also needs an authorization plane, but…
pages.markdown:
# Breakout authorization replica

ForkMesh mirrors use Git and signed repository ledgers as the replicated data
plane. Repository management during a controller outage also needs an
authorization plane, but copying D1 or password/session tables to every public
host would turn each mirror into a credential database. ForkMesh therefore uses
a narrow, signed authorization projection backed by SQLite on each node, plus
a controller-signed portable browser grant for login continuity.

## Replicated fields

Each monotonically numbered generation may contain only:

- stable opaque account id and public username;
- enabled device or passkey public keys and their capabilities;
- public repository ids and owner/collaborator roles;
- key, account, and repository revocation generations; and
- controller issue time, expiry, previous digest, and Ed25519 signature.

It must not contain email addresses, password salts or hashes, password reset
state, TOTP seeds, controller bearer/session tokens, private-message metadata, payment
state, administrator privileges, or the encrypted `users.data`/repository rows.
The source is a purpose-built D1 query and projection, never a D1 export.

## Synchronization

The node refreshes after each controller authorization event and on the normal
short reconcile interval. It verifies the controller signature, exact schema,
strictly increasing generation, previous-generation digest, size limits, and
expiry before applying one SQLite transaction. A bad or partial generation is
discarded and the last good generation remains available. Nodes exchange only
controller-signed generations, so peer catch-up does not create a new authority.

Repository code, refs, releases, issues, pulls, reviews, discussions, and signed
write events continue to synchronize through Git and durable event spools. The
authorization database decides who may create those signed changes; it is not a
second repository database.

## Login and sessions

Every successful controller login also mints a narrow Ed25519-signed portable
session grant. The grant contains only an opaque account id, public username,
opaque session/grant ids, issue/expiry times, and the mirror-dashboard audience;
it contains neither the controller bearer token nor a D1 row. On the managed
`*.forkmesh.com` fleet it is carried in a separate HttpOnly, Secure,
SameSite=Strict parent-domain cookie. An independent mirror verifies the grant
with the already-published router public key, so visiting that mirror keeps the
browser signed in even when the controller cannot answer.

The grant lives at most twelve hours and never outlives its controller session
(which lasts five years unless revoked), is reissued on authenticated
session/device reads, and is cleared with the controller cookie on logout,
current-session revocation, or current-device revocation. Signature tampering, duplicate-cookie ambiguity, future grants,
expiry, and a different signing key all fail closed. During a controller outage
an already stolen grant cannot receive a newer revocation decision, so mirrors
limit it to its signed expiry and prohibit account recovery, billing, platform
administration, and other controller-only powers. Custom-domain fleets must
configure `PORTABLE_SESSION_COOKIE_DOMAIN`; unrelated domains deliberately do
not receive the cookie.

Password-only reauthentication still never happens on a public mirror. If no
portable grant is present, an enrolled device/passkey may instead sign a node
nonce bound to the requested origin and authorization generation. That proof
creates a short-lived node-local session scoped to projected repository roles.

Password-only accounts cannot safely authenticate on a public mirror: a
password verifier distributed to every node is reusable offline attack
material. The UI must ask those users to enroll a device key or passkey while
the controller is available before breakout access can work.

## Recovery

During an outage, authorized repository mutations land in local Git and signed
spools. On recovery the node reconciles portable and breakout-session
revocations, forwards events
idempotently, fetches the newest authorization generation, and reconciles refs
according to the signed event/ref policy. Billing, password reset, account
recovery, private data, and platform administration always fail closed on a
mirror.

pages.title: Business-model rollout and recovery
pages.description: This runbook publishes the ForkMesh free-protocol / paid-services boundary without granting the hosted operator control over protocol participation.
pages.markdown:
# Business-model rollout and recovery

This runbook publishes the ForkMesh free-protocol / paid-services boundary
without granting the hosted operator control over protocol participation.

## Owners and release gate

Name a product owner, infrastructure-cost owner, support owner, and privacy or
legal reviewer before enabling a managed checkout. The initial contract is a
research preview and managed checkout must remain disabled while any gate in
`www/public/business-model.json` is open.

Run from the repository root:

```sh
python3 tools/unit_economics.py validate-contract
python3 tools/quality_gate.py run --profile core
```

For a candidate accounting window, export the admin usage report, add
invoice-backed costs and aggregate funnel counts using the period schema, then
run:

```sh
python3 tools/unit_economics.py report --input /path/to/period.json
python3 tools/unit_economics.py launch-gate --input /path/to/period.json
```

The launch gate is expected to fail until real interview evidence is marked
validated. Do not bypass it by adding synthetic research or zero-valued missing
costs.

## Supported surfaces

- Contract page and homepage pricing: current standards-based desktop and mobile
  browsers served by the WWW Worker.
- Portable proof: standard Git plus the web app in a current browser.
- Self-hosted desktop: macOS, Windows, and Linux packages covered by the release
  installer matrix.
- Managed mirror evidence: Linux headless mirror service.

Mobile and editor integrations can collaborate but are not advertised as
managed source-host controls. Self-hosted deployments receive documentation and
community support unless a separate, explicit support order names the platform.

## Deployment

1. Validate the JSON, visible matrix, docs links, analytics allowlist, and unit
   economics tests.
2. Confirm `/business-model.json`, `/docs/business-model`, `/#pricing`,
   `/privacy`, and `/terms` are in the WWW asset manifest and return on a local
   Worker smoke test.
3. Confirm the managed plan says `research-preview-not-for-sale`, contains no
   checkout control, and no variable-cost service says unlimited.
4. Deploy WWW normally. Deploy App only when the stable admin usage projection
   changed and its focused tests pass.
5. Record the commit, test run, reviewer decisions, live URLs, and screenshot or
   text capture of the entitlement matrix.

## Failure paths

| Failure | Required behavior | Recovery |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Contract JSON is malformed or drifts from the visible matrix | CI/deploy fails | Correct the source and matrix together; do not hand-edit production |
| Provider analytics is unconfigured | Usage endpoint returns `analytics_unconfigured`; cost is unknown | Restore the scoped analytics token, retry, and retain the missing interval |
| Provider analytics is unavailable | Usage endpoint returns `analytics_unavailable`; never record zero | Retry after provider recovery or reconcile the provider invoice manually |
| Invoice, host, runner, or support cost is missing | Period report is incomplete and launch gate fails | Attach an attributable source and rerun; do not estimate it as zero |
| Interview threshold is not met | Managed plan remains a research preview with no checkout | Conduct and record real qualifying interviews |
| Export or restore differs | Trial stops; no paid reliability claim | Preserve evidence, restore the last verified copy, repair the exporter, repeat on a clean deployment |
| Optional analytics is denied or blocked | No commercial product event is sent | Continue without tracking that visitor; never make analytics consent a service condition |

## Rollback

The public contract deployment changes no protocol object, repository,
identity, entitlement row, or customer data. Roll back WWW to the last reviewed
asset revision and invalidate only the changed static assets. If the App usage
projection must be rolled back, retain the newer JSON export as operational
evidence; old clients ignore unknown response fields.

Never roll back by deleting canonical repositories or signed collaboration
records. A pricing rollback cannot revoke MIT rights or make an export paid.

## Recovery and portability drill

Before the first managed trial and each material format change:

1. Select a disposable project with Git refs and signed collaboration records.
2. Export it from the managed service without using a paid-only exporter.
3. Import it into a clean self-hosted deployment with hosted routes disabled.
4. Compare all Git refs/object ids and signed `.forkmesh` records.
5. Clone and collaborate from the self-host, then restore the managed service
   from the same export.
6. Record duration, bytes, missing objects, conflicts, recovery outcome, and
   sanitized logs. Any mismatch blocks launch.

## Telemetry and privacy

The live infrastructure projection is aggregate at network level and contains
only fixed unit ids and quantities. Economics period files may contain aggregate
funnel counts, recognized revenue, and cost-source labels. They must not contain
raw account names, repository names, paths, IP addresses, request ids, provider
customer ids, interviewee identity, or confidential notes.

Pricing-page product actions use the existing default-off first-party analytics controller.
Only allowlisted action names are sent after explicit consent; denial, Global
Privacy Control, and Do Not Track continue to disable them.

pages.title: Cloudflare deployment boundaries
pages.description: ForkMesh has three product Workers. The App owns its complete control plane; there is no separate API or edge-control Worker.
pages.markdown:
# Cloudflare deployment boundaries

ForkMesh has three product Workers. The App owns its complete control plane;
there is no separate API or edge-control Worker.

| Directory | Script | Official hostnames | Responsibility |
|---|---|---|---|
| `app/` | `forkmesh-app` | `app.forkmesh.com` | Product UI, `/api/*`, health and release identity, public snapshots, WebSockets, Git Smart HTTP, ActivityPub, D1, KV, AI, Cron, migrations, and Durable Objects |
| `www/` | `forkmesh-www` | `forkmesh.com`, `forkmesh.com` | Landing pages, marketing, documentation, blog, and shared browser assets |
| `world/` | `forkmesh-world` | `world.forkmesh.com` | World shell, modules, models, soundtrack, avatars, and World media |

The canonical API base is `https://app.forkmesh.com/api`. The retired
`app.forkmesh.com` hostname has no DNS record, route, trust entry, or CORS
authority.

## Routing and snapshot contract

The App has one custom-domain route for `app.forkmesh.com`. It directly serves
the root redirect, `/health`, `/api/version`, and GET
`/api/mirrors/https`; registration POSTs and every other operational protocol
remain in the same App runtime. Identity responses are `no-store`.

Five exact anonymous GET routes (`/api/repositories`,
`/api/network/overview`, `/api/repo/forkmesh/forkmesh/mirrors`, `/api/status`,
and `/api/status/world`) read validated, fresh-only projections from the main
App `DB`. Authorization, every Cookie, query strings, cache-bypass directives,
HEAD, and non-GET methods bypass snapshots. Missing, expired, or canonical
release-mismatched rows use one no-store live fallback; corrupt rows and active
privacy-transition tombstones fail closed. Snapshot responses expose their
freshness, generated timestamp, and deploy fingerprint through the normal App
CORS policy.

`www` redirects exact `/api` to the App developer page and service-proxies
`/api/*`, Git Smart HTTP, ActivityPub, webhook bodies, and WebSocket upgrades to
`forkmesh-app`. Product routes redirect to App and `/world*` redirects to
World. `world` serves World assets, injects `APP_ORIGIN` so its HTTP and
WebSocket traffic reaches the configured App, and delegates non-World routes
to the App service binding so the App remains the canonical route owner. It
also service-proxies App-owned shell dependencies instead of duplicating them
in the World Static Assets upload.

## Asset and configuration ownership

- `app/public` owns login, signup, dashboard, repository, chat, notes, network,
  status, rewards, accounts, and file icons.
- `www/public` owns official marketing, browser docs, blog, favicons, fonts,
  video, and shared site chrome. Authored docs live under `www/docs`.
- `world/public` owns World code and World-only media.

The built World payload contains only `world/public` plus its generated
`_headers`. Shared fonts, favicons, logos, telemetry, and chat modules remain in
the App deployment and resolve through the World-to-App service binding.

`app/wrangler.toml` owns the App route, one-minute Cron Trigger, main D1
binding, KV, AI, migrations, and Durable Object classes. The checked-in WWW
and World service bindings point to `forkmesh-app`.
`app/tools/build_site_assets.py` creates ignored `app/dist`, `www/dist`, and
`world/dist` staging trees.

## Scheduled maintenance

The App scheduled handler is a doorbell: it rings the singleton
`scheduled-runner-v1` object, whose alarm runs every due phase of the minute
itself. Workers Free allows fifty subrequests per invocation, so when the
next phase's measured reserve no longer fits, the object persists its progress
(`tick_state_v5`) and re-arms its alarm for "now"; the following invocation
resumes on the same object with a fresh budget. A quiet minute is therefore one
alarm invocation on one object, and a busy one is a short chain of invocations
on that same object, never a fan-out to other objects that would be billed
while the coordinator waited for them. The status projection chain leads the
list and stays ordered, every other phase keeps its failure isolation, a phase
started by an invocation that died is reported incomplete rather than replayed
unless it is replay-safe, and the completion watchdog rides the invocation that
finishes a tick and is withheld whenever anything failed. Every tick writes one
bounded `cron_tick` row (its `batches` column now counts alarm invocations),
which is what `/api/accounts/admin-cron-report` and the desktop Log page's
Cron tab read.

The former `scheduled-batch-*`, `scheduled-phase-v2:*` and
`scheduled-status-v1:*` receivers are gone; those object names answer 404.

## Self-hosted topology

A default self-host has one complete App at
`https://forkmesh.example.com`. Set `PUBLIC_BASE_URL`, `API_ORIGIN`,
`APP_ORIGIN`, `WWW_ORIGIN`, and allowed CORS origins to that origin, and set
`SINGLE_WORKER_SITE=true`. The bootstrapper creates one App Worker, one main D1
database, one proxied hostname, and one broad App route. It does not create or
delete sibling control scripts or exact overlay routes. Any legacy overlapping
route fails closed and must be removed in a separately authorized control-plane
cutover. World remains optional.

## Skipping unchanged Workers

`./deploy.sh deploy` and `./deploy.sh changed` fingerprint each target's inputs
and compare them with the fingerprint the live Worker reports. A target whose
live fingerprint already matches is skipped, so a repeated deploy is cheap.

Pass `--force` (or `-f`) to any deploy command to bypass that check and upload
the target anyway:

```bash
cd app
./deploy.sh changed --force   # every Worker
./deploy.sh app --force       # one target
```

Forcing is the recovery path when the live Worker is wrong in a way the
fingerprint cannot see: a partially applied upload, a manually edited script, or
a Worker variable changed outside `deploy.sh`. It is equivalent to setting
`FORKMESH_FORCE_DEPLOY=1`, and on `deploy`/`changed` it carries into every
per-target run. It skips only the change check; every migration, secret, and
post-deploy verification gate still runs.

The desktop control plane exposes the same flag: the **Force** toggle in
Control → Site deployment arms `--force` for the next deploy action and clears
itself once that run starts, so it cannot silently stay on.

## Safe official consolidation cutover

The old exact edge routes continue to win until the consolidated App and all
five current snapshot rows are ready. Before running prepare, disable the
legacy edge Cron Trigger and pre-expire every normal row in the legacy
snapshots D1 database. Then use the explicit prepare stage:

```bash
cd app
FORKMESH_APP_CONSOLIDATION_PREPARE=1 \
FORKMESH_APP_WORKER_NAME=forkmesh-relay \
FORKMESH_LEGACY_EDGE_QUIESCED=1 \
./deploy.sh app
```

The acknowledgement flag does not replace the read-only D1 proof: prepare
fails unless the old schedule is acknowledged quiesced, the legacy target is
named explicitly, and every legacy normal row is explicitly expired. It then deploys
the consolidated code and secrets to the existing script, applies main-D1
migrations, verifies `/api/mainnode`, and waits for all five current rows. It
does not require the still-overlaid public routes and does not mutate or delete
external edge resources.

Complete the control-plane cutover in this recoverable order:

1. Remove (drain) all nine old exact routes: App root, health, version, mirror
   identity, and the five snapshot paths. Do not delete the old script yet.
2. Run `./deploy.sh post-deploy-verify`. It must prove the root, health,
   version, identity, and every snapshot response carry App ownership and no
   legacy edge marker. Re-confirm the old schedule remains quiesced.
3. If any takeover check fails, restore all nine routes and the old schedule
   before doing anything destructive, then diagnose and retry.
4. Export the now-unbound legacy snapshots D1 database and retain the export
   under the operator's normal recovery policy. Terminate every active tail on
   the old script so no observer outlives resource ownership.
5. Delete the old control Worker, then delete its unbound snapshots D1 database.
6. Rename the existing `forkmesh-relay` script in place to `forkmesh-app`
   through Cloudflare's UUID-preserving PATCH. Do not create a second App
   script or recreate Durable Object namespaces.
7. Re-run App verification, deploy WWW with its checked-in `forkmesh-app`
   service binding, and verify the WWW service-proxy paths.

The edge schedule, export, tail, Worker, D1, and rename steps are external
control-plane operations; `deploy.sh` never deletes those resources itself.

Normal `./deploy.sh app` deploys `forkmesh-app`, publishes secrets to that exact
same target, waits for main-D1 snapshot rows, and verifies App ownership,
release identity, router identity, and every public snapshot route. `deploy`,
`changed`, `world`, `www`, `status`, and `dry-run` retain their target-specific
roles.

## Router identity and rollback

Generic secret publication preserves the matched router signing seed and
public key already on the App. Explicit rotation validates the local pair and
publishes it atomically to the App; no separate public-key-only script exists.

Migrations are roll-forward, so an application rollback must accept the newest
schema. A rollback across consolidation must preserve privacy tombstones and
the direct phase dispatcher. If that cannot be proven, roll forward instead of
reintroducing exact overlay routes, a separate snapshots database, or the
legacy `/kick` scheduler.

pages.title: Cloudflare Free-tier request audit
pages.description: Audit date: 2026-08-12. Production baseline supplied by the operator: about 55,000 Worker invocations, 108,000 subrequests, and 23,000 asset requests per day, with 196 errors…
pages.markdown:
# Cloudflare Free-tier request audit

Audit date: 2026-08-12. Production baseline supplied by the operator: about
55,000 Worker invocations, 108,000 subrequests, and 23,000 asset requests per
day, with 196 errors (178 uncaught) and CPU-limit failures.

## Request architecture

```text
Browser, desktop, Git client
  |
  +-- app.forkmesh.com API/dynamic page
  |     -> forkmesh-app Worker
  |          +-- D1 / KV / AI
  |          +-- room, node, note, world, cron and Discord Durable Objects
  |          `-- one selected healthy mirror (bounded failover, max 4)
  |                 -> mirrorXX.forkmesh.com
  |                      -> Cloudflare Tunnel
  |                           -> loopback Python mirror_gateway
  |                                -> local bare Git / release CAS
  |
  +-- forkmesh.com static page or asset
  |     -> Cloudflare Static Assets (no Worker for ordinary static paths)
  |
  +-- forkmesh.com API/protocol/profile
  |     -> forkmesh-www Worker
  |          -> APP service binding -> forkmesh-app Worker
  |
  +-- world.forkmesh.com shell/dynamic route
  |     -> forkmesh-world Worker -> Static Assets or APP service binding
  |
  +-- app hashed asset, status document, dashboard shell/chunk
  |     -> Cloudflare Static Assets (excluded from run_worker_first)
  |
  `-- desktop Mirrors / Pulls
        +-- saved active Hosts -> mirrorXX /health directly
        +-- public branch state -> mirrorXX /v1/public/repositories/... directly
        +-- Git pull ledger -> saved Host SSH remote directly
        `-- relay Git URL only as a final fallback

Managed mirror node
  +-- one EventSocket to /api/nodes/events
  +-- one signed inbox GET and exact DELETE per changed collaboration kind
  +-- native Go materialization into Git
  +-- state/catalog publication only when changed or its lease is due
  `-- no Qt/desktop process and no fallback inbox poll
```

### Worker entry points and bindings

| Worker | Entry point | Routes | Scheduled | Storage/services |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `forkmesh-app` | `app/src_build/entry.py` (generated from `app/src/entry.py`) | `app.forkmesh.com` custom domain | `* * * * *` | D1 `DB`, KV `REPOSITORY_METADATA`, Workers AI, eight Durable Object bindings, Static Assets |
| `forkmesh-www` | `www/worker.js` | `forkmesh.com`, `forkmesh.com` | none | Static Assets, `APP` service binding |
| `forkmesh-world` | `world/worker.js` | `world.forkmesh.com` | none | Static Assets, `APP` service binding |

There are no Queue or R2 bindings in the production Wrangler manifests. The
WWW-to-App and World-to-App hops use Service Bindings, not public HTTP. The App
owns the canonical redirect decision for every non-World route delegated by
World. App-owned World shell dependencies use the same binding, so the World
Static Assets upload does not duplicate the App's shared scripts, fonts,
favicons, images, or video.

The App cron packs each minute's due phases into stable batch Durable Objects.
Four phases are due every minute (`status-sample`, alert ping/email, and
`mirror-health`), with snapshot, compaction, installer, repository, and slower
projection phases staggered. Dispatching one object per phase cost a fixed
baseline of roughly 1,440 scheduled App invocations plus at least 5,760 phase
dispatches per day before staggered work; batching collapses the phase
dispatches into as few invocations as their measured subrequest reserves allow,
typically one or two a minute. `/api/accounts/admin-cron-report` reports the
observed cost per tick against the unbatched shape.

### Are mirror domains Workers?

No project configuration routes `mirror*.forkmesh.com` to a Worker. Live HEAD
requests on 2026-08-12 to mirror20, mirror21, and mirror23 returned
`server: cloudflare`, `cf-cache-status: DYNAMIC`, and no
`x-forkmesh-worker` header. Their `/health` bodies identify the
`direct-https` mirror gateway. This is consistent with a proxied Cloudflare
Tunnel terminating at the node, not another ForkMesh Worker invocation.

By contrast, `https://app.forkmesh.com/status` returned
`x-forkmesh-worker: app` and `cf-cache-status: HIT`. Mirror HTTP traffic still
uses Cloudflare's network and Tunnel, but it does not amplify into another
`forkmesh-app`, `forkmesh-www`, or `forkmesh-world` invocation.

## Phase 1 findings

### Highest invocation sources

1. Repeated browser polling: two `/network` polls per visible tab every minute,
   repository mirror fallback polls, and homepage online-count polling.
2. Desktop mirror/catalog/reachability reads routed through App even though the
   desktop already owns the active Host inventory.
3. Legacy Qt mirror publication and collaboration intake alongside the managed
   node, creating duplicate publication and idle inbox traffic.
4. WWW API requests: one WWW invocation plus one App service-binding
   invocation. This remains necessary for requests deliberately made against
   the marketing origin; App clients should use `app.forkmesh.com` directly.
5. The fixed one-minute cron and its Durable Object phases.

### Highest subrequest sources

1. A mirror-backed cache miss previously performed two D1 cursor operations,
   a signed `/health` proof fetch, the repository fetch, and a best-effort D1
   serve-counter write.
2. Mirror failover may try up to four endpoints. It is sequential and stops on
   the first valid response; there is no visitor-path broadcast fan-out.
3. The old mirror collaboration intake polled three inbox kinds every five
   seconds. Its theoretical idle load was 51,840 relay reads/day/node.
4. Deep cron probes read several repository objects. Their routing context and
   failed-endpoint quarantine are request-scoped and reused across the suite.
5. Catalog and health publication formerly came from both Qt and Go.

### Request amplification

| Path | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| App repository cache miss | 1 App invocation + 2 D1 cursor ops + proof fetch + mirror fetch + counter write; failover could repeat proof/fetch up to four times | 1 App invocation + stateless candidate rotation + edge-cached verified proof + normally one mirror fetch + counter write; failover remains bounded at four |
| API request to `forkmesh.com` | 1 WWW invocation + 1 App service-binding invocation | unchanged; this is an internal binding, not public HTTP |
| Desktop Mirrors tab | periodic App catalog/reachability calls plus node probes | zero App calls for saved Hosts; one signed health and one branches GET per active host per five-minute visible-tab refresh |
| Desktop Pulls | App/relay Git read first | saved Host SSH remotes first; App/relay only final fallback |
| Managed collaboration | three five-second inbox polls per node, plus Qt helper process | one socket; one GET + one exact DELETE only for the changed kind |
| Visible `/network` tab | 2 requests/minute = 2,880/day/tab | 2 requests/5 minutes = 576/day/tab, paused while hidden (80% reduction) |
| Open repository Mirrors tab | 288 fallback polls/day/tab | push/reconnect/manual refresh only (100% steady-state reduction) |
| Homepage online count | 288 interval reads/day/tab | initial read and visibility resume behind a five-minute floor |

### Cache and static-asset findings

- App's hashed assets, dashboard chunks, `/status/`, login/signup, network, and
  other listed documents bypass `forkmesh-app` through Static Assets.
- WWW ordinary static pages and immutable assets use Static Assets. Only API,
  protocol, feeds, health, MCP, and the two public-profile dashboard resources
  run the WWW Worker first.
- World static asset paths bypass its Worker; the World shell and redirect
  routes run first because they inject App origin or route product pages.
- Public deterministic status and repository metadata already use
  `caches.default`; repository metadata is content-addressed by attested refs
  and persisted in KV.
- Verified repository proofs now use a 60-second per-colo Cache API entry and a
  bounded isolate memo. The key binds node, public key, owner, repository, and
  accepted refs, so key rotation or state movement cannot reuse an old proof.
- Authenticated responses, writes, private replicas, Actions output, and
  collaboration mutations remain uncached.

### Retry, polling, CPU and error findings

- Mirror fetch timeouts are bounded (6 seconds for control, 20 seconds for
  repository/Git response headers); failover is capped at four.
- Native node socket reconnect uses bounded exponential backoff. Collaboration
  failures are requeued by kind; there is no recursive or idle fallback poll.
- The installer monitor incorrectly carried a request-scoped quarantine from
  a missing optional release CAS object into its source fallback. That made a
  healthy source build read report down. The fallback now starts a fresh
  candidate suite.
- The previous per-request D1 routing cursor was a CPU/network serialization
  hot path. Stateless random rotation removes one D1 read and one D1 write per
  uncached repository request while preserving Git's two-request sticky pin.
- Mirror/network exceptions are converted to bounded 404/503 responses. Native
  intake bounds response bodies, JSON parsing, Git commands, worktrees, and
  HTTP timeouts. No normal failure path intentionally raises past the request
  boundary.
- Historical `uncaught` and CPU-limit counts cannot be attributed one-for-one
  without Cloudflare tail-event samples from that exact period. Post-deploy
  metrics must confirm zero; the primary code-level families (unbounded Qt
  intake, repeated D1 routing work, repeated proof verification, and monitor
  failover exhaustion) are removed or bounded.

## Phase 2 priority plan

### P0 — quota/outage risks (implemented)

1. Remove Qt as a server, publisher, and mirror intake process.

   - Expected impact: eliminates duplicate catalog writes and all idle Qt inbox
     traffic.
   - Risk: medium; ownership moved to native Go and is covered by real Git and
     signed-ack tests.
   - Files affected: `desktop/`, `server/`, `www/public/install.sh`.
   - Behavior change: none for users; the managed node is now the sole server.
   - Estimated request reduction: 100% of legacy desktop publication/intake.

2. Remove per-request D1 routing cursor and edge-cache verified proofs.

   - Expected impact: removes two D1 operations per uncached repository read
     and collapses repeated proof traffic per colo/state generation.
   - Risk: low; endpoint choice remains balanced and clone stickiness remains.
   - Files affected: `app/src/entry.py`.
   - Behavior change: none.
   - Estimated request reduction: 40–60% of mirror-proxy subrequests on typical
     multi-object repository page loads.

3. Fix installer fallback quarantine.

   - Expected impact: source fallback stays green when optional release CAS
     bytes are unavailable.
   - Risk: low; the fallback still performs fresh signed health and refs checks.
   - Files affected: `app/src/entry.py`.
   - Behavior change: removes a false outage only.
   - Estimated request reduction: avoids repeated failing monitor/fallback
     chains and continual outage alert work.

### P1 — major request reduction (implemented)

1. Direct desktop Mirrors and Pulls to active saved Hosts.

   - Expected impact: near-100% App Worker reduction for those views when a
     direct host succeeds.
   - Risk: low/medium; public read route is GET/HEAD-only and private/mutating
     operations remain router-capability protected.
   - Files affected: `desktop/src/MainWindowReleases.cpp`,
     `desktop/src/MainWindowPulls.cpp`, `tools/mirror_gateway.py`.
   - Behavior change: views continue working during a relay outage.
   - Estimated request reduction: 80–100% of desktop relay reads on these tabs.

2. Remove or widen browser polls and pause hidden tabs.

   - Expected impact: 80–100% reduction on the affected page loops.
   - Risk: low; account/repository changes already have push channels and
     reconnect catch-up.
   - Files affected: dashboard modules, `app/public/network.html`, homepage
     documents.
   - Behavior change: none; explicit refresh and push remain immediate.
   - Estimated request reduction: 2,304 requests/day per continuously visible
     network tab, plus eliminated idle homepage/repository-tab requests.

3. Keep active Hosts authoritative for Status.

   - Expected impact: no monitoring work for retired/stale nodes.
   - Risk: low; signed freshness and active-host membership are both required.
   - Files affected: `app/src/entry.py` and status tests.
   - Behavior change: retired mirror17, mirror19, and mirror22 disappear.
   - Estimated request reduction: three retired health targets plus their
     status sampling/history work.

### P2 — follow-up after production measurement

1. Profile cron phase dispatches and consolidate only phases whose CPU and
   replay rules safely fit one invocation. **Implemented** first as the
   `scheduled-batch-v3:*` objects, then (2026-09-13) folded into the
   coordinator's own alarm with alarm continuation, because a coordinator
   waiting on batch objects was billed for every second they worked.

   - Expected impact: up to several thousand Durable Object executions/day.
   - Risk: medium/high; isolation currently prevents one phase from exhausting
     another's CPU/subrequest budget. Mitigated by reserving each phase's
     measured high-water subrequest cost before it is packed, by giving a
     never-measured phase the whole budget so it can only lead a batch, and by
     handing the rest of a claim back to a fresh object the moment a budget is
     spent.
   - Files affected: App cron runner and status scheduling.
   - Behavior change: none intended. Phase order inside the status chain,
     per-phase failure isolation, replay rules and the completion heartbeat are
     reproduced inside the coordinator's tick.
   - Estimated request reduction: measurement-dependent; the observed figure is
     reported per tick by `/api/accounts/admin-cron-report`.

2. Consider serving the two public-profile dashboard assets directly from WWW
   instead of proxying them through WWW -> App.

   - Expected impact: removes one App service invocation for each such asset on
     a `forkmesh.com/@user` visit.
   - Risk: medium; asset fingerprints must stay exactly synchronized.
   - Files affected: WWW/App asset build pipeline and CSP tests.
   - Behavior change: none intended.
   - Estimated request reduction: two App invocations per uncached profile
     asset load.

3. Apply Cloudflare rate-limit/WAF rules only after sampled logs identify
   abusive paths or agents. Reject malformed paths before D1/mirror work.

   - Expected impact: traffic-dependent.
   - Risk: legitimate Git clients and search crawlers must be excluded.
   - Files affected: Cloudflare zone configuration, not application behavior.
   - Behavior change: abusive/malformed traffic only.
   - Estimated request reduction: unknown until bot attribution exists.

### P3 — cleanup

Rename legacy in-memory `catalogMirrors*` desktop members now that they cache a
direct Host fleet, and retire the unused D1 `edge_route_cursor` table in a later
backward-compatible migration. Neither cleanup should block rollout.

## Production verification and projection

After deployment, mirror20, mirror21, mirror23, mirror24, and mirror25 all
returned valid signed `forkmesh/forkmesh` proofs with `integrity=ok`, fourteen
advertised operations, and the same refs digest prefix `1ea332d1021c`. The
native service and direct gateway were rolled out to those five saved Hosts;
each direct branches endpoint returned HTTP 200 with the same 53 branches and
the same `main` commit. The live Status API listed exactly those five mirror
systems as operational; mirror17, mirror19, and mirror22 were absent.

The live installer monitor is operational because the signed installer and its
independently verified source fallback are reachable. The release manifest's
older authenticated prebuilt CAS objects were not republished from this dirty
development worktree: publishing desktop binaries remains intentionally gated
on a clean, exact source commit. Do not describe the new desktop build as
released until it is committed and the release publisher has generated,
signed, and replicated its new CAS objects.

```text
Current observed:
  ~55,000 Worker invocations/day
  ~108,000 subrequests/day

Projected after deployment (traffic-mix dependent):
  ~15,000–25,000 Worker invocations/day
  ~25,000–40,000 subrequests/day

Projected reduction:
  invocations: ~55–73%
  subrequests: ~63–77%
```

The upper end meets the 70% target if the supplied production traffic is, as
the code paths suggest, dominated by the removed polling and mirror-proxy work.
Confirm with a 24-hour before/after comparison split by route, cache hit/miss,
selected mirror, retry count, upstream duration, and failure reason. Do not
treat a plan upgrade as the fix; it is only optional operational headroom.

pages.title: Community reward pool
pages.description: ForkMesh's reward system is non-custodial. Production coordinates public Solana mainnet-beta state and unsigned transfer intents; it does not create, accept, store, decrypt, or…
pages.markdown:
# Community reward pool

ForkMesh's reward system is non-custodial. Production coordinates public Solana
mainnet-beta state and unsigned transfer intents; it does not create, accept, store,
decrypt, or use a wallet private key in the Cloudflare Worker or D1.

## Custody boundaries

- A contributor signs a direct transfer from their own self-custodial wallet
  to the configured public reward destination. New deployments may name it
  `COMMUNITY_REWARD_POOL_ADDRESS`; existing one-click deployments may keep
  supplying the same public address as `TREASURY_SOLANA_ADDRESS`.
- The public pool private key is imported only into the first instance owner's
  local Qt client. It must use that client's encrypted local vault/keychain
  boundary.
- D1 stores public pool addresses, public Solana Pay references, eligibility
  snapshots, unsigned transfer plans, transaction signatures, and status.
- The Qt client must show and validate every source, destination, amount,
  network, and expiry before explicit owner approval.
- The Worker independently retrieves the finalized transaction and requires
  its exact System Program transfer list to match the approved intent.
- A node operator supplies only a public payout address. ForkMesh never asks
  for a node operator's seed, recovery phrase, or private key.

User-owned funds, community-pool funds, pending rewards, and completed
on-chain transfers are separate states in the APIs and interfaces. Community
incentives are voluntary and are not investments or guaranteed returns.

## Configuration

Production configuration:

```text
COMMUNITY_REWARD_NETWORK=mainnet-beta
COMMUNITY_REWARD_RPC_URL=https://api.mainnet-beta.solana.com
# Existing ForkMesh/one-click deployment name:
TREASURY_SOLANA_ADDRESS=<existing public mainnet address>
# Optional explicit modern override:
COMMUNITY_REWARD_POOL_ADDRESS=<same or replacement public mainnet address>
REWARD_SIGNER_ACCOUNT=<instance owner account>
REWARD_INTERVAL_MS=3600000
REWARD_JITTER_MAX_MS=2700000
REWARD_AMOUNT_LAMPORTS=100000
REWARD_MIN_UPTIME_MS=1800000
REWARD_MIN_CONTRIBUTION_UNITS=0
REWARD_HEALTH_FRESH_MS=600000
```

`COMMUNITY_REWARD_POOL_ADDRESS` has priority when it is non-empty.
`TREASURY_SOLANA_ADDRESS` remains a supported compatibility fallback, so an
existing instance does not lose its configured reward destination. If the
explicit modern value is non-empty but invalid, ForkMesh fails closed instead
of silently falling back to another address. Both variables contain only a
public Solana address. A seed, recovery phrase, private key, or signed
transaction must never be placed in either variable.

The Worker refuses to expose or schedule the pool unless the network is known,
the RPC is credential-free HTTPS, `getGenesisHash` matches that exact cluster,
and `getAccountInfo` proves the configured public pool account exists there.
Known canonical RPC/cluster mismatches fail before any request. The Worker
still never signs or broadcasts. Devnet remains available only through an
explicit development configuration; it is never a production fallback.

## Voluntary contribution choices

`POST /api/rewards/contributions` with `action=prepare` creates a bounded,
one-hour public intent. The response is a reference-bound Solana Pay URI:

- `trickle` leaves the finalized contribution in the public pool for
  configurable randomized rounds.
- `instant_all_nodes` creates an unsigned, equal all-eligible-node plan after
  the incoming transfer is finalized. Size-safe batches contain at most eight
  System transfers per transaction, so every eligible node remains included
  without exceeding the legacy Solana message limit. A small explicit
  remainder covers one network fee per batch chunk and integer division.

Confirmation requires the intent ID and the public transaction signature. The
Worker checks finality, the unique reference account, exact destination, exact
amount, source address validity, replay protection, and an ordinary System
Program transfer. No outgoing plan is created while finality is unknown.

The product may describe this action as joining or funding the reward program.
It is voluntary community support, not the purchase of equity, a tokenized
ownership interest, an investment contract, or a promise of profit. Preparing
the request does not move funds: the contributor reviews and signs the direct
transfer in their own wallet, and ForkMesh never signs that incoming transfer.

## Randomized mirror rewards

Every configured interval the Worker records a public round and a reproducible
jitter offset. At execution it freezes a fresh eligibility snapshot and selects
one candidate with SHA-256 modulo using a finalized Solana blockhash. The
intent includes:

- the full accepted snapshot and its hash;
- generalized rejection reasons;
- the public blockhash and entropy source;
- the selection algorithm and selected index;
- the selected public node and payout address;
- the configured amount and expiry.

Eligibility requires all of the following:

- a fresh signed node heartbeat;
- a fresh healthy direct HTTPS endpoint;
- signed node identity registration;
- an independently challenged `forkmesh/forkmesh` refs proof matching the
  configured integrity pin;
- a valid public self-custodial payout address;
- minimum server-observed continuous uptime; and
- the optional minimum contribution-unit threshold.

Approved federated relays use the same frozen snapshot for both randomized and
`instant_all_nodes` plans. A relay may not submit a wallet-only presence claim.
It must forward the node's original signed HTTPS registration and exact
node-signed, nonce-bound `forkmesh/forkmesh` repository-health message. The
main relay independently verifies both signatures, freshness, the current refs
digest, integrity, required-operation claim, relay approval, and
its own consecutive-observation history before the row can be eligible.
Migration 0057 deletes all pre-attestation federated presence rows.
The approved relay remains a disclosed, revocable trust boundary for whether
the remote network challenge was actually performed; its approval is not proof
of personhood or universal node trust. Remove relay approval to exclude its
forwarded nodes from future snapshots.

The policy de-duplicates node identity, operator identity, device public key,
and wallet. Signup throttles, signed device identity, external health checks,
server-observed uptime, integrity proofs, and those
de-duplication gates raise the cost of fake nodes, repeated accounts,
artificial uptime, wallet farming, and reward manipulation. They reduce but do
not eliminate Sybil risk; the public policy says so explicitly.

## Pending walletless rewards

The configured instance owner may create a signed pending allocation through
`POST /api/rewards/pending-awards`. It is metadata only:

- no wallet is created;
- no funds move out of the external pool;
- only an active recipient without a payout wallet is eligible;
- the allocation expires exactly 24 hours after creation;
- the recipient may submit only a public address through
  `POST /api/rewards/pending`; and
- expiry releases the reservation while funds remain at the source.

After an address is supplied, a separate unsigned intent enters the same local
signer and finalized-transaction verification flow.

## Public inspection

`GET /api/rewards/pool` and the World fountain display:

- network, public address, explorer link, and live public balance;
- randomized timing/amount configuration;
- contribution modes;
- recent finalized incoming contributions;
- recent finalized recipient transfers; and
- explicit fund-state and non-custodial notices.

The 3D fountain's light and coin particles are illustrative. Only a finalized
transaction signature linked to the configured cluster is an on-chain event.

`GET /api/accounts/central-fund` remains a compatibility alias for that same
canonical public payload, including its non-custodial notice and four explicit
fund states. It never reads the historical encrypted `central_fund` row.

`GET /api/accounts/treasury-address` and the relay-to-relay
`/api/federation/treasury-address` alias are retired. They return HTTP 410,
an empty address, and migration-only guidance instead of exposing an
operational legacy custodial deposit target. This does not remove
`TREASURY_SOLANA_ADDRESS`: that deployment variable remains a public-address-only
compatibility input for the non-custodial community reward pool described
above. Historical treasury, signup-deposit, bounty, and central-fund keys are
handled only by
`www/docs/operations/legacy-solana-custody-migration.md`.

pages.title: Community reward-pool local signer
