pages.markdown:
# Mirror node service

`forkmesh-mirror-node` is the small, headless runtime for public mirror hosts.
It replaces Git synchronization, gateway configuration, gateway/tunnel process
supervision, signed health/capability helpers, catalog publication, telemetry,
and local readiness reporting that previously ran inside the Qt event loop.

The service binds its operator API to loopback only:

- `GET /healthz` reports that the daemon event loop is alive;
- `GET /readyz` requires a running gateway and a recent successful sync; and
- `GET /v1/status` returns bounded, secret-free process, restart, sync, and
  repository-ref state.

The gateway stays on `127.0.0.1:8790` behind an operator-managed HTTPS reverse
proxy. Set `disableCloudflared` when that public origin is independently
reachable; otherwise the daemon continues to supervise Cloudflare Tunnel as a
fallback. An optional `mirrorUrl` advertises a separate direct Git origin while
`publicOrigin` remains the Tunnel control endpoint. The daemon reuses the
existing owner-only Ed25519 identity and, when enabled, connector token; it
never accepts either value in argv, JSON, an HTTP request, or a catalog record.
Its two gateway helper modes accept only the bounded ForkMesh health and masked
proxy protocols on stdin.

The daemon holds one WebSocket to the relay's
per-owner node event channel (`wss://…/api/nodes/events`, the ForkMeshNodes
Durable Object) authenticated with the node's own Ed25519 identity. The relay
pushes a payload-free `{"type":"event","topic","repo"}` frame the instant an
issue, pull, or discussion submission lands. The Go daemon leases only that
changed inbox, writes the repository-native record in a temporary Git worktree,
commits it, and acknowledges the exact durable row with a signed refs
attestation. There is **no** polling, fallback poll, desktop binary, or GUI
process in this path. Missed pushes are covered by the socket itself: every
reconnect fires one catch-up wake that drains whatever queued while the channel
was down.

Repository sync rides the same channel: the relay pushes a `commits` event
when a source node publishes changed public heads or tags, and the daemon
fetches on that push (plus one catch-up per reconnect). The event carries the
source's signed refs digest, so a successful fetch from a stale round-robin
peer is retried on a 2s→15s backoff until the advertised generation lands.
The source desktop also pushes every changed head and tag in the canonical
`forkmesh/forkmesh` working copy directly to each saved, installed managed
host, even when that host has no working-copy Git remote. A service-owned
`post-receive` hook rings the daemon's loopback-only `POST /v1/control/sync`
doorbell as soon as Git makes those refs durable; the desktop sends the same
authenticated wake explicitly for older installed daemons. An all-up-to-date
safety pass sends no wake, so this path remains change-driven.
Because notification fan-out is best-effort, an all-relay node also reconciles
once every 30 minutes; this bounds a completely lost live event without turning
the recovery path back into the fleet's normal workload.
Bootstrap records each exact managed peer URL in `eventDrivenUpstreams`, so a
direct `mirrorN` peer is treated like every other WebSocket-notified source
instead of falling back to the legacy 15-second external-upstream poll.
Third-party upstreams that cannot push and nodes with the catalog disabled
still use `syncInterval` directly. A
four-minute heartbeat cycle republishes the catalog record and renews the HTTPS
endpoint lease from local refs reads. The signed endpoint proof rides the
already-open node event WebSocket and uses HTTPS only when the socket or relay
does not advertise that frame.
If a tunnel health challenge is temporarily pending, its bounded retry repeats
only this local-state/lease publication. It does not fetch upstream Git data,
check web fork jobs, or consume queued collaboration work.

## Owner-authorized web merges

Every served public repository also advertises the gateway's `merge-preview`,
`merge-pull`, and `update-pull-branch` operations. The daemon upgrades an
existing gateway configuration in place at startup and points the gateway's
`mergeExecutorCommand` at this same binary
(`forkmesh-mirror-node --config … --execute-mirror-merge`). When an
organization owner merges a pull request on the web, the relay authenticates
the owner, signs the exact-OID request, and hands it to one healthy mirror;
the executor verifies the pinned pull record on the `forkmesh/pulls` ledger,
the current base branch tip, and (for a branch-backed pull) the current head
tip, enforces the same independent peer-review gate as the desktop (a
repository owner may waive it with `overrideReview`) and any
`.forkmesh/required-checks.json` policy on the base commit, and then moves the
base branch, the ledger and the pull's `forkmesh/pull/<n>` metadata branch in
one atomic `update-ref` transaction.
A patch-backed pull (a web or cross-node submission whose reviewed commits
travel as `commits.mbox` / `changes.patch` in the ledger) is replayed onto the
exact base tip in a temporary detached worktree, so the contributor's
authorship is preserved.

The result carries a fresh node-signed attestation of the refs the mirror
serves afterwards. The relay verifies it against the mirror's registered
endpoint key, admits that state into the repository's pin history, treats it
as the repository's *current* generation while the source-of-truth record is
unchanged (the source is typically offline), and pushes a `commits` event
naming that digest so every other mirror keeps fetching through the relay
route until the merge lands on it. The source desktop converges from the mesh
(fast-forward only) when it reconnects and its next publish supersedes the
override automatically. Nothing in this path rewinds a ref: a stale base,
head, or ledger pin fails closed and the owner reloads the pull.

Idempotency results and the temporary merge worktree live beside the gateway
configuration under `mirror-gateway/pull-jobs/` (owner-only). Set
`"disableMergeExecutor": true` in `mirror-node.json` to keep a node strictly
read-only; the gateway then advertises no write capability and the relay never
selects that node for a merge.

## Operator storage and legal-response policy

Operators who want to limit what their node stores and serves, and handle
reports, quarantines, appeals and removals, add an `operatorPolicy` entry to
the gateway configuration. See the
[node operator policy guide](node-operator-policy.md). The policy is local to
this node: anything it refuses stays available from other mirrors.

## Signing the agent CLIs in from the website

A node that finds `claude` or `codex` on its PATH advertises those providers in
its catalog record, which is what puts it in the website's "Run on" list. Those
CLIs still have to be signed in, and until now the only way to do that on a
headless mirror was an SSH shell opened from the ForkMesh desktop app — the
website's "Sign in to Claude Code on <node>" button was a `forkmesh://` link
that the browser handed to the operating system, so on any machine without
that app installed it resolved to nothing at all.

The owner's browser now streams the sign-in from the node itself. Both ends
hold a WebSocket to one per-owner relay object — this daemon with its signed
drain token, the browser with a short-lived account event ticket — and the
relay forwards the terminal frames between them without keeping a copy of
anything. Which object that is depends on the node: a managed mirror is its
own node account and opens the socket under that name, while a desktop node
opens it under the person's account and calls itself by its machine name. So
the browser names the machine it wants when it connects, and the relay — after
checking that the account owns it — joins the tab to whichever of the two
objects that machine is actually attached to. The daemon runs the provider's
own login command (`claude auth login`, `codex login`) on a pseudo-terminal as
its own service account, so the credential lands in `/var/lib/forkmesh` where
the agent CLIs look for it. Only that one command can be started: no argument
comes from the frame, there is no shell, and the browser chooses nothing but
the provider.
One session runs at a time and ends when the browser closes it, when the
command exits, or after thirty minutes.

Set `"disableAgentLogin": true` in `mirror-node.json` to refuse these sessions;
the SSH path from the desktop app then remains the only way in.

The unit ships with `MemoryDenyWriteExecute=false` for this reason alone: the
provider CLIs are V8 programs whose JIT maps executable pages and will not
start under that restriction. Every other confinement in the unit still applies
to the sign-in — no new privileges, an empty capability set, a read-only system
outside `/var/lib/forkmesh`, and a private `/dev` and `/tmp`.

## Running website agent jobs

A node that advertises a provider also runs the agent sessions the website
queues for it; the ForkMesh desktop app is not required. To offer Gemma, install
[Ollama](https://ollama.com/download) next to the Codex CLI: the node then
advertises `local-llama` and runs Gemma 4 through `codex exec --oss`. Pull the
models you want to serve ahead of time (`ollama pull gemma4:e4b`) so the first
run does not spend its time downloading. The relay rings the
node's event socket with an `org-agents` push, and the daemon claims the job
over the same signed `org-agent-jobs` lease the desktop uses, signing with the
node key its owner claimed. A five-minute safety read covers a push lost while
the node was offline.

For each job the daemon:

- rejects any envelope outside the desktop's rules: provider `claude-code`,
  `codex` or `local-llama` (Gemma), a model from the website allowlist (`agentWebsiteModels` in
  `server/agents.go`), a prompt of at most 8,000 characters, a kind of
  `start`, `continue` or `steer`, valid image attachments, and a job addressed
  to this node and repository;
- downloads any images attached to the prompt (at most five, 5 MiB each) over
  the job's signed lease, checks size, digest and magic bytes, and writes them
  into the working tree as `.forkmesh/attachments/<uuid>.<ext>`, which is
  excluded from commits (`server/agent_attachments.go`). A job whose images
  cannot be fetched fails instead of running without them;
- clones the repository into `mirror-gateway/agent-jobs/work/` and runs
  `claude -p --output-format stream-json --verbose
  --dangerously-skip-permissions` (or `codex -a never exec --sandbox
  danger-full-access`; `workspace-write` would also block the loopback
  sockets a test server needs) on a new `agent/web-<job>-<title>` branch. The
  agent never works inside the served repository and never touches `main`;
- pushes the finished branch back as one ref update, opens a node-signed pull
  when the session asked for one, and reports running, then completed or
  failed, with the transcript, token counts and cost.

There is no model safety preflight any more. `agentOwner` is still accepted in
`mirror-node.json` so older configurations keep parsing, but nothing reads it.

A run is bounded to two hours. A `continue` job (a session moved from a
desktop with **To cloud**) waits up to ten minutes for the moved branch to
reach this node, asking for a sync every 15 seconds, before it fails.

### What a failed run reports

A failed run reports one `lastError`; clients show it next to the transcript,
and it is no longer appended to the transcript as well. `server/agent_errors.go`
picks it, in order, from the Claude result event's `errors`/`result` text, an
API-error assistant message, the last non-empty lines of stderr, and only then
"Claude Code exited with status N". It is capped at 600 characters, and the
stream-json init event is never quoted. Codex gets the same stderr-tail order.

When the provider refuses the model because the host's CLI is too old ("does
not support this model; version X or newer is required", or Codex's "requires
a newer version of Codex"), the error reads "Claude Code on <node> is <ver>;
<model> needs <X> or newer. Update the host (Hosts → Update)." The runner then
remembers the refused version per provider and model, in memory; the next run
for that model checks `claude --version` (or `codex --version`) and fails at
once with the same message until the CLI has moved past it. An outdated CLI is
not retried with a fresh conversation, because the binary would be the same.

### Keeping the agent CLIs current

The service runs as `forkmesh-node` and cannot update the root-owned copies in
`/usr/local/bin`. The desktop does it: every host update pipeline (the per-host
**Update** in Hosts, **Install (binary)**, the fleet runs, and the verified
native mirror-node update) ends, after a successful update, with a root-only,
never-fatal refresh of each CLI already present in `/usr/local/bin`. It runs
the official installer, installs the new binary as `/usr/local/bin/<name>.new`
and renames it over the old one, so a running job keeps the binary it opened.
The update's own exit status is what the command returns. The script is
`agentCliServiceRefreshScript()` in `desktop/src/ControlNode.cpp`.

Every session the website queued appears in the ForkMesh desktop's Agents list
for the repository's owner, marked with a cloud on the row's avatar — the ones
a node is running, and the ones still waiting for a node, including work queued
for that desktop itself while it was closed. The Cloud
control in the list's toolbar narrows the list to cloud runs or to the
desktop's own sessions, and searching for a node's name finds its runs.
Opening one shows its conversation, branch and pull request; typing under it
queues a follow-up for the node, and the row's trash button deletes the session
from the relay (a run already in flight on the node is not interrupted). A
desktop that signed in with its account key rather than a password reads and
steers these sessions with a key-signed `user`/`ts`/`sig` request; each
operation has its own proof (`forkmesh-owner-agent-list-v1`, `-read-v1`,
`-prompt-v1`, `-delete-v1`) bound to the exact path, and a follow-up's proof
also binds the SHA-256 of its prompt. Queueing new work is not key-signable.

The other direction starts on the desktop: right-click a session in the Agents
list and choose **Continue in the cloud** (or press **To cloud** in the
session's header). The desktop commits the session's worktree, publishes its
branch to the served mirror, queues the continuation for the account's other
nodes and stops running it locally; the session then shows up on the website
and in the list as a cloud run. Only Claude Code and Codex sessions on a
published repository the desktop can sign for can move; for any other row the
menu entry is disabled and its tooltip says why.

A run that is still waiting can go the other way at any time: right-click it
and choose **Continue on this desktop** (or press **Continue here** in its
header). The desktop asks the relay for that session by name — `POST
/api/repo/{owner}/{repo}/agent-sessions/{id}/claim`, signed with the same node
proof the job queue answers to — and the relay hands over the same lease the
periodic drain would have given it, re-targeting the job and the session at
that node. The run then starts, reports and opens its pull request exactly as
it would have on the mirror, and the list shows it once, as a local session.
This is the answer to a job the chosen mirror never picked up: the claim works
whichever of the account's nodes it was queued for, but only while no node has
started it — once one has, the conversation lives there and a follow-up is the
way to reach it. A desktop that cannot run it (no checkout of the repository,
no provider CLI, no signing key for the account) says so and leaves the run
queued rather than claiming a job it would only fail.

Set `"disableAgentJobs": true` in `mirror-node.json` to refuse these jobs. The
node then stops advertising its providers, so the website no longer offers it as
an agent target.

## Host hardening and logs

New Vultr mirrors installed from the desktop get these at install time
(`desktop/src/MainWindowHostInstall.cpp` carries the same lines inline, so
change both copies together):

- **Key-only SSH.** `server/packaging/ssh/10-forkmesh-hardening.conf` goes to
  `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/`: no password or keyboard-interactive logins, root
  by key only, `MaxAuthTries 3`, `LoginGraceTime 20`. It is applied only when
  root has an authorized key and `sshd -t` accepts it. For an existing host,
  run `tools/harden_mirror_sshd.sh <host-ip>...`; it also proves a fresh key
  login works and a password login is refused afterwards.
- **fail2ban.** `server/packaging/fail2ban/forkmesh-sshd.local` enables the
  `sshd` jail in aggressive mode, reading the systemd journal (Debian 13 has no
  `auth.log`): 5 failures in 10 minutes bans for 1 hour, growing up to a week
  for repeat offenders. For an existing host, run
  `tools/mirror_fail2ban.sh <host-ip>...` after the sshd hardening.
- **Host logs over HTTP/3.** The gateway serves the host's journal as
  server-sent events at `GET /v1/node/logs` to Ed25519 viewer keys listed in
  `/etc/forkmesh/log-viewer-keys` (one single-use signed request,
  `forkmesh-node-logs-v1`, 60-second window; see `tools/mirror_gateway.py`).
  Caddy serves it on HTTP/3, so the installer opens 443/udp and lists the
  deploying desktop's key; the unit joins `systemd-journal` to read it. The
  desktop reads it with its own QUIC client (`desktop/src/Http3Get.cpp`) and
  falls back to SSH when a host has no endpoint.

## Build and test

```sh
cd server
go test -race -cover ./...
CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -ldflags='-s -w' \
  -o forkmesh-mirror-node ./cmd/forkmesh-mirror-node
```

## Desktop companion

Vultr/host deploys upload the deploying desktop's own local
`forkmesh-mirror-node`, looked up in `PATH`, beside the running executable,
beside the installed client (`~/.local/bin/forkmesh`), then in the source
checkout. The desktop installer (`desktop/install.sh`), the public release
installer, and both in-app update flows (the source rebuild and the prebuilt
auto-update) install or refresh the companion beside the client. A desktop
whose Vultr install fails with "The Go mirror-node package is incomplete
(forkmesh-mirror-node is missing)" therefore heals by running Update & restart
(with a Go toolchain available for source installs) or by reinstalling a
release that publishes the `forkmesh-mirror-node-<os>-<arch>` asset.

Use `server/packaging/systemd/mirror-node.json.example` as the configuration template.
Every upstream list may contain multiple URLs; the daemon tries them in order,
and the public ForkMesh URL itself routes across the currently healthy mirror
set rather than pinning mirror2.

For a tunnel-free bootstrap, pass `--disable-cloudflared` with the public HTTPS
origin. The service writes a signed direct-origin manifest and advertises
`https://<origin>/<owner>/<repository>.git`. A stable ForkMesh clone URL remains
the repository identity and redirects only while this direct URL passes the
same signed refs and operation proof. When a Tunnel endpoint is also configured,
its existing masked proxy path remains the fallback.

To retain the Tunnel while advertising a separate public Git origin, set
`mirrorUrl` in the service configuration (or pass `--mirror-url` at bootstrap)
and route that HTTPS hostname to the same loopback gateway.

## Independent dashboard, SSH writes, and forks

A mirror on its own subdomain (for example `mirror33.forkmesh.com`) can run a
fully independent public Git service — website, SSH push, PR submission, and
forking — that keeps working even when the control-plane Worker is unreachable.
See [direct-https-mirror-gateway.md](direct-https-mirror-gateway.md#independent-mirror-operation)
for the gateway `dashboard` block, the SSH `localAuthorization` broker mode, and
the fork registry. Fresh native ForkMesh bootstraps enable this dashboard by
default when their catalog uses a credential-free HTTPS origin. Existing nodes
can set `dashboard.replicaPath` to retain the controller's last
validated public status/network projections locally; the daemon refreshes the
bundle after normal repository synchronization and retains it through an
outage. Repository identity is unchanged: the dashboard, SSH origin, and mirror
URLs are all replaceable, discoverable metadata layered over the same canonical
repositories. D1 account rows, password hashes, and controller bearer tokens
are never replicated. A controller login issues a separate signed,
expiry-bounded portable browser grant containing only an opaque account/session
identity and public username; direct mirrors verify it with the router public
key so the same browser remains signed in during a controller outage. Breakout
repository management uses a minimal signed SQLite authorization projection
containing only enrolled public authentication keys, repository roles, and
revocation generations; successful key proof mints a short node-local session.

## Backup, recovery, and preflight

`--preflight` checks a node without changing it: configuration, identity,
compatibility, disk space, and whether backups and drills are recent.
`--backup`, `--restore-drill`, and `--restore` handle encrypted whole-node
backups. `--export-identity` and `--import-identity` move the node key. See
[node backup, recovery, and key moves](node-backup-and-recovery.md).

## Rolling migration

1. Install the binary, configuration, and unit without stopping the old node.
2. Run `forkmesh-mirror-node --config ... --check` and
   `forkmesh-mirror-node --config ... --preflight` as `forkmesh-node`.
3. Start `forkmesh-mirror-node` and confirm `/readyz`.
4. Remove any retired `forkmesh-node` or `forkmesh-qt-intake` compatibility
   unit; the Go daemon owns serving and native collaboration intake.
5. Confirm signed external health, one pushed collaboration submission, and one clone before
   moving to the next host.

Keep the prior unit and binaries as rollback artifacts until the whole fleet has
passed reachability checks.

## A new mirror that never publishes

`journalctl -u forkmesh-mirror-node` shows the whole failure chain when a fresh
node stays invisible. A first clone that drops mid-pack ("fetch-pack: unexpected
disconnect", "early EOF") leaves `/var/lib/forkmesh/repositories` empty, and the
rest follows from that: the gateway exits every five seconds with "enabled
public repository requires integrity.expectedRefsSha256" because it will not
serve a repository whose refs it cannot read, and each cycle reports "read
stable refs: exit status 128" and "repository head or state hash unavailable".
The daemon now retries that clone on 15s→5m backoff until one lands; restarting
the service forces an immediate attempt.

pages.markdown:
# Mobile push notifications (APNs)

The iOS app is woken by Apple Push Notification service when iOS has
suspended or killed it, which is the one case the account event socket cannot
cover. Everything else about account events stays as documented in
[polling elimination](polling-elimination.md): a write that moves an unread
count calls `notify_account_event`, which fans a payload-free frame to the
owner's `ForkMeshNodes` Durable Object and, for the topics below, one
payload-free alert to every phone registered for that account.

There is no Firebase and no third-party push provider. The Worker signs its
own APNs provider token and posts to Apple directly (`app/src/apns.py`). On
the phone, the iOS app uses
`native/ios/ForkMesh/Platform/ApplePushBridge.swift` and the extension
`native/ios/NotificationService`. The extension adds the portrait and badge.

## What Apple sees

Every alert names its event; there is no generic "New activity" banner, and a
push with nothing specific to say is not sent at all. A ping carries its
headline, repository, actor and body. A direct message names its sender and a
channel message its channel; their text is sealed end to end, so the body says
it is encrypted instead. The push test says it is a test. Device tokens are
stored like every other sensitive value: the row key is a blind index of the
token and the token itself is encrypted in `data`.

## What the user sees

The Worker renders a ping's alert from the notification row it just wrote
(`_apns_ping_alert` → `_push_alert_item` in `app/src/entry.py`), so the banner
reads right even if nothing on the phone runs:

| Line | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| Title | The record and its headline — `#42 Issue submitted`. |
| Subtitle | `owner/repo · by actor`, with the organization's public name when an alias fronts the repository. |
| Body | The notification body in full, up to 900 characters. |
| Image | The actor's avatar, as an attachment thumbnail (added on the phone). |
| Badge | The account's unread count (added on the phone). |

Banners are grouped per repository (`thread-id`). Every alert sets
`mutable-content`, so iOS runs the bundled notification service extension
before drawing the banner; it reads `GET /api/push/alert` with the signed-in
session and, for the row the push names (`alertId`), adds the actor's portrait
and the unread badge — neither fits Apple's 4 KB payload. If that read fails,
the banner keeps the text the Worker sent.

That route is the alert inbox rendered for a lock screen: unread rows only,
newest first, behind the same gate as `GET /api/notifications` — a session
bearer token or an account-key signature, for the caller's own account only.
Composition lives in `push_alert_handler` / `_push_alert_item` in
`app/src/entry.py`, on the same helpers the digest email uses, so a phone, an
inbox row and a digest describe one event identically.

The session travels between the app and the extension through the keychain
group `$(AppIdentifierPrefix)com.forkmesh.forkmesh`, which both targets'
entitlements list. Two things about that are load-bearing:

* The **Keychain Sharing** capability must be enabled for both App IDs
  (`com.forkmesh.forkmesh` and `com.forkmesh.forkmesh.NotificationService`)
  in Apple Developer → Identifiers, or the extension reads an empty keychain
  and every banner silently stays generic.
* The item is stored `AfterFirstUnlock`, because the common case for a push
  is a phone sitting locked; `WhenUnlocked` would fail those reads.

The app writes it on every successful device registration and clears it on
sign-out. Anything that stops the read — signed out, offline inside the
extension, an older build with no extension — falls back to the generic alert
above rather than to no banner.

Chat and direct messages are the exception: the relay stores ciphertext and
can describe a message no better than Apple can, so it does not ask the relay
for text. Those alerts name their topic beside `aps` and carry the relay `ref`
and `keyVersion` of the stored ciphertext (plus `channelId` for a channel).
The notification service extension fetches that ciphertext from a read-only
route and decrypts it on the phone, the way Signal does; when it cannot, the
banner stays "Direct message from alice" / "New message in #design" with an
"End-to-end encrypted" body. See
[docs/app/chat-push-previews.md](../../../docs/app/chat-push-previews.md).

Topics that wake a phone (`APNS_PUSH_TOPICS` in `app/src/apns.py`): `pings`
(the alert inbox), `code-push`, `direct-messages`, and `chat` (a message in a
channel or public room). `catalog` and `issues` are UI freshness hints and
never buzz: an issue event the user should hear about raises a ping of its
own, and that ping carries the text.

`code-push` is a ping (kind `code_push`, raised by `notify_code_push` in
`app/src/entry.py`) sent under its own topic so the phone can tell a push
banner from an inbox one. Every observed push raises it: an owner-signed
catalog publication whose refs moved, or a receive-pack to a hosted
repository. It reads "Pushed to owner/repo" and links to
`/owner/repo/commits/<branch>`. Recipients are the hosting account and
organization members with read access or better; an identified pusher who is
not the owner is skipped. A storm guard allows one banner per recipient per
repository branch per 60 seconds; later pushes fold into the unread ping
without buzzing. The **Code pushes** ping setting (default on) turns it off.

Every ping is its own alert. The socket frame only means "re-read your inbox",
so frames for one account coalesce inside a two-second window; the APNs alert
for `pings` and `code-push` deliberately does not, and carries no collapse id,
so two pings are two notifications. Since 2026-10-13 `direct-messages` is
not coalesced or collapsed either: each message shows its own text, so each
is its own banner, grouped per conversation by `thread-id`. `chat` still
collapses on the phone and is still limited to one push per room every two
seconds.

Every payload carries `origin` (the Worker's `APP_ORIGIN`) beside the topic,
`alertId` and `href`, so a phone signed in to several ForkMesh projects (for
example production and ForkMesh Next) routes the tap to the right one.

## Chat messages

The relay only ever sees ciphertext, so it cannot tell a message from a
retained edit, a reaction, or the key advertisement a desktop sends on every
connect. The sender says so instead: a client sets a plaintext `notify: true`
on the envelope of a `chat` or `thread-reply` frame, and `ForkMeshRoom` wakes
phones for retained frames that carry it and for nothing else. A client that
predates the field still chats normally; its messages just do not buzz anyone.

The audience comes from the room, not the message:

| Room | Who is woken |
| --- | --- |
| Direct message | The other participant (`direct-messages`). |
| Private channel | Its creator and members, minus the sender. |
| Public channel | Every registered phone, minus the sender. |
| Public room (`world-general`, repository rooms) | Every registered phone. |

A public room's socket is anonymous, so the relay cannot leave the sender's
own phone out. The alert for room chat therefore carries `"topic": "chat"`
beside `aps` (a direct message carries `"topic": "direct-messages"` the same
way), and the app does not present chat while it is in the foreground, where
the live socket has already shown the message. At most 32 phones are
contacted per message, from a device list cached for a minute per isolate.

## Secrets the Worker needs

`push_account_apns` is a silent no-op unless all three are set on the App
Worker. `./deploy.sh app` and `./deploy.sh secrets` refuse to run without
them; the deploying control node writes them into `app/.env.production`.

| Secret | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `APNS_AUTH_KEY` | The `.p8` key downloaded from Apple Developer → Certificates, Identifiers & Profiles → Keys, created with the Apple Push Notifications service enabled. Paste it with its `-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----` armour; literal `\n` sequences are accepted. Apple lets you download it exactly once. |  <!-- forkmesh-secret-scan:ignore-line -->
| `APNS_KEY_ID` | The ten-character Key ID shown next to that key. |
| `APNS_TEAM_ID` | The ten-character Team ID of the developer account (`742ZANCB57` for the store build). |

The App ID `com.forkmesh.forkmesh` must have the Push Notifications
capability, and the key must belong to the same team. A key that imports but
does not match the key id answers `InvalidProviderToken`; a key from another
team answers `DeviceTokenNotForTopic`.

## Sandbox versus production

Apple runs two gateways, and a token is only valid against the one that
minted it. Sending to the wrong one is a hard `400 BadDeviceToken`, after which
the Worker prunes the token and the phone re-registers on its next launch.

| Build | Entitlement | Gateway the token belongs to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Debug or Profile on a device | `aps-environment = development` | `api.sandbox.push.apple.com` |
| Simulator (Apple silicon, iOS 16+) | none embedded | `api.sandbox.push.apple.com` |
| Release, TestFlight, App Store | `aps-environment = production` | `api.push.apple.com` |

The app reports the environment with its token (`environment` in the
`register-device` body) and the Worker routes each token to the matching
gateway, so both kinds can be registered for one account at the same time.

## Proving it works

Settings → Notifications on the phone shows each link of the chain
(permission, token and gateway, relay credentials) and has **Send test
notification**, which calls `POST /api/accounts/push-test` with the session
and shows the result. The same route can be called by hand:

```bash
curl -s -X POST https://app.forkmesh.com/api/accounts/push-test \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $SESSION_TOKEN" -H "User-Agent: ForkMeshMCP/0.1"
```

It answers with `configured`, `devices`, `delivered`, and one `results` entry
per registered device carrying Apple's status and reason. It sends a fixed
"ForkMesh test notification" alert, is limited to one call per account every ten
seconds, and is bound to the session's account exactly like registration.

A real ping that arrives with its text but without the actor's portrait
means the push chain is fine and the extension's read is not: check that the
build embeds the extension, that Keychain Sharing is on for both App IDs, and
that `GET /api/push/alert` answers 200 for the session.

| Answer | Meaning | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `configured: false`, `configProblem: missing_secrets` | One of the three secrets is missing on the Worker. | Set them and redeploy. |
| `configured: false`, `configProblem: key_id_malformed` or `team_id_malformed` | `APNS_KEY_ID` or `APNS_TEAM_ID` is not ten characters of `A-Z0-9`. Apple would refuse every push with `403 InvalidProviderToken`, so the Worker does not try. `./deploy.sh secrets` prints a warning for the same condition. | Copy the Key ID from Apple Developer → Keys (it is also the `XXXXXXXXXX` in the downloaded `AuthKey_XXXXXXXXXX.p8` file name) and the Team ID from Membership details, then run `./deploy.sh secrets`. |
| `devices: 0` | The phone never registered a token. | Allow notifications on the phone, or sign in again; the settings card shows why registration stopped. |
| `status: 400`, `reason: BadDeviceToken` | The token belongs to the other gateway. | Rare after the Simulator fix; reopen the app so it re-registers with the right environment. |
| `status: 400`, `reason: DeviceTokenNotForTopic` or `TopicDisallowed` | Key or bundle id mismatch. | Check the key's team and that the App ID has push enabled. |
| `status: 403`, `reason: InvalidProviderToken` or `ExpiredProviderToken` | `APNS_KEY_ID` or `APNS_TEAM_ID` does not match the key. | Correct them; the Worker re-mints its provider token on the next send. |
| `status: 410`, `reason: Unregistered` | The app was uninstalled. | Nothing; the row was pruned. |
| `status: 0` | Apple's gateway was not reached. | Retry; see the local-development note below. |
| HTTP `502`, `error: apns_provider_key` | The key is present but will not import or sign. | Re-paste the `.p8` with its armour intact. |

The register-device reply also carries `pushConfigured` and `configProblem`,
so the settings card can say "No APNs credentials configured" straight after
sign-in rather than waiting for a test.

## Android

There is no Android push transport. Android delivery would need either
Firebase Cloud Messaging, which this project has not taken on, or a foreground
service holding the account event socket. The native Android app
reports push as unsupported and receive events only while they are open.

## Limits

Delivery is best effort and runs inline on the request that produced the
event, since Python Workers have no `waitUntil` here. Apart from pings, one
account event buzzes each phone at most once per two-second coalescing
window. At most eight devices are contacted per event within a three-second
budget, at most
twenty tokens are kept per account, and a token that has not checked in for
180 days is dropped. Apple holds an alert for a phone it cannot reach for 24
hours, and only the newest one per app, so a phone that was offline overnight
gets one banner when it reconnects. Apple's provider token is cached for forty minutes per
isolate and re-minted early when Apple reports it expired.

## Local development

APNs only speaks HTTP/2. Production Workers reach it, but local `workerd` on
macOS does not negotiate HTTP/2 for outbound fetches
([cloudflare/workerd#4841](https://github.com/cloudflare/workerd/issues/4841)),
so a self-test against `wrangler dev` reports `status: 0` for every device.
Registration, routing, and the `configured` answer can still be exercised
locally; delivery has to be checked against a deployed Worker.

pages.title: Node backup, recovery, and key moves
pages.description: forkmesh-mirror-node backs up, restores, and checks the node it runs, with no extra tooling. The operations are
pages.markdown:
# Node backup, recovery, and key moves

`forkmesh-mirror-node` backs up, restores, and checks the node it runs, with no
extra tooling. The operations are:

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--preflight` | Read-only checks of configuration, identity, Git version, disk space, and backup/drill freshness |
| `--backup PATH` | Writes one encrypted archive of everything the node needs to come back |
| `--restore-drill PATH` | Restores an archive into scratch space, checks it, times it against the recovery time objective, then deletes it |
| `--restore PATH` | Restores an archive onto a host, checks it, and removes what it created if any check fails |
| `--export-identity PATH` / `--import-identity PATH` | Moves only the node's Ed25519 identity key |

Every command also takes `--config` (the service configuration, which is
`/var/lib/forkmesh/mirror-node.json` on installer-managed hosts). Results are
printed as JSON. Run these commands as the service account so that files keep
the owner the service needs:

```sh
node() {
  runuser -u forkmesh-node -- /usr/local/bin/forkmesh-mirror-node \
    --config /var/lib/forkmesh/mirror-node.json "$@"
}
```

## Passphrases

Archives and identity exports contain the node's private key and its connector
token, so they are always encrypted: AES-256-GCM in 1 MiB authenticated chunks,
with the key derived from a passphrase using PBKDF2-SHA256. A wrong passphrase,
a changed byte, a missing chunk, or a cut-off file all fail to open.

The passphrase is read only from `--passphrase-file`. That file must belong to
the account running the command, must not be readable by anyone else, and must
hold at least 12 bytes. It is never accepted as a command-line argument or an
environment variable. Keep a copy of the passphrase **somewhere other than the
node**: a backup cannot be opened without it.

```sh
install -o forkmesh-node -g forkmesh-node -m 0600 /dev/null /var/lib/forkmesh/backup.passphrase
openssl rand -base64 32 > /var/lib/forkmesh/backup.passphrase   # then store a copy off-host
```

## Preflight

```sh
node --preflight          # human-readable
node --preflight --json   # for scripts and monitoring
```

Each check reports `ok`, `warn`, or `error`. The command exits `2` only when
there is an error, meaning the service cannot work as configured:

- the configuration or gateway configuration does not load;
- the gateway script, Python, the identity key, or `git` is missing;
- `git` is older than 2.27, which atomic merges and restores need;
- the identity key does not match the public key the gateway advertises (the
  daemon will refuse to start);
- the connector token is not owner-only;
- a volume holding node state has less than 512 MiB free.

Warnings need attention but do not stop the service:

- the node reports version `dev`;
- no connector token has been written yet;
- a repository has not been cloned yet;
- free space is under 10% of the volume, or is less than the repositories take
  up (a backup or repack needs about that much again);
- fewer than 5% of inodes are free;
- the last backup is older than 24 hours (the recovery point objective);
- the last restore drill is more than 92 days old, took longer than its
  objective, or has never been run.

Run preflight before and after installing or updating a node, and from
monitoring. If it fails after an update, reinstall the previous release binary
(see [rolling migration](mirror-node.md#rolling-migration)) before you debug.

## Backups

```sh
node --passphrase-file /var/lib/forkmesh/backup.passphrase \
  --backup /var/backups/forkmesh/node-$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ).fmbackup
```

The service can keep running during a backup. A backup contains:

- the service configuration and the gateway configuration;
- the identity key and the connector token;
- the whole gateway state directory (`mirror-gateway/`): the signed mirror
  manifest, dashboard replica, pull-ledger job results, agent job state, and
  node-ops records;
- every path the gateway configuration names: repository `gitDir`s, release
  stores, `privateReplicaStore`, `dynamicRepositoriesPath` (the fork
  registry), `writableRepositoryRoot`, and operator policy state.

Each bare repository is stored as a `git bundle --all`, which is a consistent
snapshot of its refs and objects even while pushes are arriving. The
repository's `HEAD`, `config`, hooks, and release store are stored beside the
bundle.

Temporary data is left out: `tmp/` and `.cache/` directories, agent job
worktrees (`agent-jobs/work/`), merge worktrees (`pull-jobs/.apply-*`), and
half-written temporary files. Sign-ins for agent CLIs (Claude Code, Codex) are
also left out. They are third-party credentials, so sign in again after a
restore.

The archive is written under a temporary name and then linked into place, so
it never replaces an existing file. Symbolic links inside the backed-up state
are refused. The one exception is a configured path that is itself a link to
another disk; its contents are backed up under the configured name.

Each backup is recorded in `mirror-gateway/node-ops/last-backup.json`. That
record contains the size, SHA-256, duration, and ref count, and no secrets.

### Scheduling

```ini
# /etc/systemd/system/forkmesh-node-backup.service
[Unit]
Description=ForkMesh node backup

[Service]
Type=oneshot
User=forkmesh-node
Group=forkmesh-node
ExecStart=/bin/sh -c 'exec /usr/local/bin/forkmesh-mirror-node --config /var/lib/forkmesh/mirror-node.json --passphrase-file /var/lib/forkmesh/backup.passphrase --backup /var/backups/forkmesh/node-$(date -u +%%Y%%m%%dT%%H%%M%%SZ).fmbackup'
ExecStartPost=/usr/bin/find /var/backups/forkmesh -name 'node-*.fmbackup' -mtime +14 -delete

# /etc/systemd/system/forkmesh-node-backup.timer
[Timer]
OnCalendar=daily
RandomizedDelaySec=1h
Persistent=true

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target
```

Copy archives off the host as well. A backup that exists only on the node does
not survive losing the node.

## Restore drills

```sh
node --passphrase-file /var/lib/forkmesh/backup.passphrase \
  --restore-drill /var/backups/forkmesh/node-20260913T020000Z.fmbackup --rto 30m
```

A drill decrypts the whole archive into a scratch directory under `--work-dir`
(default `TMPDIR`). It then checks all of the following:

- every file's size, mode, and SHA-256;
- that each repository's refs digest matches the backup, and that
  `git fsck --connectivity-only` passes;
- that the identity key loads and matches the recorded public key;
- that the service and gateway configurations load and name that identity.

The drill then deletes the scratch directory. It changes nothing on the node
except the record in `mirror-gateway/node-ops/last-restore-drill.json`. It
exits `3` if it took longer than `--rto` (default 30 minutes).

Run a drill at least once a quarter. Preflight warns once the last drill is
more than 92 days old. `/v1/status` shows both objectives under `recovery`:

```json
"recovery": {
  "lastBackupAt": "2026-09-13T02:00:04.1Z",
  "lastBackupAgeSeconds": 3600,
  "lastBackupBytes": 734003200,
  "lastBackupDurationMs": 81234,
  "lastRestoreDrillAt": "2026-09-01T03:10:12.9Z",
  "lastRestoreDrillAgeSeconds": 1036800,
  "lastRestoreDrillDurationMs": 95310,
  "recoveryTimeObjectiveMs": 1800000,
  "lastRestoreDrillWithinObjective": true
}
```

## Restoring a node

To replace a lost or broken host:

1. Install ForkMesh on the new host as usual, but do **not** bootstrap a new
   identity or start `forkmesh-mirror-node.service`. The service account and
   `/var/lib/forkmesh` must exist; the repositories and configuration must
   not.
2. Copy the archive and the passphrase file to the new host, owned by
   `forkmesh-node` with mode `0600`.
3. Optionally rehearse with `--dry-run`, which runs the same checks as a drill
   without touching the host:

   ```sh
   node --passphrase-file /var/lib/forkmesh/backup.passphrase \
     --restore /var/lib/forkmesh/node.fmbackup --dry-run
   ```

4. Restore:

   ```sh
   node --passphrase-file /var/lib/forkmesh/backup.passphrase \
     --restore /var/lib/forkmesh/node.fmbackup
   ```

5. Run `node --preflight`, then `systemctl enable --now forkmesh-mirror-node`,
   and confirm `/readyz`.

A restore puts every file back at its original absolute path. Use
`--restore-root DIR` to place them all under another directory instead. It
**never overwrites** an existing file. It refuses to restore into an existing
repository directory, and it refuses to run as root (restored files would
belong to root, and the service could not read them). After the files are
written it runs the same checks as a drill. If any step fails, it deletes
every file and directory it created and nothing else, so you can fix the
problem and run it again. `--config` must match the configuration path stored
in the backup.

The restored node has the same name and key, so it takes over the old node's
catalog entry, endpoint lease, and account without re-linking. Do not run the
old host and its restored copy at the same time.

## Moving or replacing an identity key

To move only the key, for example onto a node that already has its
repositories:

```sh
# on the old host
node --passphrase-file /var/lib/forkmesh/backup.passphrase \
  --export-identity /var/lib/forkmesh/mirror17.fmkey

# on the new host (same node name)
node --passphrase-file /var/lib/forkmesh/backup.passphrase \
  --import-identity /var/lib/forkmesh/mirror17.fmkey --dry-run
node --passphrase-file /var/lib/forkmesh/backup.passphrase \
  --import-identity /var/lib/forkmesh/mirror17.fmkey --replace-identity
```

An export is tied to its node name, and importing it into a node with any other
name is refused. The import reports one of three actions:

- `install`: the host had no key, so the imported key is installed.
- `unchanged`: the host already has this exact key.
- `replace`: the host has a different key. This requires `--replace-identity`.
  The current key is kept beside the new one as `ed25519.pem.replaced-<unix
  time>` and is never deleted.

When the key changes, the import also updates the public key in the gateway
configuration (the daemon refuses to start if they differ). On a tunnel-free
node it also re-signs the direct-origin manifest. Restart the service
afterwards.

pages.title: Node operator policy and legal response
pages.description: A ForkMesh node operator decides, for their own machine only, what the node stores and serves, how much disk it may use, and how it answers an abuse report or a legal request.…
pages.markdown:
# Node operator policy and legal response

A ForkMesh node operator decides, for their own machine only, what the node
stores and serves, how much disk it may use, and how it answers an abuse report
or a legal request. None of these choices is a network-wide rule. When this
node refuses or quarantines a repository, every other mirror that carries it
keeps serving it. The gateway reports the repository as unavailable here, so
the router sends readers to another mirror.

The policy is opt-in. A gateway configured without `operatorPolicy` behaves
exactly as before.

## Enabling it

1. Create an owner-only state directory and policy file for the gateway's
   service user:

   ```sh
   install -d -m 0700 /var/lib/forkmesh-mirror/operator-policy
   install -m 0600 /dev/stdin /var/lib/forkmesh-mirror/operator-policy.json <<'JSON'
   {"schemaVersion": 1, "profile": "home", "jurisdiction": "eu"}
   JSON
   ```

2. Add the policy to `mirror-gateway.json`:

   ```json
   "operatorPolicy": {
     "policyPath": "/var/lib/forkmesh-mirror/operator-policy.json",
     "stateDirectory": "/var/lib/forkmesh-mirror/operator-policy"
   }
   ```

3. `mirror_gateway.py --check` validates the policy. Then restart the gateway.
   `node_operator_policy.py` must be installed beside `mirror_gateway.py`. The
   Vultr installer ships it. If the module is missing, a configuration that
   names `operatorPolicy` fails validation instead of running without a
   policy.

All commands below are `python3 -I tools/node_operator_policy.py <command>`
and print JSON.

## Profiles and safe defaults

`profile` chooses defaults for the kind of machine. Any field can be
overridden. Every limit is finite, so an unedited profile cannot fill a disk.

| Setting | home | community | commercial |
|---|---|---|---|
| `limits.maxRepositoryBytes` | 1 GiB | 4 GiB | 20 GiB |
| `limits.maxBlobBytes` | 50 MiB | 100 MiB | 400 MiB |
| `limits.maxPushBytes` (uncompressed new objects) | 512 MiB | 2 GiB | 8 GiB |
| `limits.maxRepositories` | 50 | 1000 | 10000 |
| `limits.storageBudgetBytes` (whole node) | 20 GiB | 500 GiB | 5000 GiB |
| `seeding.privateReplicas` | false | false | true |
| `violationAction` | quarantine | quarantine | quarantine |
| `retention.evidenceDays` | 90 | 180 | 365 |

Home and community nodes do not serve other people's encrypted private
replicas by default. Their operators usually cannot staff abuse review for
content they cannot inspect.

## Policy reference

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "profile": "community",
  "limits": {"maxBlobBytes": 104857600},
  "content": {
    "blockedExtensions": [".iso", ".exe"],
    "blockedPathPatterns": ["*.mp4", "datasets/*.parquet"],
    "blockedObjectIds": ["<40- or 64-hex object id from a takedown>"]
  },
  "repositories": {
    "allow": [],
    "block": ["spam-owner", "alice/leaked-keys"]
  },
  "seeding": {"privateReplicas": false},
  "violationAction": "quarantine",
  "retention": {"evidenceDays": 180},
  "jurisdiction": "eu"
}
```

- **Repositories and communities.** `repositories.allow` and `.block` take an
  owner (a person, an organization, or a community) or `owner/repository`. A
  non-empty `allow` list means the node stores only those repositories. The
  gateway also refuses to *create* a blocked or unlisted repository, or one
  past `maxRepositories`.
- **Content.** Unknown fields, duplicate keys, and group- or world-writable
  policy files are refused.
  - `blockedExtensions` is checked against every entry name in every new tree,
    so renaming an accepted file to a refused name is caught.
  - A pattern without `/` matches file names the same way.
  - A pattern with `/` matches the first path at which Git reaches the object.
  - `blockedObjectIds` names exact content, for example the blob a copyright
    notice identifies.
- **`violationAction`.** `quarantine` lets `enforce --apply` stop serving
  stored violators. `report` lists them only. Pushes that violate the policy
  are always refused.
- **`jurisdiction`.** One of `us`, `eu`, `uk`, `other`. It chooses the runbook
  attached to every case.
- **`secrets`.** Optional. It holds an organization secret policy, for example
  `"secrets": {"mode": "block"}`. `secret_gate.py` must be installed beside
  this module; the Vultr installer, `install.sh`, and
  `provision_ssh_gateway.sh` ship it. If the module is missing, a policy that
  names `secrets` fails validation and the hook refuses every push. See
  [Secret scanning before replication](../security/secret-scanning.md) for
  rules, repository policy, and signed overrides.

## Protected branches

`branches` protects refs on this node's writable repositories. The same
pre-receive hook enforces it for the HTTPS mirror gateway and for the SSH
gateway (see [Git SSH public-key authentication](git-ssh-gateway.md)).

```json
"branches": {
  "rules": [
    {"pattern": "main", "requireSignedCommits": true},
    {"pattern": "release/*", "repositories": ["alice/app"]},
    {"pattern": "refs/tags/v*", "blockForcePush": false}
  ],
  "allowedSignersPath": "/var/lib/forkmesh-mirror/allowed_signers"
}
```

- `pattern` is a glob. A bare name means `refs/heads/<name>`; start it with
  `refs/` for tags or other refs. `*` also matches `/`.
- `repositories` limits a rule to owners or `owner/repository`. An empty list
  covers every repository on the node.
- `blockDeletion` (default `true`) refuses deleting a matching ref.
- `blockForcePush` (default `true`) refuses any update whose new tip does not
  contain the current tip.
- `requireSignedCommits` (default `false`) refuses every commit the update
  adds unless an SSH key in `allowedSignersPath` signed it. The file uses
  OpenSSH's allowed signers format (`principal namespaces="git" <key>`), must
  be owned by the gateway account, and must not be group- or world-writable.
  A new protected ref checks the commits that are new to the repository. An
  update checks every commit between the old and new tips, so an unsigned
  commit already stored on another branch cannot be fast-forwarded in. Only
  SSH signatures are verified: OpenPGP and X.509 signatures are refused.
- A protected update whose expected old value no longer matches the ref is
  refused as `stale-ref`. Git also re-checks the old value under its ref lock
  after the hook, so a push that loses a race never moves the ref.

A refused push changes no ref and stores no object. The pusher sees each rule,
the evidence reference, and copy-ready recovery steps. For example:

```text
remote: This node's operator policy refused the push (other ForkMesh nodes may accept it):
remote:   protected-branch-force-update: refs/heads/main is protected and 3f1c… does not contain its tip 9ab2…
remote:   to recover (protected-branch-force-update):
remote:     git fetch origin
remote:     git rebase origin/main
remote:     git push origin HEAD:main
```

Every admitted push that updates a protected ref appends an `admit-push`
record, and every refusal appends `reject-push`. Both go to the hash-chained
audit log. Records name the repository, refs, old and new object ids, the
matching patterns, and the policy digest. They never contain file content,
keys, or the pusher's credentials. If the admit record cannot be written, the
push is refused.

Adding or tightening a branch rule counts as availability-reducing, so
`apply` needs `--confirm`.

The HTTPS mirror gateway already refuses every deletion and non-fast-forward
update, whatever the policy says. On that path, branch rules add the
signed-commit and stale-write checks and the audit trail.

## How enforcement works

**Pushes.** The gateway points `core.hooksPath` at a directory it owns
(`<stateDirectory>/hooks`), which holds only a `pre-receive` hook that runs
this module. Hooks planted inside a repository still never run.

Git has already staged the pushed objects in its receive quarantine when the
hook runs. The hook checks them against the policy:

- repository allow/block lists and quarantine
- push size, projected repository size, and the node storage budget
- blob sizes, names, paths, and blocked object ids
- probable secrets, when `secrets` is set. Blocked findings refuse the push.
  Warnings and signed overrides are admitted, shown to the pusher, and
  audited.

If anything fails, the hook exits non-zero and Git deletes the staged objects.
The repository's refs and existing objects, and every other repository, are
untouched. The pusher sees each reason as a `remote:` line with an evidence
reference.

If the policy cannot be read, the hook refuses every push (it fails closed).

**Stored data.** Upstream fetches and older data never pass through the hook.
Run `enforce` after tightening a policy, or on a timer:

```sh
node_operator_policy.py enforce --policy P --state S --root R          # preview
node_operator_policy.py enforce --policy P --state S --root R --apply  # act
```

With `secrets` set, `enforce` also scans stored history. Anything it finds
has already been replicated, so each affected repository in the output
carries a `secretResponse` plan: containment, rotation, notification, and
residual risk. Under `block` the repository is quarantined; under `warn` it
is only reported. With `--apply`, every detection is audited as
`secret-detected-stored`.

A quarantine writes `<state>/quarantine/<owner>/<repo>.json`. From that moment
the gateway answers that repository as not found, its signed health proof says
`available: false` (so the router routes elsewhere), and pushes to it are
refused. Its bytes stay on disk, so a quarantine can always be lifted with
`release`.

**Private replicas.** When `seeding.privateReplicas` is false, the gateway
serves no private replica, even if the store holds some.

## Preview, apply, and roll back

Never edit the active policy file in place. Write a candidate and apply it:

```sh
node_operator_policy.py preview --policy candidate.json --current active.json --state S --root R
node_operator_policy.py apply   --policy candidate.json --target active.json --state S --root R [--confirm]
node_operator_policy.py history --state S
node_operator_policy.py rollback --target active.json --state S --root R [--confirm]
```

`preview` reports capacity:

- stored bytes, storage budget, headroom, and utilization
- repository slots used and allowed
- the largest repository

It also lists the repositories that would become unavailable here and states
the consequences in plain language. A repository that only this node seeds
becomes unavailable to the whole network.

`apply` refuses any change that reduces availability until you pass
`--confirm`. That includes lower limits, new block rules, a narrower allow
list, dropping private replicas, or violators that would be quarantined.
Loosening a policy needs no confirmation.

Each apply archives the previous file under `<state>/policy-history/`, and
`rollback` restores the newest archive through the same preview and
confirmation step. Rolling back archives the policy being replaced, so you can
roll forward again.

## Reports, appeals, and removal

```sh
node_operator_policy.py report  --policy P --state S --owner alice --name app \
    --category copyright --reporter "rights@example.org" --details "..." [--legal-hold]
node_operator_policy.py action  --policy P --state S --case <id> --note "notice verified"
node_operator_policy.py appeal  --state S --case <id> --appellant alice --details "licensed MIT"
node_operator_policy.py resolve --state S --case <id> --decision reverse|uphold|dismiss --note "..."
node_operator_policy.py remove  --state S --root R --owner alice --name app --reason "court order" [--confirm]
```

- A case records the report, the jurisdiction runbook, and every step in its
  history.
- `action` quarantines the repository under the case.
- `resolve --decision reverse` or `dismiss` lifts a quarantine that case
  created.
- `remove` permanently deletes a repository from this node only. It works only
  on a quarantined repository, needs `--confirm`, and is recorded as
  irreversible.

**Evidence.** Evidence records hold only metadata: rules, object ids, paths,
sizes, refs, and the policy digest. They never hold the refused content. Keep
any legally required copy outside ForkMesh under counsel's direction.

`prune-evidence` deletes evidence past `retention.evidenceDays`. It never
deletes evidence for an open or appealed case, or for a case with a legal hold.

### Jurisdiction runbooks

`runbook --policy P` prints the checklist for the configured jurisdiction. The
checklists are process reminders, not legal advice:

- **us.** DMCA notice elements (17 U.S.C. §512(c)(3)), prompt quarantine, and
  restore 10–14 business days after a valid counter-notice unless suit is
  filed. CSAM is reported to NCMEC and its content is not retained.
- **eu.** Digital Services Act notice-and-action (Art. 16), statement of
  reasons (Art. 17), internal complaint handling (Art. 20), and notifying
  authorities of threats to life or safety (Art. 18).
- **uk.** Online Safety Act 2023 illegal-content assessment, a complaint route,
  and IWF/NCA reporting for CSAM.
- **other.** Record the legal basis, quarantine rather than delete until the
  request is verified, and take local advice.

## Audit and telemetry

Every quarantine, release, removal, policy apply or rollback, report, case
step, refused push, admitted protected-branch push, and evidence prune is appended to `<state>/audit.jsonl`.
Each record carries the SHA-256 of the record before it.

- `verify-audit` checks the chain and exits 4 at the first altered or missing
  record.
- `status` returns secret-free counters for local dashboards: quarantined
  repositories, open, appealed, and resolved cases, refused pushes, admitted
  protected-branch pushes, evidence records, and the audit state.
- `status` also returns `secrets` counters: blocked and warned pushes,
  overridden and allowlisted findings, invalid overrides, and detections in
  stored data.

## Not covered yet

- Bandwidth and egress caps are not enforced. Use the gateway's service
  counters and your reverse proxy.
- Upstream fetches by the Go daemon are not checked before they land. Run
  `enforce` after sync. That includes secret scanning, which there is
  detection after replication.
- The desktop app has no policy editor. The policy is a file plus this CLI.
- Branch rules do not know who is pushing. Per-collaborator roles come from the
  Worker or local SSH authorization (owner, `write`, `maintain`, `admin`, and
  pull-request namespaces). Required reviews and required checks are not
  enforced by the hook.

pages.title: Non-custodial organization succession
pages.description: ForkMesh organization succession is a governance mechanism for one organization roster. It is not inheritance, account recovery, custody, or an asset-transfer service.
pages.markdown:
# Non-custodial organization succession

ForkMesh organization succession is a governance mechanism for one
organization roster. It is not inheritance, account recovery, custody, or an
asset-transfer service.

## Transfer boundary

A completed succession performs exactly two scoped changes:

1. the configured organization owner becomes an organization administrator;
2. the explicitly named successor becomes that organization's owner.

The database completion trigger updates only those two `org_members.role`
values for the configured organization. Repository records, organization
repository links, teams, memberships, private-repository shares and encryption
recipients are not rewritten.

The following never transfer:

- wallets, wallet addresses, funds, rewards, transactions, or signing ability;
- private keys, account credentials, agent credentials, or private agent data;
- user accounts, profile/personal data, devices, or device ownership;
- repository ownership, repository content, or public/private repository ACLs.

ForkMesh does not create a custodial account or wallet for an organization or
successor. A succession response always includes this technical boundary.

## Configuration and lifecycle

Only the organization's sole current owner can configure a policy with
`PUT /api/orgs/{org}/succession`. The successor must be an explicitly named,
active user who is already an administrator or member of that organization.
Unknown fields fail closed, and transfer-shaped fields are rejected.

Configuration is bounded:

- inactivity threshold: 30–730 days (default 180);
- grace period: 7–90 days (default 30);
- independent approvals: 2–20 (default 2).

The approval threshold cannot exceed the current eligible roster. The owner
and successor are excluded from approvers, so approvals are independent.

The current owner can use `POST .../check-in`. A check-in refreshes the
succession activity timestamp and cancels an open grace case. Generalized
enabled-device and owned-node `last_seen` maxima also count as owner activity;
device identifiers, labels, platforms, locations and payloads never enter the
succession tables or API.

An hourly bounded job issues one deduplicated warning as the inactivity
deadline approaches. It never opens a case or transfers a role. A currently
authorized organization member must explicitly call `POST .../activate` after
the threshold to open the grace period.

During grace:

- the current owner may call `POST .../cancel` or `POST .../check-in`;
- independent current members call `POST .../approve`;
- duplicate approvals are idempotent;
- removed members' prior approvals stop counting immediately;
- the owner and successor cannot approve.

After grace, a current organization member may call `POST .../finalize`. D1
rechecks the grace deadline, current owner, current successor, and threshold of
currently authorized approvers inside the same transaction that changes the two
roles and appends completion history. A changed roster or stale approval fails
closed.

`DELETE /api/orgs/{org}/succession` disables the policy and cancels an active
case. Deleting an organization also disables/cancels current succession state;
its audit history remains append-only.

## Authorization and audit

The succession API receives organization-session and organization-roster
helpers only. It has no platform-administrator authorization method. Platform
administrators who are not current organization members receive `403`, and the
succession tables are hidden from the generic administrator table editor.

Cases and approvals are immutable snapshots. Approval, case, and completion
triggers protect transitions at the database boundary. Every configuration,
warning, grace opening, approval, cancellation, check-in, denied completion,
and completion adds a metadata-only event. Update/delete triggers make event
and approval history append-only.

Authorized organization members can read current status and bounded history
with `GET /api/orgs/{org}/succession`. The endpoint is `no-store`; it returns
counts and policy dates, not device data or sensitive account activity.

pages.description: Organization owners can save Claude Code and Codex work for the desktop linked to an organization repository even while that desktop is offline. The queue is durable in D1 and…
pages.markdown:
# Organization agent offline queue

Organization owners can save Claude Code and Codex work for the desktop linked
to an organization repository even while that desktop is offline. The queue is
durable in D1 and has no admission-count limit. List responses remain bounded;
that response bound is not a queue or task-creation cap.

## Authorization and execution boundary

Offline admission requires all of the following:

- the requester has the current organization `owner` role;
- the repository has an exact `org_repos` link;
- the requester's account owns the linked source node;
- the retained signed catalog record identifies that repository on a
  `desktop` runtime; and
- the record advertises the requested provider.

An explicitly selected owner target must be that linked desktop. Engineering
members retain the existing fresh, provider-capable mirror route.

Admission does not authorize execution. A reconnecting desktop must still
prove current node ownership when it claims the oldest job. It validates the
exact lease envelope and rechecks the provider binary and login locally before
dispatch. There is no model-based safety preflight: the Claude Haiku gate was
removed on 2026-09-13 (`a7dfa7936`), and leased jobs now dispatch directly
(`desktop/src/MainWindowAgents.cpp`, `server/agents.go`). Haiku remains
selectable as a model. Job and session rows remain encrypted at rest.

## Drain and recovery

The Worker leases one job per repository at a time in ascending row order and
verifies the conditional queued-to-leased update before returning it. The
desktop asks for the next job only after the Worker acknowledges the current
result. A lease abandoned for two minutes (`ORG_AGENT_JOB_LEASE_MS` in
`app/src/entry.py`) returns to `queued`; queued and running rows are never
removed by this flow.

The Qt client starts a drain after normal consolidated sync, including the
startup/reconnect fallback. It persists a running organization's job id, lease,
and repository envelope with the local agent session, restores that binding
after restart, and retries the terminal report. Resumed local sessions are
queued oldest first.

## Operator diagnostics

Queue rejections include a stable `error`, a safe user-facing `message`,
`retryable`, and—when relevant—`requiredAction`, `provider`, and `targetNode`.
Common actions are:

- `link_repository` or `publish_repository`;
- `link_owned_desktop` or `link_desktop_target`;
- `publish_provider_capability`;
- `select_linked_desktop` or `select_eligible_target`;
- `bring_agent_mirror_online`; and
- `relink_desktop`.

The Dashboard, chat composer, and World display the server message without
replacing it with a generic queue failure.

## Verification and rollback

Before deployment, run:

```bash
python3 tools/quality_gate.py validate
python3 tools/quality_gate.py run --profile core
python3 tools/quality_gate.py run --profile release
```

Focused QA should save several Claude Code and Codex tasks while the linked
desktop is offline, reconnect it, and confirm the jobs enter preflight in
creation order. Also exercise a non-owner, an unlinked repository, a foreign or
non-desktop target, and a missing provider capability; each UI must show the
exact server-authored remedy.

Rollback the Worker and web assets to the prior deployment revision if needed.
The `0114_remove_organization_task_limit.sql` migration only drops an admission
trigger and does not rewrite or delete task data, so rollback does not require
a reverse data migration. Do not recreate the old trigger: doing so would make
new durable work fail again once an organization retained 2,000 tasks.

pages.markdown:
# Paid microjobs

A microjob is a small piece of work anybody with a ForkMesh account can pick
up and be paid a fixed, deliberately tiny amount of SOL for. The section lives
at `/microjobs`; the API is `/api/microjobs`, and the policy module is
`app/src/microjobs.py`.

Microjobs reuse the community reward pool's custody boundary exactly. The
Worker never holds a key, never signs, and never broadcasts. An approved claim
becomes a public, unsigned `chain_intents` plan; the repository owner's own
desktop client re-validates that plan locally, signs it inside its encrypted
vault, and broadcasts it. See
[community-reward-pool.md](community-reward-pool.md) for the custody rules the
payout path inherits.

## The jobs and what they pay

| Job | Amount | Paid when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `issue_report` | 0.005 SOL | A Workers AI reviewer finds no existing issue covering it and no code already addressing it |
| `merged_pull` | 0.05 SOL | The pull request is merged **and** its record carries the MCP agent tool's signed marker |
| `referral_post` | 0.01 SOL | The public page still contains the referral link **and** the hostname has already sent counted visitors |

Amounts are fixed in `microjobs.JOBS`, not operator-configurable per claim, so
the number a contributor reads on the page is exactly the number that reaches
the payout plan. They are small on purpose: a microjob is a thank-you for a
small piece of verified work, not employment, an investment, or a promise of
future payment. The page states that explicitly.

## Claim lifecycle

```
submitted -> pending_review | approved | rejected
             pending_review -> (re-verified later) -> approved
             approved -> queued -> paid
```

* `pending_review` — a posted referral's counters have not caught up yet. The
  hourly payout phase rechecks a bounded set; nothing is paid meanwhile.
* `approved` — verified, waiting for the next payout batch.
* `queued` — batched into a public unsigned plan the owner's desktop may sign.
* `paid` — a finalized transfer matched the exact public plan. The claim keeps
  the public transaction signature so the contributor can check it on-chain.
* `rejected` — verification said no, and the reason is returned to the
  claimant.

`microjob_claims.subject_bi` is a blind index over the exact piece of work
(repo + issue title, repo + pull number, or the posted URL). Its UNIQUE index
is the de-duplication: one issue, one merged pull, or one posted page can be
claimed once, by whoever got there first.

## Duplicate review for reported issues

`POST /api/microjobs/claims` with `job=issue_report` runs before anything
reaches the repository:

1. The repository's existing issue numbers are listed over the public mirror
   gateway, and their records are read in one batched call.
2. The most distinctive words of the report drive a fixed-string repository
   `git grep`, so the reviewer can see code that already addresses it.
3. Workers AI (the `AI` binding, same models as ForkBot) is asked one question
   in JSON mode: is this `new`, a `duplicate`, `already_addressed`, or
   `unclear`?

Only a `new` verdict files the issue and approves the claim. `duplicate` and
`already_addressed` file nothing, and the claim is rejected with the reviewer's
own one-sentence reason.

`unclear` — including an unparseable answer, a missing `AI` binding, and "no
online host could serve the existing issues" — fails closed with a retryable
response. It files no issue and records no claim, so only a report affirmatively
classified as `new` can reach the repository.

The gate is scoped to the microjobs path. The ordinary
`POST /api/repo/<owner>/<repo>/issues` endpoint is untouched: filing an issue
normally still costs nothing, waits for nothing, and is never turned away by a
model.

## Why pull requests must come from the MCP agent tool

`tools/forkmesh_mcp_server.py` stamps two extra fields into the `pull.md` it
writes:

```
client: forkmesh-mcp-v1
clientSig: <base64url Ed25519 signature>
```

`clientSig` covers `forkmesh-mcp-pull-v1\n<number>\n<base>\n<head>\n<author>\n<ts>`
— see `mcp_pull_canonical`, which is reproduced byte-for-byte in
`app/src/microjobs.py`. The plain `client` field proves nothing on its own
(anybody can type it); the signature binds the marker to this exact pull, and
the Worker additionally checks that the signing node belongs to the account
claiming the payout.

`desktop/src/PullStore.cpp` carries both fields through every rewrite. It never
authors them and never interprets them — but a merge rewrites `pull.md`, and
dropping the marker there would silently make an MCP-opened pull unpayable long
after the work was done.

A pull request opened by hand, from the website composer, or from the desktop
UI is a perfectly good pull request. It is simply not a paid microjob, and both
the pull composer and the microjobs page say so with the exact command to run.

## Referral-post validation

Both halves are required before a referral post is payable:

1. **The link is really posted.** The Worker fetches the submitted page once,
   bounded, and looks for the claimant's `/r/<name>` link in any spelling. The
   URL is first reduced by `normalize_public_url` to an ordinary public HTTPS
   page — no credentials, no bare IP literal, no non-443 port, no
   internal/loopback name — so this can never become a probe for anything on
   the inside.
2. **It actually sent people.** `site_referrers` must show at least
   `MIN_REFERRAL_SITE_VISITS` counted visits for that hostname, and
   `referral_stats` must show at least `MIN_REFERRAL_CLICKS` clicks on the
   claimant's own link.

A post that passes (1) but not yet (2) is held at `pending_review` with the
current numbers in its detail line, so the claimant can see exactly what is
missing rather than being rejected for being early. Each hourly payout phase
re-fetches up to four oldest pending pages and promotes a claim only when the
link is still present and both counters now pass.

## Payout batching

The `microjob-payouts` cron phase (minute 7 of each hour) calls
`microjobs.queue_payouts`. It:

* reads approved claims oldest-first;
* looks up each claimant's own public payout address from their account
  record — ForkMesh never creates a wallet, so a claim without one just stays
  approved;
* collapses multiple approved claims by the same person into one transfer,
  because a legacy Solana message may not repeat a destination;
* writes one `chain_intents` row of kind `microjob_payout` with policy
  `microjob-payout-v1`, at most 8 transfers, expiring in 4 hours; and
* flips those claims to `queued`.

The owner's desktop picks the plan up from the existing
`GET /api/rewards/signing-jobs` queue. On a finalized transfer matching the
exact plan, `_complete_chain_intent` marks every batched claim `paid` and
records the public signature. On a rejected or expired plan,
`_mark_chain_intent_failed` returns the claims to `approved` so the work is not
stranded behind a plan nobody will sign.

## Anti-farming bounds

* at most 12 open claims per account;
* at most 8 claims per account per day;
* at most 0.12 SOL per account per day;
* one claim per exact piece of work, globally.

These raise the cost of grinding a job and cap the blast radius of a
verification bug. They are not proof of personhood, and the public policy
payload says so in those words.

## Operating notes

* The `AI` binding is required for `issue_report` to approve. Without it the
  microjobs endpoint fails closed: no issue and no claim are created.
* Payouts require the same `COMMUNITY_REWARD_POOL_ADDRESS` /
  `TREASURY_SOLANA_ADDRESS`, `COMMUNITY_REWARD_NETWORK` and
  `REWARD_SIGNER_ACCOUNT` configuration the reward pool already uses. Without
  them `queue_payouts` returns `pool_not_configured` and does nothing.
* `microjob_claims` is on the admin console's restricted list. Editing a claim
  over HTTP would be authoring a transfer, so claims move only through their
  own verified API and the owner-signed batcher.
